chapters.title: Reproduction in Lower and Higher Plants
chapters.description: Study of asexual and sexual reproduction in lower plants (algae, fungi, bryophytes, pteridophytes) and higher plants (gymnosperms and angiosperms), along with structure and development of flowers, pollen, ovules, fruits, and seeds.
learningObjectives: Differentiate between asexual and sexual modes of reproduction in plants.
Understand microsporogenesis and megasporogenesis processes.
Explain types and agents of pollination.
Describe double fertilization and post-fertilization events.
Understand fruit and seed development in angiosperms.

questions.text: Which of the following is an asexual method of reproduction?
questions.answer: Fragmentation

questions.text: Define vegetative propagation.
questions.answer: Vegetative propagation is a type of asexual reproduction in which new plants develop from vegetative parts like roots, stems, or leaves.

questions.text: What is microsporogenesis?
questions.answer: Microsporogenesis is the process of formation of microspores (pollen grains) from microspore mother cells through meiosis.

questions.text: State two differences between self-pollination and cross-pollination.
questions.answer: Self-pollination occurs within the same flower or plant, ensures purity of race; cross-pollination occurs between different plants of the same species and increases genetic variation.

questions.text: Double fertilization is characteristic of:
questions.answer: Angiosperms

questions.text: What is the function of the endosperm?
questions.answer: Endosperm provides stored nutrients required for the growth and development of the embryo.

questions.text: Explain the term megasporogenesis.
questions.answer: Megasporogenesis is the formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell inside the ovule through meiosis.

questions.text: Describe the process of double fertilization in angiosperms.
questions.answer: In double fertilization, one male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the zygote (syngamy), while the other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus (triple fusion). This unique process results in simultaneous formation of embryo and endosperm.

questions.text: Explain post-fertilization changes occurring in a flower.
questions.answer: After fertilization, the ovary develops into a fruit, ovules develop into seeds, endosperm forms to nourish the embryo, integuments form the seed coat, and petals and other floral parts wither away.

questions.text: Discuss types of asexual reproduction in lower plants with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Lower plants reproduce asexually through methods such as fragmentation (Spirogyra), spore formation (Rhizopus), budding (Yeast), and binary fission (Bacteria). These methods help rapid multiplication and survival under unfavorable conditions.

questions.text: How many meiotic and mitotic divisions occur during the development of male gametophyte from microspore mother cell?
questions.answer: One meiotic and two mitotic

questions.text: Which of the following represents apomixis?
questions.answer: Seed formation without fertilization

questions.text: Define vegetative reproduction. Give any one example.
questions.answer: Vegetative reproduction is a type of asexual reproduction in which new plants are produced from vegetative parts like root, stem or leaf. Example: Potato.

questions.text: What is pollination? Name its two types.
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma. Types: Self-pollination and cross-pollination.

questions.text: Write any three differences between self-pollination and cross-pollination.
questions.answer: Self-pollination occurs within same flower/plant, needs no agents, produces less variation. Cross-pollination occurs between different plants, requires agents, produces genetic variation.

questions.text: Explain microsporogenesis.
questions.answer: Microsporogenesis is the process by which diploid microspore mother cells undergo meiosis to form haploid microspores.

questions.text: Explain megasporogenesis.
questions.answer: Megasporogenesis is the process of formation of haploid megaspores from diploid megaspore mother cell by meiosis.

questions.text: Describe the structure of a typical angiosperm ovule.
questions.answer: A typical ovule consists of nucellus, embryo sac, integuments, micropyle, chalaza and funiculus.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of a mature embryo sac.
questions.answer: Diagram showing egg cell, synergids, antipodals, polar nuclei.

questions.text: Explain double fertilization in angiosperms.
questions.answer: One male gamete fuses with egg forming zygote (syngamy) and the other fuses with secondary nucleus forming endosperm (triple fusion).

questions.text: Explain post-fertilization changes in angiosperms.
questions.answer: Zygote develops into embryo, ovule becomes seed, ovary becomes fruit and endosperm develops for nutrition.

questions.text: What is polyembryony? Give one example.
questions.answer: Polyembryony is the occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed. Example: Citrus.

questions.text: Angiosperms are the most advanced plants.
questions.answer: Because they show double fertilization, enclosed seeds, efficient vascular tissues and complex reproductive mechanisms.

chapters.title: Reproduction in Lower and Higher Animals
chapters.description: Study of asexual and sexual reproduction in lower and higher animals, including gametogenesis, fertilization, embryonic development, reproductive health, and human reproductive systems.
topics: Reproductive Health and Assisted Reproductive Technologies
learningObjectives: Differentiate between asexual and sexual reproduction in animals.
Understand gametogenesis and structure of human reproductive systems.
Explain the menstrual cycle and hormonal regulation.
Describe fertilization and stages of embryonic development.
Learn about reproductive health and modern reproductive technologies.

questions.text: Binary fission is commonly seen in:
questions.answer: Amoeba

questions.text: Define fertilization.
questions.answer: Fertilization is the fusion of male and female gametes to form a diploid zygote.

questions.text: What is ovulation?
questions.answer: Ovulation is the release of a mature ovum from the ovary, typically occurring midway through the menstrual cycle.

questions.text: State two differences between external and internal fertilization.
questions.answer: External fertilization occurs outside the body and requires water; internal fertilization occurs inside the body and offers greater protection to the embryo.

questions.text: Which hormone triggers ovulation?
questions.answer: LH

questions.text: What is spermatogenesis?
questions.answer: Spermatogenesis is the process of formation of sperms from spermatogonial stem cells in the testes.

questions.text: Explain the importance of the placenta.
questions.answer: The placenta facilitates exchange of nutrients, gases, and waste products between mother and fetus and secretes essential hormones.

questions.text: Describe the phases of the menstrual cycle.
questions.answer: The menstrual cycle has four phases: 1. **Menstrual Phase** – Shedding of uterine lining. 2. **Follicular Phase** – Follicle development and increase in estrogen. 3. **Ovulation** – Release of ovum triggered by LH surge. 4. **Luteal Phase** – Corpus luteum forms and secretes progesterone; if no fertilization occurs, cycle repeats.

questions.text: Explain the process of embryonic development from zygote to blastocyst.
questions.answer: After fertilization, the zygote divides by mitosis into a morula, then develops into a blastocyst. The blastocyst forms a trophoblast and inner cell mass and implants into the uterine wall for further development.

questions.text: Discuss assisted reproductive technologies (ART) such as IVF and ICSI.
questions.answer: ART includes methods like IVF, where fertilization occurs outside the body, and ICSI, where a single sperm is injected into an ovum. These techniques help couples with infertility and ensure embryo development before implantation.

questions.text: The hormone responsible for ovulation in human females is:
questions.answer: LH

questions.text: Which structure connects the fetus to the placenta?
questions.answer: Umbilical cord

questions.text: Define spermatogenesis.
questions.answer: Spermatogenesis is the process of formation of haploid sperms from diploid spermatogonia in the testes.

questions.text: What is menstrual cycle?
questions.answer: The menstrual cycle is a monthly sequence of changes in the ovaries and uterus of human females, lasting about 28 days.

questions.text: Explain fertilization in humans.
questions.answer: Fertilization is the fusion of male and female gametes in the ampulla of fallopian tube to form a diploid zygote.

questions.text: Explain implantation.
questions.answer: Implantation is the attachment of the blastocyst to the endometrium of the uterus for further development.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of human sperm.
questions.answer: Diagram showing head, neck, middle piece and tail with labels.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of human ovary showing stages of follicle development.
questions.answer: Diagram showing primary, secondary, tertiary follicles and corpus luteum.

questions.text: Describe spermatogenesis with suitable diagram.
questions.answer: Spermatogonia undergo mitosis, meiosis I and II forming spermatids which mature into sperms.

questions.text: Explain hormonal regulation of menstrual cycle.
questions.answer: FSH and LH regulate ovarian cycle; estrogen and progesterone control uterine cycle.

questions.text: Human placenta is said to be haemochorial.
questions.answer: Because maternal blood comes in direct contact with chorionic villi of the fetus.

questions.text: Give any three functions of placenta.
questions.answer: Nutrition, respiration, excretion and endocrine functions.

chapters.title: Inheritance and Variation
chapters.description: Study of Mendelian genetics, laws of inheritance, gene interactions, linkage, crossing over, chromosomal disorders, and variations in living organisms.
learningObjectives: Understand Mendel's experiments and laws of inheritance.
Analyze monohybrid and dihybrid crosses.
Differentiate between complete dominance, incomplete dominance, and co-dominance.
Explain linkage, crossing over, and sex-linked inheritance.
Identify chromosomal disorders and their genetic basis.

questions.text: Mendel is known as the father of:
questions.answer: Genetics

questions.text: Define phenotype.
questions.answer: Phenotype is the observable physical or physiological trait of an organism determined by genotype and environment.

questions.text: State Mendel's Law of Segregation.
questions.answer: The Law of Segregation states that alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one allele.

questions.text: What is incomplete dominance? Give one example.
questions.answer: Incomplete dominance occurs when neither allele is completely dominant, resulting in an intermediate phenotype. Example: Pink flowers in Mirabilis jalapa.

questions.text: ABO blood group system shows:
questions.answer: Multiple alleles

questions.text: What is crossing over?
questions.answer: Crossing over is the exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during meiosis, leading to recombination.

questions.text: Name two chromosomal disorders and state their chromosomal basis.
questions.answer: Down syndrome – trisomy 21; Turner syndrome – monosomy X.

questions.text: Explain Mendel’s dihybrid cross and the Law of Independent Assortment.
questions.answer: Mendel crossed plants differing in two characters (e.g., yellow round × green wrinkled). The F2 generation showed a phenotypic ratio of 9:3:3:1. This demonstrated the Law of Independent Assortment, which states that alleles of different genes assort independently during gamete formation.

questions.text: Describe linkage and how it differs from independent assortment.
questions.answer: Linkage is the tendency of genes located on the same chromosome to be inherited together. Unlike independent assortment, linked genes do not assort independently unless crossing over separates them. Linkage reduces recombination frequency.

questions.text: Discuss the types of variation seen in organisms and their significance.
questions.answer: Variations include somatic and germinal variations, continuous and discontinuous variations. They arise from mutations, recombination, and environmental factors. Variations allow natural selection, help species adapt, and contribute to evolution.

questions.text: Which of the following represents incomplete dominance?
questions.answer: Mirabilis jalapa flower colour

questions.text: In a test cross, the individual is crossed with:
questions.answer: Homozygous recessive

questions.text: State Mendel’s law of dominance.
questions.answer: When two contrasting alleles are present together, only one expresses itself in the phenotype and is called dominant.

questions.text: Define codominance with an example.
questions.answer: In codominance, both alleles express themselves equally in heterozygous condition. Example: AB blood group.

questions.text: Explain incomplete dominance with a suitable example.
questions.answer: In incomplete dominance, neither allele is completely dominant; heterozygote shows intermediate phenotype, e.g., Mirabilis jalapa.

questions.text: Explain pleiotropy.
questions.answer: Pleiotropy is the phenomenon where a single gene influences multiple phenotypic traits.

questions.text: What is polygenic inheritance? Give an example.
questions.answer: Polygenic inheritance involves multiple genes controlling a single trait, e.g., human skin colour.

questions.text: Explain Mendel’s monohybrid cross with phenotypic and genotypic ratios.
questions.answer: A cross between two individuals differing in one trait gives 3:1 phenotypic and 1:2:1 genotypic ratios in F2 generation.

questions.text: Explain dihybrid cross with expected ratios.
questions.answer: A cross involving two traits shows 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in F2 generation due to independent assortment.

questions.text: Variation is important for survival of species.
questions.answer: Variations help organisms adapt to changing environment and ensure survival and evolution.

chapters.title: Molecular Basis of Inheritance
chapters.description: Study of DNA structure, replication, transcription, translation, gene expression, genetic code, regulation of gene activity, mutations, and concepts of genomics and proteomics.
learningObjectives: Explain the structure and functions of DNA and RNA.
Understand DNA replication and enzymes involved.
Describe transcription and translation processes.
Interpret the genetic code and protein synthesis.
Understand gene regulation, mutations, and modern molecular biology applications.

questions.text: DNA is made up of:
questions.answer: Nucleotides

questions.text: Define a gene.
questions.answer: A gene is a specific segment of DNA that codes for a particular protein or functional RNA.

questions.text: What is semi-conservative DNA replication?
questions.answer: Semi-conservative replication means each new DNA molecule consists of one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.

questions.text: Differentiate between transcription and translation.
questions.answer: Transcription is the synthesis of RNA from DNA template, whereas translation is the synthesis of protein from mRNA with the help of tRNA and ribosomes.

questions.text: Which codon is a start codon?
questions.answer: AUG

questions.text: Explain the role of helicase enzyme in DNA replication.
questions.answer: Helicase unwinds and separates the two DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds, creating the replication fork.

questions.text: What is a mutation? Give an example.
questions.answer: A mutation is a sudden heritable change in DNA sequence. Example: Sickle-cell anemia caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene.

questions.text: Describe the process of transcription in detail.
questions.answer: Transcription involves: 1. **Initiation** – RNA polymerase binds to promoter and unwinds DNA. 2. **Elongation** – RNA nucleotides pair with complementary DNA bases forming mRNA. 3. **Termination** – Polymerase reaches terminator sequence and releases mRNA. In eukaryotes, mRNA undergoes capping, polyadenylation, and splicing.

questions.text: Explain the lac operon model of gene regulation.
questions.answer: The lac operon in bacteria is regulated by lactose availability. - In absence of lactose, the repressor binds operator preventing transcription. - In presence of lactose, it binds repressor, inactivating it, allowing transcription of genes for lactose metabolism. This demonstrates inducible gene regulation.

questions.text: Discuss the central dogma of molecular biology.
questions.answer: The central dogma states that genetic information flows from DNA → RNA → Protein. DNA replicates, is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into proteins, which determine phenotype. It explains gene expression at molecular level.

questions.text: The bonds that hold the two strands of DNA together are:
questions.answer: Hydrogen bonds

questions.text: Which enzyme is responsible for the synthesis of RNA on a DNA template?
questions.answer: RNA polymerase

questions.text: Define transcription.
questions.answer: Transcription is the process of synthesis of RNA from a DNA template.

questions.text: What is genetic code?
questions.answer: Genetic code is a sequence of three nucleotides (codon) that codes for a specific amino acid.

questions.text: Explain the concept of degeneracy of genetic code.
questions.answer: Degeneracy means that more than one codon can code for the same amino acid.

questions.text: Explain the role of tRNA in protein synthesis.
questions.answer: tRNA carries specific amino acids to ribosomes and matches its anticodon with codon on mRNA during translation.

questions.text: Explain DNA replication with suitable examples.
questions.answer: DNA replication is a semi-conservative process involving unwinding, complementary base pairing and synthesis of new strands.

questions.text: Explain transcription in prokaryotes.
questions.answer: In prokaryotes, transcription occurs in cytoplasm and involves initiation, elongation and termination by RNA polymerase.

questions.text: Describe translation process in protein synthesis.
questions.answer: Translation occurs on ribosomes involving initiation, elongation and termination to form polypeptide chain.

questions.text: Genetic code is universal.
questions.answer: Because the same codon specifies the same amino acid in almost all organisms.

chapters.title: Origin and Evolution of Life
chapters.description: Study of theories of origin of life, early earth conditions, chemical evolution, biological evolution, Darwinism, Lamarckism, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, and evidences of evolution.
learningObjectives: Understand early conditions on Earth and theories of origin of life.
Explain chemical evolution and Miller-Urey's experiment.
Differentiate between Lamarckism and Darwinism.
Interpret Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and factors affecting it.
Recognize evidences of evolution and human evolutionary stages.

questions.text: Which scientist performed the experiment supporting chemical evolution?
questions.answer: Miller and Urey

questions.text: Define evolution.
questions.answer: Evolution is the gradual change in the heritable characteristics of populations over generations.

questions.text: State any two evidences supporting evolution.
questions.answer: Fossil records and homologous organs are strong evidences supporting evolution.

questions.text: What is natural selection according to Darwin?
questions.answer: Natural selection is the process where organisms with favorable traits survive and reproduce, passing those traits to the next generation.

questions.text: Which of the following violates Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
questions.answer: Migration

questions.text: Explain Lamarck’s theory with an example.
questions.answer: Lamarck proposed that acquired characters are inherited. Example: Giraffes developed long necks because they stretched to reach leaves, and this trait was passed to offspring.

questions.text: What is speciation?
questions.answer: Speciation is the formation of new species through genetic divergence, often due to isolation and natural selection.

questions.text: Describe the Miller-Urey experiment and its significance.
questions.answer: Miller and Urey created an apparatus simulating early Earth conditions with gases like methane, ammonia, hydrogen, and water vapor. Electric sparks simulated lightning. After several days, organic molecules like amino acids formed. This supported chemical evolution and the idea that life originated from simple organic compounds.

questions.text: Explain the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and factors affecting it.
questions.answer: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium states that allele frequencies remain constant in a population if conditions like random mating, no mutation, no migration, large population, and no selection are met. Factors disrupting equilibrium include mutation, migration, genetic drift, natural selection, and non-random mating.

questions.text: Discuss the major stages in human evolution.
questions.answer: Human evolution includes: 1. **Australopithecus** – bipedal, small brain. 2. **Homo habilis** – tool user. 3. **Homo erectus** – upright posture, fire use. 4. **Neanderthals** – strong build, cultural development. 5. **Homo sapiens** – modern humans with advanced intelligence and culture.

questions.text: The theory of chemical evolution was proposed by:
questions.answer: Oparin and Haldane

questions.text: Which experiment provided experimental evidence for chemical evolution?
questions.answer: Miller–Urey experiment

questions.text: What is abiogenesis?
questions.answer: Abiogenesis is the origin of life from non-living matter.

questions.text: Define homologous organs.
questions.answer: Homologous organs are organs with similar origin and basic structure but different functions.

questions.text: Explain Lamarckism.
questions.answer: Lamarckism proposes that characters acquired during lifetime are inherited by next generation.

questions.text: Explain natural selection with reference to industrial melanism.
questions.answer: Dark coloured moths survived better in polluted environment due to camouflage, proving natural selection.

questions.text: What is adaptive radiation? Give an example.
questions.answer: Adaptive radiation is evolution of multiple species from a common ancestor adapting to different habitats. Example: Darwin’s finches.

questions.text: Explain Darwin’s theory of natural selection.
questions.answer: Organisms produce more offspring; struggle for existence; survival of the fittest; favourable variations are selected.

questions.text: Explain evidences of evolution from morphology and anatomy.
questions.answer: Homologous organs show common ancestry; analogous organs show convergent evolution.

questions.text: Evolution is a continuous process.
questions.answer: Because organisms constantly undergo genetic variations and natural selection over generations.

chapters.title: Plant Water Relation
chapters.description: Study of water absorption, water potential, diffusion, osmosis, plasmolysis, transpiration, ascent of sap, and factors regulating water movement in plants.
learningObjectives: Understand basic principles of water movement in plants.
Explain osmosis, diffusion, imbibition, and water potential.
Describe mechanisms of absorption and conduction of water.
Understand transpiration and its significance.
Explain ascent of sap and forces involved in water transport.

questions.text: Movement of molecules from higher concentration to lower concentration is called:
questions.answer: Diffusion

questions.text: Define osmosis.
questions.answer: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential across a semipermeable membrane.

questions.text: What is water potential?
questions.answer: Water potential (Ψ) is the potential energy of water, determining the direction of its movement. Pure water has the highest water potential (Ψ = 0).

questions.text: Explain plasmolysis with an example.
questions.answer: Plasmolysis is the shrinkage of the cytoplasm away from the cell wall when a cell is placed in a hypertonic solution. Example: Onion peel cells in concentrated salt solution.

questions.text: Which tissue is mainly responsible for upward conduction of water?
questions.answer: Xylem

questions.text: What is transpiration?
questions.answer: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapor from aerial parts of plants, mainly through stomata.

questions.text: Explain imbibition.
questions.answer: Imbibition is the adsorption of water by hydrophilic substances like cellulose and seeds, causing them to swell.

questions.text: Describe the cohesion-tension theory of ascent of sap.
questions.answer: The cohesion-tension theory states that water molecules stick together by cohesion and adhere to xylem vessels. Transpiration pull creates negative pressure, which pulls water upward through the plant from roots to leaves.

questions.text: Explain the apoplast and symplast pathways of water movement.
questions.answer: In the apoplast pathway, water moves through cell walls and intercellular spaces. In the symplast pathway, water moves from cell to cell through the cytoplasm via plasmodesmata. The endodermis forces water into the symplast before entering the xylem.

questions.text: Discuss the significance of transpiration in plants.
questions.answer: Transpiration helps in cooling the plant, maintaining turgor, absorption and upward movement of water, mineral transport, and creating transpiration pull for ascent of sap.

questions.text: The movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from higher water potential to lower water potential is called:
questions.answer: Osmosis

questions.text: Which of the following is responsible for ascent of sap in tall trees?
questions.answer: Transpiration pull

questions.text: Define diffusion.
questions.answer: Diffusion is the passive movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.

questions.text: What is water potential?
questions.answer: Water potential is the potential energy of water which determines the direction of movement of water.

questions.text: Explain imbibition.
questions.answer: Imbibition is the absorption of water by hydrophilic colloids causing swelling, e.g., swelling of seeds.

questions.text: Explain root pressure.
questions.answer: Root pressure is the positive pressure developed in roots due to osmotic absorption of water, pushing sap upwards.

questions.text: Explain transpiration.
questions.answer: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapour from aerial parts of plants, mainly through stomata.

questions.text: Explain ascent of sap with reference to transpiration pull theory.
questions.answer: According to transpiration pull theory, evaporation of water from leaves creates negative pressure which pulls water upward through xylem.

questions.text: Describe factors affecting transpiration.
questions.answer: Light, temperature, humidity, wind velocity and leaf area affect transpiration rate.

questions.text: Transpiration is called a necessary evil.
questions.answer: Because it causes water loss but is essential for ascent of sap, cooling and mineral transport.

chapters.title: Plant Growth and Mineral Nutrition
chapters.description: Study of plant growth phases, growth regulators, mineral absorption, essential elements, deficiency symptoms, nitrogen cycle, and role of macronutrients and micronutrients.
learningObjectives: Understand phases and characteristics of plant growth.
Identify essential mineral nutrients and their functions.
Explain mechanisms of mineral absorption.
Describe nitrogen cycle and nitrogen fixation.
Recognize deficiency symptoms of various nutrients.

questions.text: Which of the following is a micronutrient?
questions.answer: Iron

questions.text: Define meristematic growth.
questions.answer: Meristematic growth refers to growth due to continuous cell division in meristematic tissues.

questions.text: Name any two plant growth regulators and state their functions.
questions.answer: Auxins promote cell elongation; cytokinins promote cell division.

questions.text: What is the significance of nitrogen in plant nutrition?
questions.answer: Nitrogen is essential for synthesis of proteins, nucleic acids, chlorophyll, and enzymes.

questions.text: Chlorosis is caused due to deficiency of:
questions.answer: Iron

questions.text: Differentiate between macronutrients and micronutrients.
questions.answer: Macronutrients are required in large amounts (e.g., N, P, K), whereas micronutrients are needed in trace amounts (e.g., Fe, Zn, Cu).

questions.text: What is biological nitrogen fixation?
questions.answer: Biological nitrogen fixation is conversion of atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia by microorganisms like Rhizobium.

questions.text: Describe the sigmoid (S-shaped) growth curve in plants.
questions.answer: The sigmoid growth curve consists of lag phase (slow growth), log phase (rapid exponential growth), and stationary phase (growth slows due to limited resources). It represents the typical growth pattern of plant tissues.

questions.text: Explain passive and active absorption of minerals by plants.
questions.answer: Passive absorption occurs without energy expenditure through diffusion. Active absorption requires ATP and involves carrier proteins moving ions against concentration gradients.

questions.text: Discuss the nitrogen cycle and its significance in plant growth.
questions.answer: The nitrogen cycle includes nitrogen fixation, ammonification, nitrification, and denitrification. It converts atmospheric nitrogen into usable forms like nitrates. This maintains soil fertility and supports plant growth.

questions.text: Which of the following is a micronutrient essential for plants?
questions.answer: Zinc

questions.text: The hormone responsible for cell elongation in plants is:
questions.answer: Auxin

questions.text: Define macronutrients in plants.
questions.answer: Macronutrients are elements required by plants in large quantities for normal growth and development.

questions.text: What are plant growth regulators?
questions.answer: Plant growth regulators are organic substances that influence physiological processes of plants at low concentrations.

questions.text: Explain nitrogen cycle.
questions.answer: Nitrogen cycle involves nitrogen fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification.

questions.text: Explain role of auxins in plant growth.
questions.answer: Auxins promote cell elongation, apical dominance, root initiation and tropic responses.

questions.text: Explain deficiency symptoms of nitrogen in plants.
questions.answer: Nitrogen deficiency causes chlorosis, stunted growth and reduced protein synthesis.

questions.text: Explain the role of plant growth regulators with examples.
questions.answer: Auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, ethylene and ABA regulate growth, flowering, senescence and dormancy.

questions.text: Describe biological nitrogen fixation.
questions.answer: Nitrogen fixation is conversion of atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia by Rhizobium in legume root nodules.

questions.text: Micronutrients are required in very small quantities.
questions.answer: Because they act mainly as enzyme activators and cofactors.

chapters.title: Respiration and Circulation
chapters.description: Study of respiratory mechanisms in humans, exchange and transport of gases, structure and working of the heart, cardiac cycle, blood vessels, and regulation of circulation.
topics: Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide
learningObjectives: Understand the structure and mechanism of human respiration.
Explain gaseous exchange at lungs and tissues.
Describe oxygen and carbon dioxide transport in blood.
Understand structure of the heart and working of cardiac cycle.
Explain blood circulation routes and blood pressure regulation.

questions.text: Which pigment is responsible for transport of oxygen in humans?
questions.answer: Hemoglobin

questions.text: Define tidal volume.
questions.answer: Tidal volume is the amount of air inhaled or exhaled during normal quiet breathing, approximately 500 mL.

questions.text: What is double circulation?
questions.answer: Double circulation refers to the separate pulmonary and systemic circuits in which blood passes through the heart twice during one complete circulation.

questions.text: Name the stages of the cardiac cycle.
questions.answer: Atrial systole, ventricular systole, and joint diastole.

questions.text: Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood from lungs to heart?
questions.answer: Pulmonary vein

questions.text: Explain Bohr effect.
questions.answer: Bohr effect refers to the decrease in hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen due to increased CO₂ concentration or lowered pH, enhancing oxygen release in tissues.

questions.text: What is systolic and diastolic blood pressure?
questions.answer: Systolic pressure is the pressure in arteries during ventricular contraction; diastolic pressure is the pressure during ventricular relaxation.

questions.text: Describe the mechanism of breathing in humans.
questions.answer: Breathing involves inspiration and expiration. During inspiration, diaphragm contracts and flattens, external intercostal muscles raise ribs, increasing thoracic volume, causing air to flow into lungs. During expiration, diaphragm relaxes, ribs move down, thoracic volume decreases, forcing air out.

questions.text: Explain the exchange of gases at alveoli and tissues.
questions.answer: At alveoli: O₂ diffuses from alveolar air to blood due to higher partial pressure, while CO₂ diffuses from blood to alveoli. At tissues: O₂ diffuses from blood to cells and CO₂ diffuses from cells to blood due to concentration gradients.

questions.text: Describe the structure of the human heart and its working.
questions.answer: The heart has four chambers: right and left atria, right and left ventricles. Valves ensure one-way flow. Deoxygenated blood enters right atrium → right ventricle → lungs. Oxygenated blood from lungs enters left atrium → left ventricle → pumped to body. Heart functions through rhythmic contraction and relaxation known as the cardiac cycle.

questions.text: Which pigment is responsible for oxygen transport in human blood?
questions.answer: Haemoglobin

questions.text: The pacemaker of human heart is:
questions.answer: SA node

questions.text: Define respiration.
questions.answer: Respiration is the biochemical process of oxidation of food substances to release energy.

questions.text: What is cardiac cycle?
questions.answer: Cardiac cycle is the sequence of events occurring during one complete heartbeat, including systole and diastole.

questions.text: Explain aerobic respiration.
questions.answer: Aerobic respiration is the complete oxidation of glucose in presence of oxygen to release energy, CO₂ and water.

questions.text: Explain transport of oxygen in blood.
questions.answer: Oxygen is transported mainly by haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin and partly dissolved in plasma.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of the conducting system of human heart.
questions.answer: Diagram showing SA node, AV node, Bundle of His and Purkinje fibres.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of alveolus.
questions.answer: Diagram showing alveolar wall, capillaries and air space.

questions.text: Explain the mechanism of breathing in humans.
questions.answer: Inspiration occurs by contraction of diaphragm and intercostal muscles; expiration is passive due to relaxation.

questions.text: Describe double circulation in humans.
questions.answer: Blood passes twice through the heart in one cycle: pulmonary and systemic circulation.

questions.text: Human heart is called myogenic.
questions.answer: Because the heartbeat originates within the heart muscle itself from SA node.

chapters.title: Control and Coordination
chapters.description: Study of the nervous system, endocrine system, neurons, synapses, reflex action, hormones, and regulation of physiological processes in animals.
topics: Coordination Between Nervous and Endocrine Systems
learningObjectives: Understand the structure of neurons and the mechanism of nerve impulse transmission.
Differentiate between CNS, PNS, and ANS.
Explain reflex action and reflex arc.
Describe endocrine glands and hormone functions.
Understand feedback systems and coordination between nervous and endocrine systems.

questions.text: The structural and functional unit of the nervous system is:
questions.answer: Neuron

questions.text: What is a synapse?
questions.answer: A synapse is a junction between two neurons where nerve impulses are transmitted chemically or electrically.

questions.text: Explain the term reflex action.
questions.answer: Reflex action is an automatic, immediate response to a stimulus, controlled by the spinal cord without involvement of the brain.

questions.text: State any two functions of the autonomic nervous system.
questions.answer: The autonomic nervous system regulates involuntary activities such as heartbeat, digestion, glandular secretion, and smooth muscle contraction.

questions.text: Which gland is known as the master gland?
questions.answer: Pituitary

questions.text: What is the role of myelin sheath in neurons?
questions.answer: The myelin sheath insulates axons, increases speed of nerve impulse conduction, and prevents signal loss.

questions.text: Name two hormones secreted by the adrenal gland and state their functions.
questions.answer: Adrenaline – prepares body for 'fight or flight'; Aldosterone – regulates sodium and potassium balance.

questions.text: Describe the mechanism of nerve impulse transmission across a synapse.
questions.answer: When an impulse reaches the axon terminal, calcium ions enter, causing synaptic vesicles to release neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft. These bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, generating a new impulse. Neurotransmitters are then broken down or reabsorbed.

questions.text: Explain the endocrine system with examples of glands and hormones they secrete.
questions.answer: The endocrine system consists of glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream. Examples: Thyroid secretes thyroxine; Pancreas secretes insulin and glucagon; Pituitary secretes growth hormone; Adrenal secretes adrenaline and aldosterone.

questions.text: Discuss coordination between the nervous and endocrine systems with an example.
questions.answer: Both systems work together to maintain homeostasis. Example: Stress triggers hypothalamus, which stimulates adrenal glands via neural signals to release adrenaline, increasing heart rate and respiration. This illustrates neuroendocrine coordination.

questions.text: The functional unit of nervous system is:
questions.answer: Neuron

questions.text: Which hormone regulates blood glucose level?
questions.answer: Insulin

questions.text: Define hormone.
questions.answer: Hormones are chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands and transported through blood to target organs.

questions.text: What is synapse?
questions.answer: Synapse is the junction between two neurons where transmission of nerve impulse occurs.

questions.text: Explain reflex action.
questions.answer: Reflex action is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus mediated by spinal cord without conscious control.

questions.text: Explain mechanism of hormone action.
questions.answer: Hormones bind to specific receptors, triggering signal transduction that alters cellular activity.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of a neuron.
questions.answer: Diagram showing dendrites, cell body, axon and synaptic knobs.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of human brain.
questions.answer: Diagram showing cerebrum, cerebellum, pons and medulla.

questions.text: Explain nervous coordination in humans.
questions.answer: Nervous coordination involves reception of stimulus, transmission via neurons and response through effectors.

questions.text: Describe endocrine glands and their functions.
questions.answer: Endocrine glands secrete hormones like pituitary, thyroid, adrenal controlling growth, metabolism and stress.

questions.text: Hormonal coordination is slower than nervous coordination.
questions.answer: Because hormones travel through blood and take more time to reach target organs.

chapters.title: Human Health and Diseases
chapters.description: Study of infectious and non-infectious diseases, immunity, vaccines, immune response, AIDS, cancer, addiction, and strategies for disease prevention.
learningObjectives: Differentiate between infectious and non-infectious diseases.
Understand the structure and functioning of the immune system.
Explain types of immunity and principles of vaccination.
Recognize major diseases such as AIDS, cancer, and their causes.
Understand causes and consequences of drug and alcohol abuse.

questions.text: The pathogen that causes tuberculosis is:
questions.answer: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

questions.text: Define immunity.
questions.answer: Immunity is the ability of the body to resist and fight infections through defense mechanisms.

questions.text: What is the difference between innate and acquired immunity?
questions.answer: Innate immunity is present from birth and provides immediate defense, while acquired immunity develops after exposure to pathogens and is highly specific.

questions.text: Name any two sexually transmitted diseases (STDs).
questions.answer: AIDS and syphilis are two sexually transmitted diseases.

questions.text: Which cells produce antibodies?
questions.answer: B-lymphocytes

questions.text: Explain the term vaccination.
questions.answer: Vaccination is the process of administering weakened or inactive pathogens to stimulate immunity without causing disease.

questions.text: What is AIDS? How is it transmitted?
questions.answer: AIDS is Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome caused by HIV. It is transmitted through unprotected sex, contaminated needles, infected blood, and mother-to-child transmission.

questions.text: Describe the structure of the human immune system.
questions.answer: The immune system consists of lymphoid organs such as thymus, spleen, lymph nodes, bone marrow, and circulating immune cells like T-cells, B-cells, macrophages, and antigen-presenting cells. These organs and cells coordinate to detect, attack, and eliminate pathogens.

questions.text: Explain the causes and symptoms of cancer.
questions.answer: Cancer is caused by uncontrolled cell division due to mutations, carcinogens, radiation, viruses, or genetic factors. Symptoms include formation of tumors, weight loss, fatigue, abnormal bleeding, and organ dysfunction.

questions.text: Discuss the effects of drug and alcohol addiction on human health.
questions.answer: Drug and alcohol addiction affect the nervous system, cause liver damage, impair judgment, weaken immunity, lead to mental disorders, social problems, accidents, and long-term physiological damage.

questions.text: The causative agent of AIDS is:
questions.answer: HIV

questions.text: Which of the following is a bacterial disease?
questions.answer: Typhoid

questions.text: Define immunity.
questions.answer: Immunity is the ability of the body to resist and fight against pathogens and diseases.

questions.text: What are vaccines?
questions.answer: Vaccines are biological preparations that provide active acquired immunity against specific diseases.

questions.text: Explain acquired immunity.
questions.answer: Acquired immunity develops after exposure to antigens and can be active or passive.

questions.text: Explain the mode of transmission and symptoms of malaria.
questions.answer: Malaria is transmitted by bite of infected female Anopheles mosquito; symptoms include fever, chills and headache.

questions.text: Explain the mode of transmission and prevention of AIDS.
questions.answer: AIDS spreads through unprotected sex, blood transfusion and infected needles; prevention includes safe sex and screened blood.

questions.text: Describe the structure and functions of antibodies.
questions.answer: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins with antigen binding sites; they neutralize toxins and pathogens.

questions.text: Explain innate immunity in humans.
questions.answer: Innate immunity includes physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine barriers that provide non-specific defense.

questions.text: Vaccination is an effective method of disease prevention.
questions.answer: Because vaccines stimulate immune memory and protect against future infections.

chapters.title: Enhancement of Food Production
chapters.description: Study of crop improvement, plant breeding, animal husbandry, dairy and poultry management, fisheries, biofortification, tissue culture, and modern agricultural technologies.
learningObjectives: Understand methods of improving crop yield and quality.
Explain plant breeding techniques like hybridization and mutation breeding.
Recognize the importance of animal husbandry and fisheries.
Understand biofortification and its role in nutrition.
Explain tissue culture and modern biotechnological tools in food production.

questions.text: Single-cell protein (SCP) is obtained from:
questions.answer: Bacteria and fungi

questions.text: Define plant breeding.
questions.answer: Plant breeding is the purposeful manipulation of plant species to create desired varieties with improved yield, quality, and resistance.

questions.text: What is biofortification?
questions.answer: Biofortification is the process of increasing the nutritional value of crops through breeding, genetic engineering, or agronomic practices.

questions.text: Name two applications of tissue culture in agriculture.
questions.answer: Micropropagation for mass production of disease-free plants and production of somaclones with desirable traits.

questions.text: Which of the following is a high-yielding variety (HYV) crop?
questions.answer: IR-8 rice

questions.text: What is animal husbandry?
questions.answer: Animal husbandry is the science of breeding, feeding, and caring for domestic animals to obtain useful products like milk, eggs, meat, and wool.

questions.text: Explain the importance of fishery development.
questions.answer: Fishery provides protein-rich food, employment, foreign exchange, and supports rural economies through aquaculture and marine fishing.

questions.text: Describe the steps involved in hybridization in plants.
questions.answer: Steps include selection of parents, emasculation, bagging, pollination, tagging, and collection of hybrid seeds. The resulting hybrids show improved traits such as yield, disease resistance, and stress tolerance.

questions.text: Explain mutation breeding and give an example.
questions.answer: Mutation breeding involves exposing seeds or tissues to chemicals or radiation to induce mutations, followed by selection of desirable mutants. Example: Sharbati Sonora wheat variety developed through gamma radiation.

questions.text: Discuss the role of biotechnology in enhancing food production.
questions.answer: Biotechnology helps increase yield and nutritional value through genetic modification, tissue culture, microbial fermentation (SCP), pest-resistant GM crops, improved varieties through marker-assisted selection, and biofertilizers improving soil fertility.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of biofertilizer?
questions.answer: Rhizobium

questions.text: The technique of producing disease-resistant varieties of crops is known as:
questions.answer: Plant breeding

questions.text: Define plant breeding.
questions.answer: Plant breeding is the science of improving crop plants by selecting and crossing plants with desirable traits.

questions.text: What is animal husbandry?
questions.answer: Animal husbandry is the branch of agriculture concerned with breeding, feeding and management of domestic animals.

questions.text: Explain hybridization in plant breeding.
questions.answer: Hybridization involves crossing two genetically different plants to obtain hybrids with desirable traits.

questions.text: Explain advantages of tissue culture technique.
questions.answer: Tissue culture enables rapid multiplication, disease-free plants and conservation of rare species.

questions.text: Explain single cell protein (SCP).
questions.answer: Single cell protein refers to microbial biomass used as protein source for humans and animals.

questions.text: Describe the steps involved in plant breeding programme.
questions.answer: Collection of variability, evaluation, selection, hybridization, testing and release of varieties.

questions.text: Explain role of biofertilizers and biopesticides in agriculture.
questions.answer: They enhance soil fertility and control pests without environmental pollution.

questions.text: Use of biofertilizers is encouraged in sustainable agriculture.
questions.answer: Because they are eco-friendly, cost-effective and improve soil health.

chapters.title: Biotechnology
chapters.description: Study of principles, tools, and applications of biotechnology including recombinant DNA technology, plasmids, restriction enzymes, PCR, transgenic organisms, and ethical issues.
learningObjectives: Understand the principles and steps of recombinant DNA technology.
Explain the role of restriction enzymes and vectors.
Describe PCR, cloning, and electrophoresis techniques.
Explore applications of biotechnology in various fields.
Understand ethical concerns and biosafety measures.

questions.text: The enzyme used to cut DNA at specific sites is called:
questions.answer: Restriction endonuclease

questions.text: Define biotechnology.
questions.answer: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms, cells, or biological systems to develop products or processes for human welfare.

questions.text: What is a cloning vector? Give an example.
questions.answer: A cloning vector is a DNA molecule that carries foreign DNA into a host cell for replication. Example: Plasmid pBR322.

questions.text: Explain the function of DNA ligase.
questions.answer: DNA ligase joins DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds, sealing nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone.

questions.text: Which technique is used to amplify DNA fragments?
questions.answer: PCR

questions.text: What is recombinant DNA?
questions.answer: Recombinant DNA is artificially created DNA formed by combining DNA from two different organisms or sources.

questions.text: Name two applications of biotechnology in medicine.
questions.answer: Production of insulin using recombinant DNA technology and development of vaccines.

questions.text: Explain the steps involved in recombinant DNA technology.
questions.answer: Steps include: 1. Isolation of DNA. 2. Cutting DNA with restriction enzymes. 3. Insertion into a cloning vector. 4. Introduction of recombinant DNA into host cells. 5. Selection of transformed cells. 6. Expression of the inserted gene to obtain the desired product.

questions.text: Describe the process and significance of gel electrophoresis.
questions.answer: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments based on size. DNA samples are loaded into agarose gel and subjected to electric current. Smaller fragments move faster towards the positive electrode. It is used in DNA fingerprinting, PCR analysis, and gene cloning.

questions.text: Discuss ethical issues related to genetic engineering and GM crops.
questions.answer: Concerns include ecological risks, gene transfer to wild species, loss of biodiversity, food safety issues, labeling requirements, and ethical debate over manipulating life forms. Biosafety regulations are necessary to prevent misuse.

questions.text: Which enzyme is used to cut DNA at specific sites?
questions.answer: Restriction endonuclease

questions.text: The vector commonly used in genetic engineering is:
questions.answer: Plasmid

questions.text: Define biotechnology.
questions.answer: Biotechnology is the application of biological systems, organisms or derivatives to develop useful products and processes.

questions.text: What is recombinant DNA?
questions.answer: Recombinant DNA is DNA formed by combining DNA segments from two different sources.

questions.text: Explain the role of plasmids in genetic engineering.
questions.answer: Plasmids act as vectors to transfer foreign DNA into host cells for replication and expression.

questions.text: Explain polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
questions.answer: PCR is a technique used to amplify specific DNA sequences using primers, DNA polymerase and thermal cycling.

questions.text: State applications of biotechnology in medicine.
questions.answer: Production of insulin, vaccines, antibiotics, gene therapy and diagnostic techniques.

questions.text: Describe the steps involved in recombinant DNA technology.
questions.answer: Isolation of DNA, restriction digestion, ligation, transformation, selection and expression of recombinant DNA.

questions.text: Explain applications of biotechnology in agriculture.
questions.answer: Development of GM crops, pest resistance, improved yield and nutritional quality.

questions.text: Biotechnology is considered a multidisciplinary science.
questions.answer: Because it integrates biology with chemistry, physics, engineering and computer science.

chapters.title: Organisms and Populations
chapters.description: Study of ecological levels, abiotic factors, adaptations, population attributes, population interactions, and growth models.
topics: Population Interactions (Competition, Predation, Parasitism, Commensalism, Mutualism)
learningObjectives: Understand how organisms interact with their environment.
Explain adaptations to various abiotic factors.
Analyze population attributes such as size, density, and age structure.
Differentiate population interactions and their ecological significance.
Interpret population growth curves and survivorship patterns.

questions.text: The study of interaction between organisms and their environment is called:
questions.answer: Ecology

questions.text: Define habitat.
questions.answer: Habitat is the natural living place of an organism where it obtains food, shelter, and reproduces.

questions.text: What is acclimatization? Give an example.
questions.answer: Acclimatization is the reversible adjustment of an organism to a change in its environment. Example: Humans adjusting to high altitudes.

questions.text: Differentiate between natality and mortality.
questions.answer: Natality is the birth rate of a population, whereas mortality is the death rate.

questions.text: The logistic growth curve is:
questions.answer: S-shaped

questions.text: Explain mutualism with an example.
questions.answer: Mutualism is an interaction where both species benefit. Example: Lichens consist of algae and fungi living together.

questions.text: What are age pyramids? Name their types.
questions.answer: Age pyramids show the age distribution of a population. Types: Expanding, stable, and declining.

questions.text: Describe the exponential growth model.
questions.answer: In exponential growth, resources are unlimited and population grows at its maximum rate, forming a J-shaped curve. The growth rate is proportional to the existing population, represented by the equation dN/dt = rN.

questions.text: Explain predation and its ecological importance.
questions.answer: Predation is the interaction where one organism (predator) kills and consumes another (prey). It maintains population balance, drives evolution through natural selection, and regulates energy flow in ecosystems.

questions.text: Discuss adaptations of organisms to extreme environments.
questions.answer: Adaptations include morphological (thick fur in polar animals), physiological (heat tolerance in desert plants), and behavioral (burrowing in rodents). These enable survival under extreme temperature, salinity, pressure, or light conditions.

questions.text: The relationship where one organism benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited is called:
questions.answer: Commensalism

questions.text: Exponential population growth is represented by:
questions.answer: J-shaped curve

questions.text: Define population density.
questions.answer: Population density is the number of individuals of a species per unit area or volume at a given time.

questions.text: What is mutualism?
questions.answer: Mutualism is an interaction where both participating species benefit from each other.

questions.text: Explain logistic population growth.
questions.answer: Logistic growth shows initial exponential growth followed by stabilization at carrying capacity, forming an S-shaped curve.

questions.text: Explain predator-prey relationship with an example.
questions.answer: In predator-prey interaction, predator feeds on prey, regulating population size; e.g., lion and deer.

questions.text: Explain adaptations in desert plants.
questions.answer: Desert plants show thick cuticle, reduced leaves, deep roots and CAM pathway to reduce water loss.

questions.text: Describe population interactions in an ecosystem.
questions.answer: Interactions include mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, predation and competition.

questions.text: Explain population growth curves with suitable diagrams.
questions.answer: Exponential growth shows J-curve; logistic growth shows S-curve due to carrying capacity.

questions.text: Carrying capacity regulates population size.
questions.answer: Because it represents maximum population an environment can sustain with available resources.

chapters.title: Ecosystems and Energy Flow
chapters.description: Study of ecosystem structure, biotic and abiotic components, food chains and food webs, ecological pyramids, productivity, energy flow, and nutrient cycles.
learningObjectives: Understand the structure and components of ecosystems.
Differentiate between food chains and food webs.
Interpret ecological pyramids and energy flow models.
Explain primary and secondary productivity.
Understand the importance of nutrient cycles.

questions.text: The primary source of energy in an ecosystem is:
questions.answer: Sunlight

questions.text: Define ecosystem.
questions.answer: An ecosystem is a functional unit consisting of living organisms interacting with each other and with the physical environment.

questions.text: What is a food web?
questions.answer: A food web is a network of interconnected food chains that shows multiple feeding relationships in an ecosystem.

questions.text: Explain Gross Primary Productivity (GPP).
questions.answer: GPP is the total amount of energy captured by producers through photosynthesis in a given time.

questions.text: Ecological pyramids represent:
questions.answer: Number, biomass, or energy

questions.text: What is decomposition?
questions.answer: Decomposition is the breakdown of organic matter by microorganisms, releasing nutrients back into the environment.

questions.text: State the 10% law of energy transfer.
questions.answer: According to the 10% law, only about 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next; the rest is lost as heat.

questions.text: Describe the nitrogen cycle in an ecosystem.
questions.answer: The nitrogen cycle includes nitrogen fixation (conversion of N₂ to ammonia), nitrification (ammonia to nitrates), assimilation by plants, ammonification (decomposition releasing ammonia), and denitrification (conversion of nitrates back to N₂). This cycle maintains soil fertility.

questions.text: Explain the flow of energy in an ecosystem.
questions.answer: Energy flows unidirectionally from the sun to producers and then to consumers and decomposers. At each trophic level, most energy is lost as heat, making the energy pyramid always upright.

questions.text: Discuss differences between food chains and food webs.
questions.answer: A food chain shows a single linear pathway of energy flow. A food web consists of multiple interconnected chains, offering greater stability to the ecosystem by providing alternative feeding routes.

questions.text: The primary producers in an ecosystem are:
questions.answer: Green plants

questions.text: The ten percent law of energy transfer was proposed by:
questions.answer: Lindeman

questions.text: Define ecosystem.
questions.answer: An ecosystem is a functional unit where living organisms interact with each other and with their physical environment.

questions.text: What are decomposers?
questions.answer: Decomposers are organisms like bacteria and fungi that break down dead organic matter into simpler substances.

questions.text: Explain food chain with an example.
questions.answer: A food chain shows transfer of energy from producers to consumers, e.g., grass → deer → lion.

questions.text: Explain food web.
questions.answer: A food web is a network of interconnected food chains showing complex feeding relationships.

questions.text: Explain ecological pyramids.
questions.answer: Ecological pyramids represent number, biomass or energy at each trophic level.

questions.text: Describe energy flow in an ecosystem.
questions.answer: Energy flows unidirectionally from sun to producers and then to consumers with loss at each trophic level.

questions.text: Explain nutrient cycling in an ecosystem.
questions.answer: Nutrients circulate through biotic and abiotic components via biogeochemical cycles like carbon and nitrogen cycles.

questions.text: Energy pyramid is always upright.
questions.answer: Because energy decreases at successive trophic levels due to loss as heat.

chapters.title: Biodiversity, Conservation and Environmental Issues
chapters.description: Study of biodiversity levels, importance of biodiversity, threats to biodiversity, conservation strategies, pollution, global warming, ozone depletion, and sustainable development.
learningObjectives: Understand biodiversity at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels.
Recognize the importance and value of biodiversity.
Identify major threats such as habitat loss, poaching, pollution, and climate change.
Differentiate between in-situ and ex-situ conservation.
Understand environmental issues and the need for sustainable development.

questions.text: Biosphere reserves, national parks, and wildlife sanctuaries are examples of:
questions.answer: In-situ conservation

questions.text: Define biodiversity.
questions.answer: Biodiversity refers to the variety of life forms at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels.

questions.text: State two major threats to biodiversity.
questions.answer: Habitat loss and fragmentation, and poaching of wildlife are major threats to biodiversity.

questions.text: What is global warming? Mention one cause.
questions.answer: Global warming is the rise in Earth's average temperature due to increased greenhouse gases such as CO₂.

questions.text: Ozone depletion is mainly caused by:
questions.answer: CFCs

questions.text: Explain ex-situ conservation with an example.
questions.answer: Ex-situ conservation involves protecting species outside their natural habitats. Example: Botanical gardens and seed banks.

questions.text: What is eutrophication?
questions.answer: Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of water bodies causing excessive algal growth, depletion of oxygen, and damage to aquatic life.

questions.text: Describe the major types of biodiversity.
questions.answer: Types include: 1. **Genetic diversity** – variation in genes within a species. 2. **Species diversity** – variety of species within a region. 3. **Ecosystem diversity** – diversity of ecosystems such as forests, deserts, wetlands. These levels reflect complexity and stability of life on Earth.

questions.text: Explain how climate change affects biodiversity.
questions.answer: Climate change alters temperature and rainfall patterns, causing habitat shifts, species migration, coral bleaching, extinction of sensitive species, and disruption of ecological interactions like pollination and migration.

questions.text: Discuss sustainable development and its importance.
questions.answer: Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising future generations by balancing economic growth, environmental protection, and social well-being. It promotes conservation of resources, renewable energy use, and pollution control.

questions.text: The variety of life forms found in a particular habitat is called:
questions.answer: Biodiversity

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of ex-situ conservation?
questions.answer: Botanical garden

questions.text: Define biodiversity hotspot.
questions.answer: A biodiversity hotspot is a region with high species richness and a high degree of endemism that is under threat.

questions.text: What is in-situ conservation?
questions.answer: In-situ conservation is the protection of species in their natural habitats.

questions.text: Explain causes of loss of biodiversity.
questions.answer: Habitat loss, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution and climate change cause loss of biodiversity.

questions.text: Explain the importance of biodiversity.
questions.answer: Biodiversity provides ecological stability, resources for food and medicine, and supports ecosystem services.

questions.text: Explain greenhouse effect.
questions.answer: Greenhouse effect is warming of Earth due to trapping of heat by greenhouse gases like CO₂ and methane.

questions.text: Describe measures for conservation of biodiversity.
questions.answer: Conservation includes in-situ and ex-situ methods, habitat protection, legal measures and public awareness.

questions.text: Explain environmental issues caused by human activities.
questions.answer: Human activities cause pollution, deforestation, global warming and ozone depletion.

questions.text: Conservation of biodiversity is essential.
questions.answer: Because biodiversity maintains ecological balance and ensures sustainable development.

chapters.title: Solid State
chapters.description: Classification of solids, crystal lattices, unit cells, packing efficiency, voids, imperfections, electrical and magnetic properties.
learningObjectives: Differentiate between crystalline and amorphous solids.
Understand types of unit cells and lattice parameters.
Calculate packing efficiency and number of voids.
Explain point defects in ionic and non-ionic solids.
Describe electrical, magnetic, and dielectric properties of solids.

questions.text: Which of the following is an amorphous solid?
questions.answer: Glass

questions.text: In a simple cubic unit cell, the number of atoms present is:
Define packing efficiency. What is the packing efficiency of a bcc lattice?
questions.answer: Packing efficiency is the percentage of space occupied by particles in a unit cell. For bcc, it is 68%.

questions.text: What is a Schottky defect? How does it affect the density of a crystal?
questions.answer: Schottky defect occurs when equal number of cations and anions are missing, creating vacancies. It reduces the density.

questions.text: Coordination number of fcc lattice is:
Explain the difference between crystalline and amorphous solids with any three points.
questions.answer: Crystalline solids have long-range order, sharp melting point, anisotropic properties; amorphous solids have short-range order, soften over a range, isotropic properties.

questions.text: Calculate the number of octahedral voids in 0.5 mol of a hcp metal.
questions.answer: Number of octahedral voids = number of atoms = 0.5 × NA = 3.011×10^23 voids.

questions.text: What is isomorphism? Give one example.
questions.answer: Two compounds having the same crystal structure are isomorphous. Example: NaNO3 and CaCO3.

questions.text: Which of the following defects does NOT change the density of the crystal?
questions.answer: Frenkel defect

questions.text: Explain tetrahedral and octahedral voids with diagrams and coordination numbers.
questions.answer: Tetrahedral voids are surrounded by 4 atoms; octahedral voids by 6 atoms. Two tetrahedral voids form per atom; one octahedral void per atom.

questions.text: The coordination number of atoms in a body centred cubic (bcc) lattice is:
The number of atoms per unit cell in face centred cubic lattice is:
Which of the following solids is a non-stoichiometric compound?
questions.answer: ZnO

questions.text: Define unit cell.
questions.answer: A unit cell is the smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice which, when repeated in three dimensions, generates the entire crystal.

questions.text: What is coordination number?
questions.answer: Coordination number is the number of nearest neighbouring particles surrounding a given particle in a crystal lattice.

questions.text: Define Schottky defect.
questions.answer: Schottky defect is a point defect in which equal number of cations and anions are missing from their lattice sites in an ionic crystal.

questions.text: Define Frenkel defect.
questions.answer: Frenkel defect is a point defect in which an ion leaves its lattice site and occupies an interstitial position.

questions.text: Distinguish between Schottky defect and Frenkel defect.
questions.answer: Schottky defect involves missing ions from lattice sites, while Frenkel defect involves displacement of an ion to interstitial site.

questions.text: Calculate the number of atoms per unit cell in a simple cubic lattice.
questions.answer: A simple cubic lattice has 8 corner atoms each contributing 1/8, so total atoms per unit cell = 1.

questions.text: Gold crystallises in a face centred cubic lattice. Calculate its density if the atomic mass is given and edge length of unit cell is known.
questions.answer: Density is calculated using ρ = (Z × M) / (a³ × NA). Substituting values gives density ≈ 19.3 g/cm³.

questions.text: An element crystallises in bcc structure. If the edge length of unit cell is given, calculate the atomic radius.
questions.answer: For bcc lattice, atomic radius r = (√3 × a) / 4.

questions.text: Explain different types of point defects found in ionic solids.
questions.answer: Point defects include Schottky defect, Frenkel defect and impurity defect affecting density and electrical properties.

questions.text: Ionic solids are hard and brittle.
questions.answer: Because shifting of layers brings like charges together causing strong repulsion and fracture.

questions.text: Frenkel defect does not affect density of a crystal.
questions.answer: Because ions are displaced within the lattice without changing total number of ions.

chapters.title: Solutions
chapters.description: Types of solutions, concentration terms, solubility, vapor pressure of solutions, Raoult’s law, ideal and non-ideal solutions, colligative properties and abnormal molar mass.
topics: Abnormal Molar Mass and van’t Hoff Factor
learningObjectives: Classify solutions based on physical state and concentration.
Use different concentration units to express composition of solutions.
Explain Raoult’s law and distinguish between ideal and non-ideal solutions.
Define and apply various colligative properties to determine molar mass.
Explain abnormal molar mass using van’t Hoff factor.

questions.text: Which concentration term is temperature independent?
questions.answer: Molality

questions.text: State Raoult’s law for a solution of volatile liquids.
questions.answer: Raoult’s law states that the partial vapour pressure of each component in an ideal solution is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution.

questions.text: Calculate the molality of a solution prepared by dissolving 18 g of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) in 90 g of water.
questions.answer: Moles of glucose = 18/180 = 0.1 mol; mass of solvent = 0.090 kg; molality = 0.1 / 0.090 ≈ 1.11 m.

questions.text: Which of the following is a colligative property?
questions.answer: Relative lowering of vapour pressure

questions.text: Differentiate between ideal and non-ideal solutions on the basis of enthalpy change of mixing.
questions.answer: In ideal solutions, enthalpy of mixing (ΔHmix) is zero, whereas in non-ideal solutions ΔHmix is not zero (it may be positive or negative).

questions.text: A solution containing 1.0 g of a non-volatile solute in 100 g of water boils at 100.15°C. Calculate the molar mass of the solute. (Kb for water = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹).
questions.answer: ΔTb = 0.15 K; molality = ΔTb / Kb = 0.15 / 0.52 ≈ 0.288 m. Moles of solute = 0.288 × 0.100 = 0.0288 mol. Molar mass = 1.0 / 0.0288 ≈ 34.7 g mol⁻¹.

questions.text: Define solubility. How does temperature affect solubility of solids in liquids?
questions.answer: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specific temperature. Generally, solubility of solids in liquids increases with increase in temperature.

questions.text: For a solution showing positive deviation from Raoult’s law:
questions.answer: ΔHmix > 0 and ΔVmix > 0

questions.text: What is van’t Hoff factor? How is it related to abnormal molar mass?
questions.answer: van’t Hoff factor (i) is the ratio of the observed colligative property to the calculated colligative property for a nonelectrolyte. Due to association or dissociation, the effective number of particles changes, giving abnormal molar mass, which is corrected by using i.

questions.text: Explain the concept of azeotropes. Distinguish between minimum boiling and maximum boiling azeotropes with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Azeotropes are constant boiling mixtures whose composition in liquid and vapour phase is the same. Minimum boiling azeotropes show positive deviation and boil at a temperature lower than that of either component (e.g. ethanol–water). Maximum boiling azeotropes show negative deviation and boil at a temperature higher than either component (e.g. HNO₃–water).

questions.text: The concentration of a solution expressed as number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent is called:
questions.answer: Molality

questions.text: Which of the following is temperature independent?
questions.answer: Molality

questions.text: Define molarity.
questions.answer: Molarity is the number of moles of solute present in one litre of solution.

questions.text: What is mole fraction?
questions.answer: Mole fraction is the ratio of number of moles of a component to total moles of all components in the solution.

questions.text: State Raoult’s law.
questions.answer: Raoult’s law states that the partial vapour pressure of a component is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution.

questions.text: Define ideal solution.
questions.answer: An ideal solution obeys Raoult’s law over the entire range of concentration and shows no enthalpy or volume change on mixing.

questions.text: What is azeotrope?
questions.answer: An azeotrope is a mixture of liquids that boils at a constant temperature and has same composition in liquid and vapour phase.

questions.text: Explain positive deviation from Raoult’s law.
questions.answer: Positive deviation occurs when solute–solvent interactions are weaker than solute–solute or solvent–solvent interactions.

questions.text: Calculate molarity of a solution containing given grams of solute dissolved in given volume of solution.
questions.answer: Molarity = moles of solute / volume of solution in litres.

questions.text: Calculate mole fraction of each component in a binary solution.
questions.answer: Mole fraction = moles of component / total moles of solution.

questions.text: Calculate the elevation in boiling point of a solution given molal concentration and ebullioscopic constant.
questions.answer: ΔTb = Kb × m.

questions.text: Calculate depression in freezing point of a solution given molality and cryoscopic constant.
questions.answer: ΔTf = Kf × m.

questions.text: Explain non-ideal solutions with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Non-ideal solutions do not obey Raoult’s law and show positive or negative deviation, e.g., ethanol–water mixture.

questions.text: Molality is preferred over molarity in colligative properties.
questions.answer: Because molality is temperature independent while molarity depends on volume which changes with temperature.

chapters.title: Ionic Equilibria
chapters.description: Concept of acids and bases, ionization of weak electrolytes, Ostwald’s dilution law, pH scale, buffer solutions, solubility product and common ion effect.
topics: Arrhenius, Bronsted–Lowry and Lewis Acids and Bases
pH, pOH and Ionic Product of Water
learningObjectives: Compare different concepts of acids and bases.
Derive and apply Ostwald’s dilution law for weak electrolytes.
Calculate pH of strong and weak acid/base solutions.
Explain the working of buffer solutions using Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.
Use solubility product to predict precipitation and solubility.

questions.text: Which of the following is a Lewis acid?
questions.answer: BF₃

questions.text: State Ostwald’s dilution law for a weak electrolyte.
questions.answer: Ostwald’s dilution law states that the degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte is inversely proportional to the square root of its concentration and relates dissociation constant K to concentration c and degree of dissociation α by K = cα² / (1 − α).

questions.text: Calculate the pH of 0.001 M HCl solution.
questions.answer: HCl is a strong acid and fully ionizes. [H⁺] = 0.001 M = 10⁻³ M; pH = −log[H⁺] = 3.

questions.text: The ionic product of water (Kw) at 25°C is approximately:
What is a buffer solution? Give one example each of acidic and basic buffer.
questions.answer: A buffer solution resists change in pH on addition of small amounts of acid or base. Example of acidic buffer: CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻Na⁺; basic buffer: NH₄OH and NH₄Cl.

questions.text: Write Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer and explain each term.
questions.answer: For an acidic buffer, pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]), where pKa is −log Ka, [salt] is concentration of conjugate base and [acid] is concentration of weak acid.

questions.text: The solubility product of AgCl at 25°C is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰. Calculate its solubility in mol L⁻¹ in pure water.
questions.answer: For AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, Ksp = s²; s = √(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 1.26 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹.

questions.text: Common ion effect is observed when:
options: A weak electrolyte is mixed with a strong electrolyte having a common ion
A salt is added to a non-aqueous solvent
questions.answer: A weak electrolyte is mixed with a strong electrolyte having a common ion

questions.text: Explain hydrolysis of salts formed from (i) strong acid and weak base, (ii) weak acid and strong base with suitable examples.
questions.answer: i) Salts of strong acid and weak base (e.g. NH₄Cl) hydrolyse to give acidic solution because the cation reacts with water to produce H⁺. ii) Salts of weak acid and strong base (e.g. CH₃COONa) hydrolyse to give basic solution because the anion reacts with water to produce OH⁻.

questions.text: Derive the expression for pH of a weak acid solution using its dissociation constant (Ka) and concentration.
questions.answer: For weak acid HA of initial concentration C, degree of dissociation α is small. Ka = Cα²/(1−α) ≈ Cα². [H⁺] = Cα = √(CKa). Hence pH = −log[H⁺] = −log(√(C Ka)) = 1/2 (pKa − log C).
