questions.text: The pH of a neutral solution at 25°C is:
Which of the following is a weak acid?
questions.answer: CH₃COOH

questions.text: Define pH.
questions.answer: pH is the negative logarithm of hydrogen ion concentration of a solution.

questions.text: What is ionic product of water?
questions.answer: Ionic product of water is the product of concentrations of hydrogen and hydroxide ions in water.

questions.text: Define dissociation constant of an acid (Ka).
questions.answer: Ka is the equilibrium constant for dissociation of a weak acid into ions in aqueous solution.

questions.text: What is buffer solution?
questions.answer: A buffer solution resists change in pH on addition of small amount of acid or base.

questions.text: Give one example of acidic buffer.
questions.answer: Acetic acid and sodium acetate mixture is an acidic buffer.

questions.text: Calculate pH of a given concentration of strong acid.
questions.answer: pH = −log[H⁺], where [H⁺] equals concentration of strong acid.

questions.text: Calculate pH of a weak acid using Ka value.
questions.answer: pH is calculated using [H⁺] = √(Ka × C).

questions.text: Calculate pH of a buffer solution containing given concentration of weak acid and its salt.
questions.answer: pH is calculated using Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]).

questions.text: Calculate solubility of a sparingly soluble salt using Ksp value.
questions.answer: Solubility is calculated using Ksp expression based on dissociation stoichiometry.

questions.text: Explain common ion effect with suitable example.
questions.answer: Common ion effect is suppression of ionisation of a weak electrolyte by addition of strong electrolyte having common ion.

questions.text: pH of pure water changes with temperature.
questions.answer: Because ionic product of water varies with temperature.

questions.text: Buffer solutions are important in biological systems.
questions.answer: Because they maintain nearly constant pH essential for biochemical reactions.

chapters.title: Chemical Thermodynamics
chapters.description: Basic thermodynamic terms, first law, enthalpy changes, Hess’s law, spontaneity, entropy, Gibbs free energy and criteria for equilibrium.
topics: System, Surroundings and Types of Systems
Heat of Reaction and Hess’s Law
Gibbs Free Energy and Work Function
Relationship between ΔG, ΔH and ΔS
learningObjectives: Define system, surroundings and types of thermodynamic systems.
Apply first law of thermodynamics to physical and chemical processes.
Explain enthalpy changes and use Hess’s law for calculation.
Describe entropy and spontaneity in terms of second law.
Use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS to predict feasibility of reactions.

questions.text: Which of the following is an extensive property?
questions.answer: Enthalpy

questions.text: State the first law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: The first law of thermodynamics states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be converted from one form to another. Mathematically, ΔU = q + w.

questions.text: An ideal gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work. Calculate the change in internal energy of the system.
State Hess’s law of constant heat summation.
questions.answer: Hess’s law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or in a series of steps.

questions.text: For a spontaneous process at constant temperature and pressure:
questions.answer: ΔG < 0

questions.text: Define entropy. What is its SI unit?
questions.answer: Entropy is a measure of randomness or disorder of a system. Its SI unit is J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

questions.text: Calculate ΔG for a reaction at 298 K if ΔH = −40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −50 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Comment on spontaneity.
questions.answer: Convert ΔS to kJ: −50 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = −0.050 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −40 − 298(−0.050) = −40 + 14.9 = −25.1 kJ mol⁻¹. Since ΔG < 0, the reaction is spontaneous.

questions.text: Which of the following processes has ΔS > 0?
options: Dissolution of a salt in water
Formation of ionic solid from gaseous ions
questions.answer: Dissolution of a salt in water

questions.text: Distinguish between reversible and irreversible processes with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Reversible processes occur infinitely slowly through a series of equilibrium states and can be reversed by an infinitesimal change (e.g. isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas). Irreversible processes occur spontaneously in a finite time with driving force; they cannot be exactly reversed (e.g. free expansion of gas, natural heat flow from hot to cold body).

questions.text: Explain the relationship ΔG = −nFE and its significance in electrochemical cells.
questions.answer: ΔG is the maximum non-expansion work obtainable from a galvanic cell. For a cell involving n moles of electrons and emf E, ΔG = −nFE (F is Faraday constant). A negative ΔG corresponds to positive E and a spontaneous cell reaction.

questions.text: Which of the following is a state function?
questions.answer: Internal energy

questions.text: The SI unit of enthalpy change is:
questions.answer: J mol⁻¹

questions.text: Define system in thermodynamics.
questions.answer: A system is that part of the universe which is under observation.

questions.text: What is enthalpy?
questions.answer: Enthalpy is the total heat content of a system and is represented by H.

questions.text: State first law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed but can be converted from one form to another.

questions.text: Define internal energy.
questions.answer: Internal energy is the total energy possessed by a system due to molecular motion and interactions.

questions.text: What is Hess’s law of constant heat summation?
questions.answer: The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the path and depends only on initial and final states.

questions.text: Calculate work done when a gas expands against constant external pressure.
questions.answer: Work done is calculated using w = −PΔV.

questions.text: Calculate change in internal energy using first law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: ΔU = q + w.

questions.text: Calculate enthalpy change of a reaction using given thermochemical equations.
questions.answer: Enthalpy change is calculated using Hess’s law by algebraic addition of equations.

questions.text: Calculate standard enthalpy of formation using given data.
questions.answer: Standard enthalpy of formation is calculated from thermochemical equations under standard conditions.

questions.text: Explain types of thermodynamic systems.
questions.answer: Thermodynamic systems are classified as open, closed and isolated systems.

questions.text: Enthalpy is a state function.
questions.answer: Because it depends only on initial and final states of the system, not on the path.

questions.text: Heat is not a state function.
questions.answer: Because heat depends on the path followed during a process.

chapters.title: Electrochemistry
chapters.description: Electrolytic and galvanic cells, electrode potential, Nernst equation, electrochemical series, conductance of electrolytes, Kohlrausch’s law and applications.
learningObjectives: Differentiate between electrolytic and galvanic cells.
Explain electrode potential and its measurement.
Apply Nernst equation to calculate cell potential.
Use electrochemical series to predict feasibility and EMF.
Describe working of important electrochemical cells and corrosion.

questions.text: Unit of molar conductance is:
questions.answer: S cm² mol⁻¹

questions.text: Define standard electrode potential.
questions.answer: Standard electrode potential is the potential difference between a metal/metal ion electrode and standard hydrogen electrode when the ionic concentration is 1 M, gas pressure 1 bar and temperature 298 K.

questions.text: Calculate the EMF of a cell: Zn | Zn²⁺ (0.1 M) || Cu²⁺ (1.0 M) | Cu. Given E°cell = 1.10 V, n = 2.
In an electrolytic cell, the electrode at which oxidation occurs is called:
questions.answer: Anode

questions.text: State Kohlrausch’s law of independent migration of ions.
questions.answer: Kohlrausch’s law states that at infinite dilution, the limiting molar conductance of an electrolyte is equal to the sum of the individual contributions of its cation and anion.

questions.text: The limiting molar conductance of NaCl, HCl and NaAc are 126.4, 426.2 and 91.0 S cm² mol⁻¹ respectively. Calculate the limiting molar conductance of CH₃COOH.
questions.answer: Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(NaAc) − Λ°(NaCl) = 426.2 + 91.0 − 126.4 = 390.8 S cm² mol⁻¹.

questions.text: What is a fuel cell? Give one example.
questions.answer: A fuel cell converts the chemical energy of a fuel directly into electrical energy by an electrochemical reaction. Example: Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.

questions.text: Rusting of iron is an example of:
questions.answer: Galvanic corrosion

questions.text: Explain the construction and working of a lead storage battery.
questions.answer: A lead storage battery consists of lead anode and lead dioxide cathode dipped in aqueous H₂SO₄. During discharge, Pb is oxidized to PbSO₄ and PbO₂ is reduced to PbSO₄, producing electrical energy. On charging, these reactions are reversed, regenerating Pb and PbO₂.

questions.text: What is electrochemical series? Give any three applications.
questions.answer: Electrochemical series is an arrangement of elements in order of their standard reduction potentials. Applications: predicting feasibility of redox reactions, calculating EMF of cells, determining the oxidizing/reducing strength of species and metal displacement reactions.

questions.text: The electrode at which oxidation occurs is called:
questions.answer: Anode

questions.text: The unit of electrical conductivity is:
questions.answer: ohm⁻¹ cm⁻¹

questions.text: Define electrode potential.
questions.answer: Electrode potential is the potential difference developed between electrode and its ions in solution.

questions.text: What is electrochemical cell?
questions.answer: An electrochemical cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy by redox reactions.

questions.text: Define standard electrode potential.
questions.answer: Standard electrode potential is electrode potential measured under standard conditions with respect to standard hydrogen electrode.

questions.text: State Nernst equation.
questions.answer: Nernst equation relates electrode potential to standard electrode potential and concentration of ions.

questions.text: What is salt bridge? State its function.
questions.answer: Salt bridge maintains electrical neutrality and completes the circuit by allowing ion flow.

questions.text: Calculate cell EMF using given standard electrode potentials.
questions.answer: Cell EMF is calculated as E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode.

questions.text: Calculate electrode potential at given concentration using Nernst equation.
questions.answer: Electrode potential is calculated using Nernst equation with given values.

questions.text: Calculate equilibrium constant of a cell reaction using EMF data.
questions.answer: Equilibrium constant is calculated using ΔG° = −nFE°cell and relation with K.

questions.text: Calculate electrical conductivity of solution given resistance and cell constant.
questions.answer: Conductivity κ = cell constant / resistance.

questions.text: Explain electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride.
questions.answer: Electrolysis produces hydrogen at cathode, chlorine at anode and sodium hydroxide in solution.

questions.text: Salt bridge is essential in galvanic cell.
questions.answer: Because it prevents charge build-up and maintains electrical neutrality.

questions.text: Conductivity of electrolyte decreases on dilution.
questions.answer: Because number of ions per unit volume decreases on dilution.

chapters.title: Chemical Kinetics
chapters.description: Rate of reaction, factors affecting rate, rate laws, order and molecularity, integrated rate equations, half-life, collision theory and catalysis.
topics: Average and Instantaneous Rate of Reaction
Integrated Rate Equations for Zero and First Order
learningObjectives: Define rate of reaction and express it mathematically.
Determine order and rate constant from experimental data.
Use integrated rate equations for zero and first order reactions.
Explain effect of temperature on rate using Arrhenius equation.
Describe collision theory and role of catalyst.

questions.text: The unit of rate constant for a first-order reaction is:
questions.answer: s⁻¹

questions.text: Define order of a reaction. How is it different from molecularity?
questions.answer: Order is the sum of powers of concentration terms in the rate law and is an experimental quantity. Molecularity is the number of molecules colliding in a single step and is a theoretical concept defined only for elementary reactions.

questions.text: For a first order reaction, the rate constant is 0.693 min⁻¹. Calculate its half-life.
questions.answer: For first order, t½ = 0.693 / k = 0.693 / 0.693 = 1 min.

questions.text: According to Arrhenius equation, rate constant k is related to temperature T as:
questions.answer: k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT)

questions.text: What is activation energy? How does a catalyst affect it?
questions.answer: Activation energy is the minimum extra energy that reacting molecules must possess to undergo a chemical reaction. A catalyst lowers the activation energy by providing an alternative pathway.

questions.text: A zero order reaction has a rate constant of 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. How long will it take for the concentration of reactant to fall from 0.10 mol L⁻¹ to 0.04 mol L⁻¹?
Write integrated rate law for first order reaction and explain the terms.
questions.answer: For A → products, ln[A]t = ln[A]0 − kt or [A]t = [A]0 e^(−kt); [A]0 is initial concentration, [A]t is concentration at time t, k is rate constant.

questions.text: Which factor does NOT affect rate of a chemical reaction?
questions.answer: Avogadro number

questions.text: Explain collision theory of bimolecular reactions.
questions.answer: According to collision theory, molecules must collide with sufficient energy (≥ activation energy) and proper orientation to react. Rate is proportional to the number of effective collisions per unit time. Temperature increases kinetic energy and collision frequency, increasing rate.

questions.text: Discuss the effect of temperature on rate constant using Arrhenius equation and explain how activation energy can be determined graphically.
questions.answer: Arrhenius equation k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT) shows that k increases with temperature. Taking log gives ln k = ln A − Eₐ/RT. A plot of ln k versus 1/T is a straight line with slope −Eₐ/R from which activation energy Eₐ is calculated.

questions.text: The rate of a chemical reaction is defined as:
options: Change in concentration per unit time
Change in temperature per unit time
Change in pressure per unit time
Change in volume per unit time
questions.answer: Change in concentration per unit time

questions.text: For a zero order reaction, the rate of reaction is:
questions.answer: Independent of concentration

questions.text: Define order of reaction.
questions.answer: Order of reaction is the sum of powers of concentration terms appearing in the rate law expression.

questions.text: What is rate constant?
questions.answer: Rate constant is the proportionality constant in the rate law equation at a given temperature.

questions.text: State integrated rate law for first order reaction.
questions.answer: For first order reaction: ln([A]₀/[A]) = kt.

questions.text: Define half-life of a reaction.
questions.answer: Half-life is the time required for the concentration of reactant to become half of its initial value.

questions.text: How does temperature affect the rate of reaction?
questions.answer: Increase in temperature increases kinetic energy of molecules, leading to higher reaction rate.

questions.text: Calculate rate constant for a first order reaction given concentration data and time.
questions.answer: Rate constant is calculated using integrated rate law: k = (2.303/t) log([A]₀/[A]).

questions.text: Calculate half-life of a first order reaction using given rate constant.
questions.answer: Half-life t½ = 0.693 / k.

questions.text: Calculate activation energy using Arrhenius equation given rate constants at two temperatures.
questions.answer: Activation energy is calculated using Arrhenius equation: ln(k₂/k₁) = Ea/R(1/T₁ − 1/T₂).

questions.text: Calculate time required for a given percentage completion of first order reaction.
questions.answer: Time is calculated using integrated first order rate law.

questions.text: Explain collision theory of chemical reactions.
questions.answer: Collision theory states that effective collisions with sufficient energy and proper orientation lead to reaction.

questions.text: Half-life of a first order reaction is independent of initial concentration.
questions.answer: Because half-life depends only on rate constant, not on initial concentration.

questions.text: Rate constant increases with increase in temperature.
questions.answer: Because more molecules acquire activation energy at higher temperature.

chapters.title: Elements of Groups 16, 17 and 18
chapters.description: Study of p-block elements of groups 16, 17 and 18, their electronic configurations, trends, important compounds and anomalous behaviour of oxygen and fluorine.
topics: Group 16 Elements: O, S and Their Compounds
Hydrogen Halides and Oxyacids of Halogens
learningObjectives: Write electronic configurations of group 16, 17 and 18 elements.
Explain trends in physical and chemical properties down the groups.
Describe preparation and properties of important compounds like O₂, O₃, SO₂, H₂SO₄, Cl₂ and HCl.
Draw structures of oxyacids of sulphur and halogens.
Explain formation and structure of xenon compounds.

questions.text: Which of the following is a group 16 element?
questions.answer: Oxygen

questions.text: Why is O–O bond weaker than S–S bond?
questions.answer: Due to small size of oxygen atoms, electron–electron repulsions in O–O bond are higher, weakening the bond, whereas sulphur has larger size and less repulsion in S–S bond.

questions.text: Write any two uses of sulphuric acid.
questions.answer: Used in manufacture of fertilizers like ammonium sulphate and superphosphate; used in petroleum refining, dyes, paints and as a dehydrating agent.

questions.text: Which hydrogen halide is the strongest acid in aqueous solution?
questions.answer: HI

questions.text: What are interhalogen compounds? Give one example.
questions.answer: Compounds formed between different halogen atoms are called interhalogen compounds, e.g. ClF₃, ICl.

questions.text: Explain the structure and bonding in ozone (O₃).
questions.answer: Ozone is angular with O–O–O bond angle about 117°. It shows resonance between two equivalent structures with one O–O single bond and one O=O double bond, giving equalized bond order of 1.5.

questions.text: Why are noble gases chemically inert?
questions.answer: They have stable ns²np⁶ configuration (except He: 1s²) with completely filled valence shell and high ionization energy, so they do not easily gain or lose electrons.

questions.text: Which xenon compound has square planar geometry around xenon?
questions.answer: XeF₄

questions.text: Describe contact process for manufacture of sulphuric acid with reactions.
questions.answer: Steps: (i) Burning S or FeS₂ in air to form SO₂. (ii) Catalytic oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃ using V₂O₅ at 720–770 K and 1–2 bar: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃. (iii) Absorption of SO₃ in conc. H₂SO₄ to form oleum, then dilution with water to get desired concentration of H₂SO₄.

questions.text: Explain anomalous behaviour of fluorine compared to other halogens.
questions.answer: Fluorine is most electronegative, smallest in size and has no d-orbitals. It forms only one oxidation state (−1), shows high reactivity, forms strong hydrogen bonds, low bond dissociation energy of F–F and does not form oxyacids like other halogens.

questions.text: Which of the following is the most electronegative element among halogens?
questions.answer: Fluorine

questions.text: Which noble gas is used in electric bulbs?
questions.answer: Argon

questions.text: Name the element of group 16 having highest electronegativity.
questions.answer: Oxygen

questions.text: What are noble gases?
questions.answer: Noble gases are elements of group 18 having completely filled valence shells and low chemical reactivity.

questions.text: Give two uses of sulphur dioxide.
questions.answer: Sulphur dioxide is used as a bleaching agent and in manufacture of sulphuric acid.

questions.text: Explain anomalous behaviour of fluorine.
questions.answer: Fluorine shows anomalous behaviour due to its small size, high electronegativity and absence of d-orbitals.

questions.text: Why noble gases are chemically inert?
questions.answer: Because they have completely filled valence shells and high ionisation energies.

questions.text: Explain preparation, properties and uses of sulphuric acid.
questions.answer: Sulphuric acid is prepared by contact process; it is a strong acid and widely used in fertilizers, batteries and industries.

questions.text: Describe preparation and properties of chlorine.
questions.answer: Chlorine is prepared by electrolysis of brine; it is a greenish-yellow gas with strong oxidising properties.

questions.text: Explain preparation and uses of ozone.
questions.answer: Ozone is prepared by silent electric discharge and is used as an oxidising agent and disinfectant.

questions.text: Fluorine does not show positive oxidation state.
questions.answer: Because fluorine is the most electronegative element and cannot lose electrons.

questions.text: Helium is used in filling weather balloons.
questions.answer: Because helium is light, non-inflammable and inert.

chapters.title: Transition and Inner Transition Elements
chapters.description: Study of d-block and f-block elements, general properties, variable oxidation states, complex formation, magnetic behaviour and lanthanoid contraction.
topics: Preparation and Properties of Important Compounds
learningObjectives: Write electronic configurations of transition and inner transition elements.
Explain general properties like variable oxidation state, catalytic activity and complex formation.
Interpret magnetic properties and colour on the basis of unpaired electrons.
Describe lanthanoid contraction and its consequences.
Differentiate between lanthanoids and actinoids.

questions.text: Which of the following is a d-block element?
questions.answer: Fe

questions.text: Why do transition metals show variable oxidation states?
questions.answer: Because of small energy difference between (n−1)d and ns orbitals, both can participate in bonding, giving multiple oxidation states.

questions.text: Explain why most transition metal salts are coloured.
questions.answer: Presence of partially filled d-orbitals allows d–d transitions of electrons under ligand field, absorbing certain wavelengths and giving colour.

questions.text: Which property generally increases with number of unpaired electrons?
questions.answer: Paramagnetism

questions.text: What is lanthanoid contraction?
questions.answer: It is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii of lanthanoids (from La³⁺ to Lu³⁺) with increasing atomic number due to poor shielding by 4f electrons.

questions.text: Give any three consequences of lanthanoid contraction.
questions.answer: i) Similarity in size of Zr and Hf and their similar properties. ii) Difficulty in separation of lanthanoids due to close radii. iii) Higher basicity of early lanthanoid hydroxides compared to later ones.

questions.text: Which of the following is an actinoid element?
questions.answer: Th

questions.text: Transition metals form alloys easily. Why?
questions.answer: Because their atomic sizes are similar and crystal structures are compatible, atoms of one metal can replace those of another in the lattice to form alloys.

questions.text: Compare lanthanoids and actinoids with respect to (i) oxidation states, (ii) radioactivity, (iii) complex formation.
questions.answer: i) Lanthanoids mainly show +3 state with few exceptions; actinoids show wider range from +3 to +6. ii) Most lanthanoids are non-radioactive (except promethium); almost all actinoids are radioactive. iii) Actinoids show stronger tendency for complex formation due to higher charge and larger size.

questions.text: An aqueous solution of a metal ion M²⁺ has three unpaired electrons. Calculate its magnetic moment (spin-only formula).
Which of the following elements shows variable oxidation states?
questions.answer: Iron

questions.text: The general electronic configuration of transition elements is:
questions.answer: (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻²

questions.text: Define transition element.
questions.answer: Transition elements are elements having partially filled d-orbitals in their atoms or common oxidation states.

questions.text: What are inner transition elements?
questions.answer: Inner transition elements are f-block elements including lanthanides and actinides.

questions.text: Why do transition elements show coloured compounds?
questions.answer: Due to d–d electronic transitions in partially filled d-orbitals.

questions.text: Explain catalytic property of transition metals.
questions.answer: Transition metals act as catalysts due to their variable oxidation states and ability to form complexes.

questions.text: What is lanthanide contraction?
questions.answer: Lanthanide contraction is the gradual decrease in atomic and ionic radii of lanthanides with increasing atomic number.

questions.text: Explain general characteristics of transition elements.
questions.answer: Transition elements show variable oxidation states, coloured compounds, catalytic activity, complex formation and magnetic properties.

questions.text: Describe properties and uses of lanthanides.
questions.answer: Lanthanides show similar properties, high reactivity and are used in alloys, catalysts and phosphors.

questions.text: Explain actinides and their radioactive nature.
questions.answer: Actinides are f-block elements that are mostly radioactive due to unstable nuclei.

questions.text: Transition metals form complexes.
questions.answer: Because of availability of vacant d-orbitals to accept electron pairs from ligands.

questions.text: Zinc is not considered a transition element.
questions.answer: Because zinc has completely filled d-orbitals in its atoms and common oxidation states.

chapters.title: Coordination Compounds
chapters.description: Werner’s theory, nomenclature, isomerism, valence bond theory, crystal field theory, stability and applications of coordination compounds.
topics: Basic Terms: Ligand, Coordination Number, Coordination Sphere
learningObjectives: Use IUPAC rules to name coordination compounds.
Classify ligands and determine coordination number.
Identify and explain different kinds of isomerism in complexes.
Apply VBT and CFT to predict geometry and magnetic properties.
Explain stability and uses of coordination compounds.

questions.text: In the complex [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃, the coordination number of Co is:
Define ligand and give one example each of monodentate and bidentate ligand.
questions.answer: Ligand is an ion or molecule capable of donating a pair of electrons to central metal atom/ion. Monodentate: Cl⁻; Bidentate: ethane-1,2-diamine (en).

questions.text: Write IUPAC name of [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻.
questions.answer: Hexacyanidoferrate(II) ion.

questions.text: Which type of isomerism is shown by [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl and [Co(NH₃)₄ClCl₂]?
questions.answer: Ionization isomerism

questions.text: Explain geometrical isomerism in square planar complex [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂].
questions.answer: In square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], ligands can be arranged as cis (two Cl⁻ adjacent) and trans (two Cl⁻ opposite). These isomers differ in physical and chemical properties; cis is more reactive and used as anticancer drug (cis-platin).

questions.text: What is effective atomic number (EAN)? State its significance.
questions.answer: EAN is the total number of electrons present around the central metal ion including those donated by ligands. Complexes with EAN equal to nearest noble gas configuration are often more stable.

questions.text: A complex with d²sp³ hybridization has which geometry?
questions.answer: Octahedral (inner orbital)

questions.text: Explain high-spin and low-spin complexes with reference to crystal field splitting.
questions.answer: In octahedral field, Δo may be small or large. For weak-field ligands (small Δo), electrons occupy higher energy t2g and eg orbitals singly, giving more unpaired electrons (high-spin complex). For strong-field ligands (large Δo), electrons pair in lower t2g orbitals before occupying eg, giving fewer unpaired electrons (low-spin complex).

questions.text: Give any two applications of coordination compounds in daily life or industry.
questions.answer: Used in metallurgy for extraction (e.g., cyanide complexes in gold extraction), as catalysts (e.g., Wilkinson’s catalyst), in medicine (e.g., cis-platin), and as complexometric indicators (EDTA in water hardness estimation).

questions.text: Calculate the oxidation state of cobalt in the complex [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂.
questions.answer: Let oxidation state of Co be x. NH₃ is neutral, Cl⁻ ligand is −1, two counter Cl⁻ are −2: x + (−1) + 0 = +2 (overall charge of complex cation). So x = +3.

questions.text: The coordination number of cobalt in [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 is:
Which of the following is a bidentate ligand?
questions.answer: C2O4²−

questions.text: Define coordination compound.
questions.answer: A coordination compound is a compound containing a central metal atom or ion surrounded by ligands linked through coordinate bonds.

questions.text: What is ligand?
questions.answer: A ligand is an ion or molecule that donates a pair of electrons to the central metal atom or ion to form a coordinate bond.

questions.text: Define coordination number.
questions.answer: Coordination number is the number of ligands directly attached to the central metal atom or ion.

questions.text: What is chelation?
questions.answer: Chelation is the formation of ring structures when a polydentate ligand binds to a central metal ion.

questions.text: Explain ionisation isomerism with an example.
questions.answer: Ionisation isomerism occurs when compounds produce different ions in solution, e.g., [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4 and [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br.

questions.text: Explain geometrical isomerism in coordination compounds.
questions.answer: Geometrical isomerism arises due to different spatial arrangements of ligands around the central metal ion.

questions.text: Explain Werner’s theory of coordination compounds.
questions.answer: Werner proposed primary and secondary valencies explaining bonding, structure and properties of coordination compounds.

questions.text: Describe different types of isomerism in coordination compounds.
questions.answer: Isomerism includes structural (ionisation, hydrate) and stereoisomerism (geometrical, optical).

questions.text: Coordination compounds show optical isomerism.
questions.answer: Due to asymmetric arrangement of ligands around the central metal ion.

questions.text: Chelated complexes are more stable than non-chelated complexes.
questions.answer: Because chelation forms ring structures which increase stability.

chapters.title: Halogen Derivatives
chapters.description: Classification, nomenclature, methods of preparation and reactions of haloalkanes and haloarenes, mechanism of nucleophilic substitution and elimination reactions.
topics: Classification and Nomenclature of Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
learningObjectives: Write IUPAC names and classify haloalkanes and haloarenes.
Describe methods of preparation and properties of halogen derivatives.
Differentiate between SN1 and SN2 mechanisms.
Explain elimination reactions and Saytzeff rule.
Discuss uses and environmental hazards of important polyhalogen compounds.

questions.text: Which of the following is a primary haloalkane?
questions.answer: 1-bromopropane

questions.text: Write IUPAC name of CH₃–CH(Br)–CH₂–CH₃.
questions.answer: 2-bromobutane.

questions.text: What is Walden inversion?
questions.answer: In SN2 reactions at a chiral carbon, the configuration inverts due to backside attack of nucleophile; this is called Walden inversion.

questions.text: SN1 reactions are favoured by:
options: Primary halides in polar protic solvents
Tertiary halides in polar protic solvents
Primary halides in polar aprotic solvents
questions.answer: Tertiary halides in polar protic solvents

questions.text: State Saytzeff’s rule with an example.
questions.answer: In dehydrohalogenation of haloalkanes, the major alkene formed is the one with greater number of alkyl substituents on doubly bonded carbon atoms. Example: 2-bromobutane gives mainly 2-butene.

questions.text: Explain the electrophilic substitution reactions of chlorobenzene.
questions.answer: Chlorobenzene undergoes substitution such as nitration, sulphonation and halogenation. Cl is deactivating but o,p-directing. Reaction conditions are harsher than benzene due to −I effect of Cl.

questions.text: Which of these is a polyhalogen compound used as a refrigerant?
questions.answer: Freon-12

questions.text: Why are aryl halides less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution than alkyl halides?
questions.answer: Due to partial double bond character of C–X bond because of resonance and because the carbon in ring is sp²-hybridized and holds halogen more strongly.

questions.text: Differentiate between SN1 and SN2 mechanisms (any three points).
questions.answer: SN1: two-step, carbocation intermediate, first order, favoured by tertiary halides and polar protic solvents, racemization at chiral centre. SN2: one-step, backside attack, second order, favoured by primary halides and polar aprotic solvents, Walden inversion.

questions.text: A chiral haloalkane undergoes SN1 reaction. If the initial optical rotation is +20°, what will be the observed rotation if complete racemization occurs?
questions.answer: For complete racemization, equal amounts of enantiomers are formed; net optical rotation becomes 0°.

questions.text: Which of the following is a secondary alkyl halide?
questions.answer: CH3CHClCH3

questions.text: Which reagent is used to convert alcohol into alkyl chloride?
questions.answer: PCl5

questions.text: Define alkyl halide.
questions.answer: Alkyl halides are organic compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane are replaced by halogen atoms.

questions.text: What is Wurtz reaction?
questions.answer: Wurtz reaction involves coupling of alkyl halides with sodium metal in dry ether to form higher alkanes.

questions.text: Explain SN1 reaction.
questions.answer: SN1 reaction is a nucleophilic substitution reaction that proceeds via carbocation intermediate and follows first order kinetics.

questions.text: Explain SN2 reaction.
questions.answer: SN2 reaction is a bimolecular nucleophilic substitution reaction occurring in a single step with inversion of configuration.

questions.text: Why tertiary alkyl halides undergo SN1 reaction?
questions.answer: Because tertiary carbocations are more stable due to inductive and hyperconjugation effects.

questions.text: Arrange alkyl halides in increasing order of reactivity towards SN2 reaction.
questions.answer: Tertiary < Secondary < Primary < Methyl.

questions.text: Explain preparation, properties and uses of chloroform.
questions.answer: Chloroform is prepared by chlorination of methane; it is a colourless liquid used as solvent and anesthetic (earlier).

questions.text: Explain preparation and uses of iodoform.
questions.answer: Iodoform is prepared by reaction of ethanol with iodine in presence of alkali and used as antiseptic.

questions.text: Alkyl iodides are more reactive than alkyl chlorides.
questions.answer: Because C–I bond is weaker than C–Cl bond.

questions.text: Polar solvents favour SN1 reaction.
questions.answer: Because they stabilize carbocation intermediate.

chapters.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
chapters.description: Nomenclature, preparation, physical and chemical properties of alcohols, phenols and ethers; acidity of alcohols and phenols; Williamson ether synthesis.
learningObjectives: Name and classify alcohols, phenols and ethers.
Describe methods of preparation of these compounds.
Explain acidity of phenols and compare with alcohols.
Discuss important reactions such as dehydration, oxidation and electrophilic substitution.
Explain Williamson synthesis and cleavage of ethers.

questions.text: Which of the following will show highest boiling point?
questions.answer: Ethanol

questions.text: Give IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃C–OH.
questions.answer: 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

questions.text: Explain why phenol is more acidic than ethanol.
questions.answer: Phenoxide ion formed after deprotonation is resonance-stabilized, whereas ethoxide ion is not; this makes phenol more acidic.

questions.text: Dehydration of ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K gives mainly:
questions.answer: Ethene

questions.text: Write equation for Williamson synthesis of ethoxybenzene (phenetole).
questions.answer: C₂H₅Br + C₆H₅O⁻Na⁺ → C₆H₅–O–C₂H₅ + NaBr.

questions.text: Describe electrophilic substitution reactions of phenol.
questions.answer: Phenol undergoes nitration, halogenation and sulphonation more readily than benzene due to +M effect of –OH. It is o,p-directing: nitration gives o- and p-nitrophenols; bromination gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol in absence of solvent.

questions.text: Which reagent is used to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols?
questions.answer: Lucas reagent

questions.text: What happens when anisole reacts with HI?
questions.answer: Anisole undergoes cleavage to give phenol and iodomethane: C₆H₅–O–CH₃ + HI → C₆H₅–OH + CH₃I.

questions.text: Explain oxidation reactions of primary and secondary alcohols.
questions.answer: Primary alcohols oxidize to aldehydes and further to acids (e.g., ethanol → ethanal → ethanoic acid). Secondary alcohols oxidize to ketones (e.g., isopropanol → acetone). Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation under mild conditions.

questions.text: 0.92 g of ethanol is completely burned. Calculate moles of CO₂ formed. (Molar mass of ethanol = 46 g mol⁻¹).
questions.answer: Moles of ethanol = 0.92/46 = 0.02 mol. Combustion: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. Moles of CO₂ = 2 × 0.02 = 0.04 mol.

questions.text: Which of the following alcohols gives Lucas test immediately?
questions.answer: Propan-2-ol

questions.text: Phenol is more acidic than alcohol because:
questions.answer: Phenoxide ion is resonance stabilized

questions.text: Define alcohol.
questions.answer: Alcohols are organic compounds in which hydroxyl group (–OH) is attached to a saturated carbon atom.

questions.text: What are phenols?
questions.answer: Phenols are organic compounds in which hydroxyl group is directly attached to an aromatic ring.

questions.text: Explain acidic nature of phenol.
questions.answer: Phenol is acidic due to resonance stabilization of phenoxide ion formed after loss of proton.

questions.text: What is Williamson ether synthesis?
questions.answer: Williamson ether synthesis is the preparation of ethers by reaction of alkyl halide with sodium alkoxide.

questions.text: Why phenol does not give Lucas test?
questions.answer: Because phenol does not form stable carbocation due to aromatic ring.

questions.text: Arrange alcohols in increasing order of acidity.
questions.answer: Tertiary < Secondary < Primary alcohols.

questions.text: Explain preparation, properties and uses of ethanol.
questions.answer: Ethanol is prepared by fermentation; it shows hydrogen bonding and is used as solvent, fuel and antiseptic.

questions.text: Explain preparation and reactions of phenol.
questions.answer: Phenol is prepared from chlorobenzene; it undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions.

questions.text: Phenol reacts with sodium hydroxide but alcohol does not.
questions.answer: Because phenol is acidic enough to react with NaOH while alcohol is not.

questions.text: Ethers are less reactive than alcohols.
questions.answer: Because ethers do not have active hydrogen and are less polar.

chapters.title: Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic acids
chapters.description: Nomenclature, preparation and reactions of aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids; nucleophilic addition, oxidation–reduction and strength of acids.
topics: Nomenclature and Structure of Carbonyl Group
Preparation and Properties of Carboxylic Acids
learningObjectives: Write IUPAC names and structures of aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids.
Explain nucleophilic addition reactions of carbonyl compounds.
Compare reactivity of aldehydes and ketones.
Describe methods of preparation and reactions of carboxylic acids.
Explain factors affecting acidity of carboxylic acids.

questions.text: The functional group present in aldehydes is:
questions.answer: –CHO

questions.text: Give IUPAC name of CH₃–CO–CH₃.
questions.answer: Propan-2-one (acetone).

questions.text: State any two differences between aldehydes and ketones.
questions.answer: Aldehydes have –CHO group at end of chain while ketones have >C=O within chain; aldehydes are generally more reactive and are easily oxidized to acids, whereas ketones resist oxidation.

questions.text: Benedict’s solution is used to distinguish:
questions.answer: Aldehydes and ketones

questions.text: Write the reaction of acetaldehyde with hydrogen cyanide.
questions.answer: CH₃–CHO + HCN → CH₃–CH(OH)–CN (cyanohydrin).

questions.text: Explain the mechanism of nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl group.
questions.answer: First, nucleophile attacks electrophilic carbon of C=O, forming a tetrahedral intermediate. Then protonation of oxygen (or deprotonation of nucleophile) occurs to give addition product. Polarization of C=O makes carbon susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

questions.text: The reaction of carboxylic acid with alcohol in presence of conc. H₂SO₄ is called:
questions.answer: Esterification

questions.text: Why are carboxylic acids stronger acids than alcohols?
questions.answer: Carboxylate ion is resonance-stabilized with negative charge delocalized over two oxygen atoms, whereas alkoxide ion is not; this stabilizes conjugate base and increases acidity.

questions.text: Explain Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction.
questions.answer: HVZ reaction is α-halogenation of carboxylic acids. Carboxylic acid is converted to its acyl halide with PCl₃/Cl₂, then halogen substitutes α-hydrogen, followed by hydrolysis to give α-halo acid.

questions.text: 0.1 mol of acetic acid is neutralized by NaOH releasing 5.7 kJ heat. Calculate molar enthalpy of neutralization.
questions.answer: ΔHneutralization = −5.7 kJ / 0.1 mol = −57 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.text: Which functional group is present in aldehydes?
questions.answer: –CHO

questions.text: Which of the following does not give Tollens’ test?
questions.answer: Acetone

questions.text: Define aldehydes.
questions.answer: Aldehydes are organic compounds containing the functional group –CHO.

questions.text: What are ketones?
questions.answer: Ketones are organic compounds containing carbonyl group (–CO–) bonded to two carbon atoms.

questions.text: Explain nucleophilic addition reaction of aldehydes.
questions.answer: Aldehydes undergo nucleophilic addition due to polar C=O bond, where nucleophile attacks carbonyl carbon.

questions.text: Distinguish between aldehydes and ketones.
questions.answer: Aldehydes have –CHO group and are easily oxidised; ketones have –CO– group and resist oxidation.

questions.text: Why aldehydes are more reactive than ketones?
questions.answer: Because aldehydes have less steric hindrance and stronger positive charge on carbonyl carbon.

questions.text: Give chemical test to distinguish aldehyde and ketone.
questions.answer: Tollens’ test gives silver mirror with aldehydes but not with ketones.

questions.text: Explain preparation and reactions of formaldehyde.
questions.answer: Formaldehyde is prepared by oxidation of methanol and shows nucleophilic addition and oxidation reactions.

questions.text: Explain preparation and properties of acetic acid.
questions.answer: Acetic acid is prepared by oxidation of ethanol; it shows acidic reactions and esterification.

questions.text: Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenols.
questions.answer: Because carboxylate ion is more stabilized by resonance than phenoxide ion.

questions.text: Ketones do not give Tollens’ test.
questions.answer: Because ketones are not easily oxidised.

chapters.title: Amines
chapters.description: Classification, nomenclature, methods of preparation, basic character, reactions and identification of primary, secondary and tertiary amines.
topics: Basicity of Amines and Factors Affecting It
Aromatic Diazonium Salts and Their Reactions
Distinction between Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Amines
learningObjectives: Classify and name aliphatic and aromatic amines.
Describe various methods of preparation of amines.
Explain basic nature of amines and compare strengths.
Discuss important reactions including diazotization and coupling.
Use chemical tests to distinguish different classes of amines.

questions.text: Which of the following is a secondary amine?
questions.answer: (CH₃)₂NH

questions.text: Write IUPAC name of aniline.
questions.answer: Benzenamine.

questions.text: State carbylamine reaction.
questions.answer: Primary amines on heating with chloroform and alcoholic KOH form isocyanides (carbylamines) with foul smell; used as a test for primary amines.

questions.text: Which amine is most basic in aqueous solution?
questions.answer: (C₂H₅)₂NH

questions.text: What is diazotization? Write equation for diazotization of aniline.
questions.answer: Conversion of primary aromatic amine into diazonium salt with nitrous acid at low temperature. C₆H₅NH₂ + HNO₂ + HCl → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + 2H₂O.

questions.text: Explain why aniline is less basic than ethylamine.
questions.answer: In aniline, lone pair on nitrogen is delocalized into benzene ring by resonance, reducing availability for protonation. In ethylamine, lone pair is localized and +I effect of ethyl group increases electron density, making it more basic.

questions.text: Which reagent is used to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amines?
questions.answer: HNO₂

questions.text: What is coupling reaction of diazonium salts?
questions.answer: Aromatic diazonium salts react with phenols or aromatic amines to form azo compounds with –N=N– linkage, often coloured dyes.

questions.text: Explain Gabriel phthalimide synthesis for preparation of primary amines.
questions.answer: Phthalimide reacts with alcoholic KOH to form potassium salt, which undergoes nucleophilic substitution with alkyl halide to form N-alkyl phthalimide. Hydrolysis of this gives primary amine and phthalic acid.

questions.text: 0.93 g of an amine neutralizes 0.1 mol of HCl. Determine molar mass of the amine assuming it is monobasic.
questions.answer: If it neutralizes 0.1 mol HCl, moles of amine = 0.1 mol. Molar mass = 0.93 / 0.1 = 9.3 g mol⁻¹ (hypothetical example for calculation practice).

questions.text: Which of the following is a primary amine?
questions.answer: CH3NH2

questions.text: Aniline on diazotisation gives:
questions.answer: Benzene diazonium chloride

questions.text: Define amines.
questions.answer: Amines are organic compounds derived from ammonia by replacement of one or more hydrogen atoms by alkyl or aryl groups.

questions.text: What are aromatic amines?
questions.answer: Aromatic amines are amines in which amino group is directly attached to an aromatic ring.

questions.text: Explain basic nature of amines.
questions.answer: Amines are basic due to availability of lone pair of electrons on nitrogen atom which can accept a proton.

questions.text: Arrange amines in increasing order of basic strength.
questions.answer: Aromatic amines < Primary aliphatic < Secondary aliphatic < Tertiary aliphatic.

questions.text: Why aniline is less basic than aliphatic amines?
questions.answer: Because lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised into benzene ring by resonance.

questions.text: Explain Hoffmann bromamide reaction.
questions.answer: In Hoffmann bromamide reaction, amide is converted to amine with one carbon less using bromine and alkali.

questions.text: Explain preparation and reactions of aniline.
questions.answer: Aniline is prepared by reduction of nitrobenzene and undergoes diazotisation and electrophilic substitution reactions.

questions.text: Explain diazotisation and coupling reactions.
questions.answer: Diazotisation converts aromatic amine into diazonium salt which undergoes coupling to form azo dyes.

questions.text: Aniline is ortho-para directing in electrophilic substitution reactions.
questions.answer: Because –NH2 group activates benzene ring and directs incoming electrophile to ortho and para positions.

questions.text: Diazonium salts are prepared at low temperature.
questions.answer: Because diazonium salts are unstable at higher temperatures.

chapters.title: Biomolecules
chapters.description: Carbohydrates, amino acids, proteins, vitamins and nucleic acids – their classification, structure and biological importance.
learningObjectives: Classify carbohydrates and represent monosaccharides using Fischer and Haworth projections.
Explain structure of amino acids and formation of peptides.
Describe different levels of protein structure.
Differentiate between DNA and RNA in structure and function.
Explain role of vitamins and enzymes in biological systems.

questions.text: Glucose is an example of:
questions.answer: Monosaccharide

questions.text: What is an essential amino acid?
questions.answer: Amino acid that cannot be synthesized by the human body and must be supplied through diet is called essential amino acid.

questions.text: Define peptide bond.
questions.answer: Peptide bond is an amide linkage formed between –COOH group of one amino acid and –NH₂ group of another with elimination of water (–CO–NH–).

questions.text: Which of the following is a storage polysaccharide in animals?
questions.answer: Glycogen

questions.text: Explain primary, secondary and tertiary structure of proteins.
questions.answer: Primary: linear sequence of amino acids. Secondary: regular folding into α-helix or β-pleated sheet due to hydrogen bonding. Tertiary: further folding into specific 3D shape stabilized by H-bonds, disulphide bonds, hydrophobic interactions and ionic interactions.

questions.text: Name the vitamin whose deficiency causes scurvy and give its chemical name.
questions.answer: Vitamin C; chemical name ascorbic acid.

questions.text: The sugar present in RNA is:
questions.answer: Ribose

questions.text: Differentiate between DNA and RNA (any three points).
questions.answer: DNA has deoxyribose sugar, RNA has ribose. DNA contains bases A, G, C, T while RNA has A, G, C, U. DNA is double stranded helix, RNA usually single stranded. DNA is genetic material; RNA involved in protein synthesis.

questions.text: What is an enzyme? Mention any one characteristic.
questions.answer: Enzymes are biocatalysts which speed up biochemical reactions. They are highly specific for substrate and work under mild conditions.

questions.text: If a tripeptide is made from three different amino acids A, B and C, how many different sequences are possible?
questions.answer: Number of permutations of 3 different amino acids = 3! = 6 sequences.

questions.text: Which of the following is a reducing sugar?
questions.answer: Glucose

questions.text: The linkage present in proteins is:
questions.answer: Peptide

questions.text: Define carbohydrates.
questions.answer: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or substances that yield them on hydrolysis.

questions.text: What are amino acids?
questions.answer: Amino acids are organic compounds containing both amino (–NH2) and carboxyl (–COOH) groups.

questions.text: Explain denaturation of proteins.
questions.answer: Denaturation is the loss of biological activity of proteins due to change in structure caused by heat, pH or chemicals.

questions.text: Distinguish between glucose and fructose.
questions.answer: Glucose is an aldohexose while fructose is a ketohexose.

questions.text: Why sucrose is a non-reducing sugar?
questions.answer: Because both aldehyde and ketone groups are involved in glycosidic bond formation.

questions.text: What is zwitter ion?
questions.answer: Zwitter ion is a dipolar ion having both positive and negative charges in the same molecule.

questions.text: Explain classification of carbohydrates with examples.
questions.answer: Carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides with suitable examples.

questions.text: Explain structure and functions of proteins.
questions.answer: Proteins are polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds and perform structural and catalytic functions.

questions.text: Proteins are optically active.
questions.answer: Because they contain chiral carbon atoms in amino acids.

questions.text: Starch gives blue colour with iodine.
questions.answer: Because iodine molecules get trapped in helical structure of starch.

chapters.title: Introduction to Polymer Chemistry
chapters.description: Classification of polymers, addition and condensation polymerization, natural and synthetic polymers, properties and uses of important polymers and biodegradable polymers.
topics: Types Based on Source and Structure
learningObjectives: Classify polymers on different bases such as source, structure and mode of polymerization.
Differentiate between addition and condensation polymerization.
Explain preparation and properties of important polymers like PVC, teflon, nylon and bakelite.
Describe vulcanization of rubber and its advantages.
Discuss significance of biodegradable polymers.

questions.text: The polymer of tetrafluoroethene is known as:
questions.answer: Teflon

questions.text: Define monomer and give one example.
questions.answer: Monomer is a small molecule that combines with similar molecules to form a polymer; e.g., ethene is monomer of polyethene.

questions.text: Differentiate between thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics.
questions.answer: Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be reshaped; thermosetting plastics harden permanently on heating and cannot be remoulded.

questions.text: Which of the following is a condensation polymer?
questions.answer: Nylon-6,6

questions.text: Explain vulcanization of rubber.
questions.answer: Natural rubber is heated with sulphur and accelerators. Sulphur forms cross-links between polyisoprene chains, increasing elasticity, tensile strength and resistance to temperature changes.

questions.text: What is a copolymer? Give one example.
questions.answer: Polymer formed from two or more different monomers is copolymer; e.g., Buna-S from butadiene and styrene.

questions.text: Which of the following is a biodegradable polymer?
questions.answer: PHBV

questions.text: State any two disadvantages of synthetic polymers.
questions.answer: They are often non-biodegradable causing environmental pollution; burning them may release toxic gases.

questions.text: Describe the preparation and uses of bakelite.
questions.answer: Bakelite is formed by condensation polymerization of phenol and formaldehyde in presence of acid or base catalyst, followed by cross-linking. It is a thermosetting plastic used in electrical switches, plugs, handles of utensils etc.

questions.text: If the average degree of polymerization of a polymer sample is 1000 and molecular mass of its monomer is 28 g mol⁻¹, calculate the approximate molecular mass of the polymer.
questions.answer: Molecular mass of polymer ≈ 1000 × 28 = 2.8 × 10⁴ g mol⁻¹.

questions.text: Which of the following is a natural polymer?
questions.answer: Cellulose

questions.text: The polymer obtained from ethene is:
questions.answer: Polythene

questions.text: Define polymer.
questions.answer: Polymer is a high molecular mass compound formed by repetition of small units called monomers.

questions.text: What is monomer?
questions.answer: Monomer is a small molecule that combines repeatedly to form a polymer.

questions.text: Explain addition polymerisation.
questions.answer: Addition polymerisation involves successive addition of monomers without elimination of small molecules.

questions.text: Explain condensation polymerisation.
questions.answer: Condensation polymerisation involves elimination of small molecules like water or HCl during polymer formation.

questions.text: What are thermoplastics?
questions.answer: Thermoplastics are polymers that soften on heating and harden on cooling repeatedly.

questions.text: What are thermosetting polymers?
questions.answer: Thermosetting polymers are polymers that become permanently hard on heating.

questions.text: Explain preparation, properties and uses of nylon-6,6.
questions.answer: Nylon-6,6 is prepared by condensation of hexamethylene diamine and adipic acid and is used in fibres and ropes.

questions.text: Explain preparation and uses of Bakelite.
questions.answer: Bakelite is prepared by condensation of phenol and formaldehyde and is used in electrical switches.

questions.text: Polythene is an addition polymer.
questions.answer: Because it is formed by addition of ethene monomers without elimination of small molecules.

questions.text: Thermosetting plastics cannot be recycled.
questions.answer: Because they have cross-linked structure and cannot be remoulded on heating.

chapters.title: Green Chemistry and Nanochemistry
chapters.description: Principles of green chemistry, sustainable development, introduction to nanoscience and nanomaterials, methods of synthesis and applications.
topics: Concept and Need of Green Chemistry
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and importance of green chemistry.
State and illustrate twelve principles of green chemistry.
Describe atom economy and its calculation.
Explain basic methods for synthesis of nanomaterials.
Discuss unique properties and applications of nanomaterials with awareness of safety aspects.

questions.text: Green chemistry aims primarily at:
options: Minimizing use and generation of hazardous substances
questions.answer: Minimizing use and generation of hazardous substances

questions.text: What is atom economy?
questions.answer: Atom economy is the percentage of reactant atoms that are incorporated into the desired product; it is calculated as (molar mass of desired product / sum of molar masses of all reactants) × 100.

questions.text: Name any two green solvents.
questions.answer: Water, supercritical CO₂, ionic liquids (any two).

questions.text: Which of the following is a bottom-up approach in nanomaterial synthesis?
questions.answer: Sol–gel method

questions.text: Write any four principles of green chemistry and explain them briefly.
questions.answer: Examples: (i) Prevention: better to prevent waste than treat it. (ii) Atom economy: design processes maximizing incorporation of materials into product. (iii) Use of safer solvents and auxiliaries. (iv) Energy efficiency: conduct reactions at ambient temperature and pressure when possible.

questions.text: What are nanomaterials? Give typical size range.
questions.answer: Materials with at least one dimension in the nanometer range, typically 1–100 nm, are called nanomaterials.

questions.text: Unique properties of nanomaterials are mainly due to:
options: Large surface area to volume ratio and quantum effects
questions.answer: Large surface area to volume ratio and quantum effects

questions.text: Explain any three applications of nanomaterials.
questions.answer: Applications: (i) In medicine for targeted drug delivery and imaging. (ii) In electronics for smaller, faster devices using nanotubes and quantum dots. (iii) In catalysis, nanoparticles offer high surface area and improved activity in environmental remediation.

questions.text: Give one example of a green chemistry practice in industry.
questions.answer: Use of supercritical CO₂ as a solvent instead of organic solvents in dry cleaning or extraction processes is a green practice.

questions.text: In a reaction A + 2B → C + D, total molar mass of reactants is 150 g and that of desired product C is 90 g. Calculate atom economy.
Green chemistry aims at:
questions.answer: Reducing environmental pollution

questions.text: The size range of nanoparticles is:
Define green chemistry.
questions.answer: Green chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances.

questions.text: What is nanochemistry?
questions.answer: Nanochemistry deals with synthesis, properties and applications of materials at nanoscale.

questions.text: State any two principles of green chemistry.
questions.answer: Prevention of waste and use of safer solvents and reaction conditions.

questions.text: What is atom economy?
questions.answer: Atom economy is the measure of efficiency of a chemical reaction in terms of utilisation of atoms of reactants into products.

questions.text: Why nanomaterials show different properties than bulk materials?
questions.answer: Due to large surface area to volume ratio and quantum size effects.

questions.text: Give two applications of nanoparticles.
questions.answer: Used in drug delivery and catalysis.

questions.text: Explain principles of green chemistry with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Green chemistry principles include waste prevention, atom economy, safer solvents and renewable feedstocks with examples.

questions.text: Explain synthesis and applications of nanoparticles.
questions.answer: Nanoparticles are synthesized by top-down and bottom-up approaches and used in medicine, electronics and catalysis.

questions.text: Green chemistry is sustainable chemistry.
questions.answer: Because it reduces environmental impact and conserves resources.

questions.text: Nanoparticles are more reactive than bulk materials.
questions.answer: Because they have larger surface area relative to volume.

chapters.title: Population: Part 1
chapters.description: Concept of population distribution, density of population, physical and human factors affecting distribution, and an introduction to population growth.
topics: Human and economic factors affecting population distribution
learningObjectives: Define population distribution and population density.
Identify regions of high and low population density in the world.
Explain how relief, climate, soil and water affect population distribution.
Explain how agriculture, mining, transport, urbanisation and government policies affect population distribution.
Relate population growth with birth rate and death rate in a basic way.

questions.text: Population density is defined as:
options: Total population divided by total area
Total area divided by total population
Total population multiplied by total area
questions.answer: Total population divided by total area

questions.text: Name any two regions of the world which are sparsely populated and state one common reason.
questions.answer: Examples: Sahara desert and Arctic region. Common reason: extreme climatic conditions make human life difficult.

questions.text: Explain how relief (landforms) influence population distribution.
questions.answer: Flat and low-lying plains favour agriculture, transport and settlement, so they have high population density, whereas mountains and steep slopes hinder agriculture and transport, so they have low population density.

questions.text: Which of the following regions generally has the highest population density?
questions.answer: River valleys and deltas

questions.text: State any two human (non-physical) factors responsible for high population density.
questions.answer: Examples: developed transportation network, industrialisation, availability of employment opportunities, urbanisation.

questions.text: A country has a population of 50 million and an area of 250,000 sq km. Calculate its population density.
questions.answer: Density = 50,000,000 ÷ 250,000 = 200 persons per sq km.

questions.text: Explain with suitable examples how climate affects population distribution in the world.
questions.answer: Equable climates (e.g., Western Europe) attract dense population as agriculture and living conditions are favourable. Extreme hot deserts (Sahara, Arabian desert) and cold regions (Greenland, Antarctica) are sparsely populated due to lack of water, difficult agriculture and harsh living conditions. Very humid equatorial regions like Amazon basin also remain sparsely populated due to dense forests and diseases.

questions.text: What is meant by distribution of population?
questions.answer: Distribution of population refers to the way people are spread or arranged over the Earth’s surface.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a physical factor affecting population distribution?
questions.answer: Government policy

questions.text: Distinguish between areas of high population density and areas of low population density on any three points.
questions.answer: Areas of high density: usually plains/coasts, fertile soils, developed transport, intensive agriculture/industry and urbanisation. Areas of low density: mountains/deserts/polar regions, infertile or thin soils, poor accessibility, limited economic activities and smaller/nucleated settlements.

questions.text: Broad base in population pyramid indicates higher number of children.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
questions.answer: Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.text: Arrange according to increase in age.
questions.answer: Children → Young people → Adults → Old people

questions.text: Population distribution is uneven.
questions.answer: Population distribution depends on physical, economic and social factors like climate, relief, soil, industries and transport.

questions.text: Distinguish between birth rate and death rate.
questions.answer: Birth rate refers to number of live births per thousand population per year, while death rate refers to number of deaths per thousand population per year.

questions.text: Explain uneven distribution of population with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Population is dense in fertile plains and industrial regions while sparse in deserts, mountains and polar regions.

questions.text: Show a country in second phase of demographic transition on the world map.
questions.howToSaveImage: Save map question image under /public/maps with standardized filename and reference it using imageUrl.
questions.answer: Example: Nigeria / India (as per map)

questions.text: Draw pyramid of underdeveloped countries.
questions.howToSaveImage: Scan diagram from answer key or textbook and store under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Broad base and narrow apex showing high birth rate.

questions.text: Explain the physical factors affecting the distribution of population.
questions.answer: Physical factors include climate, relief, soil, water availability and natural vegetation which influence settlement and population density.

chapters.title: Population: Part 2
chapters.description: Population composition including age structure, sex ratio, literacy, occupational structure, rural–urban composition, demographic dividend and migration.
learningObjectives: Interpret different types of population pyramids.
Explain age structure and dependency ratio.
Define sex ratio and discuss its spatial variation.
Explain the idea of demographic dividend with reference to India.
Classify types of migration and identify push and pull factors.

questions.text: Sex ratio in India is expressed as:
questions.answer: Number of females per 1000 males

questions.text: What is meant by age structure of population?
questions.answer: Age structure refers to the distribution of population in different age groups such as children, working-age people and the aged in a given region.

questions.text: Differentiate between expansive and constrictive population pyramids in brief.
questions.answer: Expansive pyramid has a broad base and narrow top, showing high birth and death rates and large child population. Constrictive pyramid has a narrow base and relatively wider upper part, showing low birth rate and larger proportion of older people.

questions.text: A country with very low birth and death rates and almost equal percentage in all age groups will show which type of pyramid?
questions.answer: Stationary

questions.text: Define demographic dividend.
questions.answer: Demographic dividend is the potential economic benefit that arises from a change in a country’s age structure, when the share of working-age population becomes larger than the dependent population.

questions.text: Explain any three conditions necessary for a country like India to effectively utilise its demographic dividend.
questions.answer: Conditions: (1) Investment in quality education and skill development so that working-age people are employable. (2) Adequate job opportunities through industrial and service sector growth. (3) Good health facilities to keep workforce productive. (4) Gender equality and higher participation of women in labour force. (Any three explained.)

questions.text: Which of the following is a pull factor of migration?
options: Higher wages and better jobs in destination
questions.answer: Higher wages and better jobs in destination

questions.text: What is internal migration? Give one example.
questions.answer: Migration within the boundaries of the same country is called internal migration, e.g., a person moving from rural Odisha to Mumbai for work.

questions.text: Describe the effects of migration on the donor region and the recipient region (any three effects each).
questions.answer: Donor region: (i) Loss of working-age population can reduce production. (ii) Remittances sent by migrants can improve family income. (iii) Change in sex ratio and age structure as many young males move out. Recipient region: (i) Pressure on housing, water and services. (ii) Availability of cheap labour and cultural diversity. (iii) Possible growth of slums and social tensions if planning is poor.

questions.text: In a town, there are 52,000 males and 49,400 females. Calculate the sex ratio.
questions.answer: Sex ratio = (49,400 ÷ 52,000) × 1000 ≈ 950 females per 1000 males.

questions.text: The process of movement of population from rural to urban areas is called:
questions.answer: Migration

questions.text: Which of the following is a push factor of migration?
questions.answer: Natural calamities

questions.text: Define migration.
questions.answer: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another for a temporary or permanent period.

questions.text: What is population density?
questions.answer: Population density is the number of persons living per square kilometre area.

questions.text: State the factors affecting population density.
questions.answer: Physical factors like climate, relief and soil and economic factors like industries, transport and urbanisation affect population density.

questions.text: Explain pull factors of migration.
questions.answer: Pull factors include employment opportunities, better education, healthcare, higher wages and urban amenities.

questions.text: Show any two high population density regions in the world map.
questions.howToSaveImage: Store scanned map question image in /public/maps and reference it using imageUrl.
questions.answer: East Asia and South Asia

questions.text: Draw a diagram showing rural to urban migration.
questions.howToSaveImage: Create or scan a simple migration flow diagram and save under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Flow of population from villages to cities due to push and pull factors.

questions.text: Explain causes and effects of migration.
questions.answer: Migration occurs due to push and pull factors like poverty, unemployment, education and urbanisation. It affects population distribution, urban growth and socio-economic conditions.

chapters.title: Human Settlements and Land Use
chapters.description: Types and patterns of human settlements, factors affecting their location and growth, land use types, and the relationship between settlements and land use.
topics: Concept and types of human settlements
Factors affecting location and growth of settlements
Concept of land use and land cover
Types of rural and urban land use
learningObjectives: Classify settlements into rural and urban with examples.
Describe different settlement patterns and relate them to physical factors.
Explain major types of land use in rural and urban areas.
Analyse how transport, relief and water availability influence settlement location.
Discuss the need for proper land use planning.

questions.text: A settlement in which houses are closely spaced around a central point like a market or temple is called:
questions.answer: Nucleated settlement

questions.text: Differentiate between rural and urban settlements on any two points.
questions.answer: Rural settlements: mainly engaged in primary activities, low building density and more open space. Urban settlements: mainly engaged in secondary and tertiary activities, high building density and better infrastructure.

questions.text: What is land use? Give two examples of land use in rural areas.
questions.answer: Land use refers to the purposes for which land is used by humans, such as agriculture, settlement, industry or recreation. In rural areas examples are crop cultivation and grazing land.

questions.text: Which of the following factors is most responsible for linear settlements?
questions.answer: Along transport routes or rivers

questions.text: Explain any three physical and any three human factors affecting the location and growth of human settlements.
questions.answer: Physical: (i) Relief – plains favour larger settlements; steep slopes discourage them. (ii) Climate – moderate climate attracts people, extreme climate discourages. (iii) Water – proximity to rivers, lakes and groundwater supports settlements. Human: (i) Transport routes like highways and railways stimulate growth. (ii) Availability of jobs in industries or services. (iii) Government policies such as new town development or relocation schemes.

questions.text: Why do some mountainous regions still have dense settlements despite difficult terrain?
questions.answer: Because they may have valuable resources (minerals, tourism), fertile valley floors, or strategic importance that offers employment and services, attracting population despite harsh relief.

questions.text: Conversion of agricultural land into built-up area is an example of:
options: Both land use and land cover change
questions.answer: Both land use and land cover change

questions.text: In a village, the total area is 500 hectares. Out of this, 300 ha is under agriculture, 50 ha under forest, 100 ha under settlement and roads, and 50 ha is wasteland. Calculate the percentage of land under agriculture and settlement.
questions.answer: Agriculture: (300 ÷ 500) × 100 = 60%. Settlement and roads: (100 ÷ 500) × 100 = 20%.

questions.text: List any two problems created due to unplanned urban land use.
questions.answer: Examples: traffic congestion, slums, shortage of open spaces, pollution, overburdened water supply and drainage systems.

questions.text: Describe the need for land use planning in a rapidly growing city.
questions.answer: Land use planning ensures proper location of residential, industrial and commercial areas, protects environmentally sensitive zones, provides adequate transport and public services, prevents haphazard growth and slums, and helps maintain a balance between development and quality of life.

questions.text: Which of the following is a rural settlement pattern?
questions.answer: All of the above

questions.text: The settlement pattern found along rivers and roads is:
questions.answer: Linear

questions.text: Define human settlement.
questions.answer: Human settlement is a place where people establish their dwellings and carry out economic and social activities.

questions.text: What is land use?
questions.answer: Land use refers to the way land is utilized for various purposes like agriculture, settlement, industry and transport.

questions.text: Explain factors affecting rural settlements.
questions.answer: Physical factors like relief, climate, soil and water availability and human factors like agriculture and transport affect rural settlements.

questions.text: State the factors affecting land use.
questions.answer: Physical factors include relief, climate and soil; economic and social factors include population, technology and government policies.

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram of compact settlement.
questions.howToSaveImage: Scan or draw a labelled compact settlement diagram and store it under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Houses closely built with common facilities at centre.

questions.text: Show an urban settlement on the map of India.
questions.howToSaveImage: Store scanned India map under /public/maps and mark a major city.
questions.answer: Mumbai / Delhi / Kolkata (any one)

questions.text: Explain types of rural settlements with suitable diagrams.
questions.answer: Rural settlements are compact, linear and dispersed. Each type depends on relief, water supply and agricultural practices.

chapters.title: Primary Economic Activities
chapters.description: Nature and types of primary activities like agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining, their spatial distribution and recent changes.
topics: Meaning and types of primary activities
Fishing and forestry as primary activities
Recent changes and modernisation in primary sector
learningObjectives: Define primary economic activities with examples.
Differentiate between subsistence and commercial agriculture.
Explain important types of agriculture and their regional examples.
Describe global distribution of fishing, forestry and mining regions in brief.
Discuss problems and changes in primary economic activities.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a primary activity?
questions.answer: Software development

questions.text: State any two differences between subsistence farming and commercial farming.
questions.answer: Subsistence: small land holdings, use of family labour, production mainly for own consumption. Commercial: large farms, hired labour, production for market and profit.

questions.text: What is plantation agriculture? Give two examples of plantation crops.
questions.answer: Plantation agriculture is a type of commercial farming where a single crop is grown on a large estate using modern techniques and wage labour; examples: tea, coffee, rubber, oil palm.

questions.text: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
options: Rice – intensive subsistence farming in monsoon Asia
Maize – shifting cultivation crop in Arctic
questions.answer: Rice – intensive subsistence farming in monsoon Asia

questions.text: Explain the factors affecting the development of fishing industry in the world.
questions.answer: Factors: (i) Physical – continental shelf, cold and warm current convergence, nutrient-rich waters. (ii) Climatic – suitable temperatures and absence of storms during fishing seasons. (iii) Economic – demand in domestic and foreign markets, availability of refrigeration and processing.
