(iv) Technological – modern trawlers, sonar, cold storage. (v) Government policies like subsidies and exclusive economic zones.

questions.text: Mention two major problems faced by farmers in India.
questions.answer: Examples: dependence on monsoon, fragmentation of land holdings, lack of irrigation facilities, low use of modern inputs, low and fluctuating market prices.

questions.text: Mining of which mineral is most important in the Chota Nagpur plateau?
questions.answer: Iron ore and coal

questions.text: A farmer owns 2 hectares of land. On one hectare he grows food grains only for his family, and on the other hectare he grows sugarcane for selling to a factory. Calculate the percentage of his land under subsistence and commercial farming.
questions.answer: Subsistence: (1 ÷ 2) × 100 = 50%. Commercial: (1 ÷ 2) × 100 = 50%.

questions.text: What is shifting cultivation? Mention one region where it is still practised.
questions.answer: Shifting cultivation is an agricultural system in which a plot of land is cleared, cultivated for a few years and then abandoned for another plot; examples: North-East India, Amazon basin, parts of Congo basin.

questions.text: Discuss any three environmental problems created by intensive exploitation of primary resources like forests and minerals.
questions.answer: Problems: (i) Deforestation leading to soil erosion, loss of biodiversity and climate change. (ii) Over-mining causing land degradation, subsidence and pollution of water bodies. (iii) Overfishing resulting in depletion of fish stocks and ecological imbalance in marine ecosystems.

questions.text: Which of the following is a primary economic activity?
questions.answer: Fishing

questions.text: Which type of farming is mainly practised in densely populated regions?
questions.answer: Intensive farming

questions.text: Define primary economic activities.
questions.answer: Primary economic activities involve extraction of natural resources directly from the Earth such as agriculture, fishing, forestry and mining.

questions.text: What is shifting cultivation?
questions.answer: Shifting cultivation is a farming method where land is cleared, cultivated for a few years and then abandoned to regain fertility.

questions.text: State the characteristics of commercial farming.
questions.answer: Commercial farming is market-oriented, uses modern technology, high capital input and produces crops for sale.

questions.text: Explain subsistence farming.
questions.answer: Subsistence farming is practised to meet the needs of the farmer’s family using traditional tools and methods.

questions.text: Show major wheat producing regions of the world on the map.
questions.howToSaveImage: Store scanned world map in /public/maps and mark major wheat belts.
questions.answer: North America, Europe, Asia

questions.text: Draw a diagram showing shifting cultivation.
questions.howToSaveImage: Create or scan a simple labelled diagram and store under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Forest cleared → cultivated → abandoned

questions.text: Explain different types of farming with examples.
questions.answer: Farming types include subsistence, commercial, intensive and shifting farming, each with distinct characteristics and examples.

chapters.title: Secondary Economic Activities
chapters.description: Nature of secondary activities, types of industries, factors affecting industrial location, major industrial regions of the world and emerging trends.
topics: Definition of secondary activities and industries
Classification of industries (size, ownership, raw material, product)
Major industrial regions of the world
learningObjectives: Define secondary economic activities and classify industries.
Explain physical and human factors responsible for industrial location.
Identify major industrial regions of the world and India on a map.
Describe characteristics of footloose and information technology industries.
Discuss environmental problems caused by industries.

questions.text: Which of the following is a secondary activity?
questions.answer: Steel manufacturing

questions.text: State any two factors affecting the location of industries.
questions.answer: Examples: availability of raw materials, power supply, labour, transport facilities, market, government policies.

questions.text: What are footloose industries? Give one example.
questions.answer: Footloose industries are those which are not tied to any specific raw material or market location and can be located in a wide choice of places; example: electronics assembly, software industry.

questions.text: The Ruhr region of Germany is famous for:
questions.answer: Iron and steel industry

questions.text: Explain how market and transport facilities influence industrial location.
questions.answer: Industries producing bulky or perishable finished goods prefer locations near markets to reduce transport cost and ensure quick delivery. Good transport facilities (roads, railways, ports) reduce cost of bringing raw materials and sending finished products, allow easy access to national and international markets and thus attract industries to such nodes and corridors.

questions.text: Mention any two characteristics of high-technology (hi-tech) industries.
questions.answer: Characteristics: high investment in research and development; use of advanced electronics and robotics; highly skilled workforce; clean and environment-friendly production compared to traditional heavy industries.

questions.text: Which one is an example of public sector industry in India?
questions.answer: BHEL

questions.text: In an industrial region, 40% of workers are engaged in engineering industries, 35% in textile industries and the rest in food-processing. If total industrial workers are 2,00,000, find the number working in food-processing.
questions.answer: Percentage in food-processing = 100 − (40 + 35) = 25%. Number = 25% of 2,00,000 = 50,000 workers.

questions.text: List any two environmental problems caused by concentration of industries.
questions.answer: Air pollution from smoke and gases, water pollution from industrial effluents, noise pollution, solid waste generation and land degradation.

questions.text: Describe any three advantages of industrial regions for the economic development of a country.
questions.answer: Advantages: (i) Economies of scale as industries share infrastructure and services. (ii) Large employment opportunities and urban growth. (iii) Development of transport, banking and other services. (iv) Increase in exports and tax revenue, contributing to GDP.

questions.text: Which of the following activities converts raw materials into finished goods?
questions.answer: Manufacturing

questions.text: Cottage industries are generally:
questions.answer: Household based

questions.text: Define secondary economic activities.
questions.answer: Secondary economic activities involve processing of raw materials into semi-finished or finished goods through manufacturing.

questions.text: What is manufacturing?
questions.answer: Manufacturing is the process of converting raw materials into finished products using labour, machines and power.

questions.text: State the factors affecting location of industries.
questions.answer: Availability of raw materials, power, labour, transport, market and capital affect industrial location.

questions.text: Explain small scale industries.
questions.answer: Small scale industries require less capital, use simple technology and employ local labour to produce goods for nearby markets.

questions.text: Show major iron and steel producing regions of the world on the map.
questions.howToSaveImage: Store scanned world map in /public/maps and mark major iron and steel belts.
questions.answer: USA, Europe, China, India

questions.text: Draw a flow diagram of manufacturing process.
questions.howToSaveImage: Create or scan a labelled flow diagram and store under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Raw material → Processing → Finished goods

questions.text: Explain types of industries with examples.
questions.answer: Industries are classified as cottage, small-scale and large-scale based on size, capital, technology and output with examples.

chapters.title: Tertiary Economic Activities
chapters.description: Nature and types of tertiary activities such as trade, transport, tourism and communication, their interrelationships and changing trends.
topics: Definition and types of tertiary activities
Relationship between trade, transport and tourism
Recent trends: e-commerce, digital services, globalisation
Problems and prospects of tertiary sector in developing countries
learningObjectives: Define tertiary activities and give examples.
Explain the role of transport and communication in economic development.
Differentiate between internal and international trade.
Discuss the importance and impacts of tourism.
Describe how trade, transport and tourism are interlinked.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a tertiary activity?
questions.answer: Road construction

questions.text: State any two advantages of good transport facilities to a region.
questions.answer: They help movement of raw materials and finished goods, reduce transport cost and time, promote trade and tourism and integrate remote areas with markets.

questions.text: Differentiate between internal trade and international trade.
questions.answer: Internal trade takes place within the boundaries of a country and uses national currency, whereas international trade occurs between different countries and involves foreign exchange and customs procedures.

questions.text: Which factor has recently contributed most to the growth of e-commerce?
options: Discovery of sea route to India
questions.answer: Spread of internet and smartphones

questions.text: Explain any three positive and any two negative impacts of tourism on a destination region.
questions.answer: Positive: (i) Generates employment and income. (ii) Develops infrastructure like roads, airports and hotels. (iii) Encourages preservation of culture and heritage. Negative: (i) Environmental degradation due to pollution and littering. (ii) Overcrowding and seasonal pressure on local resources, sometimes cultural commodification.

questions.text: What is meant by globalisation of services? Give one example.
questions.answer: Globalisation of services means services such as IT, banking, education and health are provided across national boundaries using communication technology, e.g., Indian IT companies providing software services to clients in USA or Europe.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
questions.answer: Banking – financial service

questions.text: A country exported goods worth ₹800 crore and imported goods worth ₹650 crore in a year. Calculate its balance of trade and state whether it is favourable or unfavourable.
questions.answer: Balance of trade = Exports − Imports = 800 − 650 = ₹150 crore (surplus). It is a favourable balance of trade.

questions.text: Explain the term ‘transport corridor’ with an example.
questions.answer: A transport corridor is a well-developed route connecting major centres with concentrated road, rail or water transport facilities, e.g., the Golden Quadrilateral in India connecting Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.

questions.text: Describe the relationship between trade, transport and tourism.
questions.answer: Efficient transport connects producers and consumers, enabling trade of goods. Developed trade encourages better transport infrastructure like ports and airports. The same transport networks allow tourists to reach destinations; in turn, growth of tourism justifies further improvements in transport and communication. Thus, trade, transport and tourism support each other’s growth.

questions.text: Which of the following is a tertiary economic activity?
questions.answer: Transport

questions.text: Which service helps in movement of goods and people?
questions.answer: Transport

questions.text: Define tertiary economic activities.
questions.answer: Tertiary economic activities provide services that support primary and secondary activities and help people directly or indirectly.

questions.text: What is trade?
questions.answer: Trade is the exchange of goods and services between producers and consumers.

questions.text: State the importance of transport.
questions.answer: Transport connects producers and consumers, promotes trade, supports industrial growth and facilitates regional development.

questions.text: Explain tourism as a tertiary activity.
questions.answer: Tourism involves travel for recreation and generates employment, foreign exchange and infrastructure development.

questions.text: Show major international air routes on the world map.
questions.howToSaveImage: Store scanned world map under /public/maps and mark major air routes.
questions.answer: North America–Europe, Asia–Europe routes

questions.text: Draw a flow diagram showing interdependence of economic activities.
questions.howToSaveImage: Create or scan a labelled flow diagram and store under /public/diagrams.
questions.answer: Primary → Secondary → Tertiary activities

questions.text: Explain different types of tertiary economic activities with examples.
questions.answer: Tertiary activities include transport, trade, tourism, communication and services which support economic development.

chapters.title: Region and Regional Development
chapters.description: Concept of region, types of regions, indicators of development, regional imbalance and measures for balanced regional development.
topics: Case examples of regional development programmes
learningObjectives: Define region and explain its characteristics.
Differentiate between various types of regions.
Explain concept of regional development and imbalance.
Identify factors responsible for regional disparities.
Suggest measures for balanced regional development.

questions.text: An area organised around a focal point such as a city and its surrounding hinterland is called a:
questions.answer: Functional region

questions.text: Define ‘region’ in geographical sense.
questions.answer: Region is an area of the earth’s surface that is homogeneous with respect to certain selected criteria such as climate, economy or culture and differs from surrounding areas.

questions.text: State any two indicators used to measure regional development.
questions.answer: Examples: per capita income, literacy rate, level of industrialisation, availability of infrastructure (roads, electricity, health services), Human Development Index.

questions.text: A state boundary in India is an example of which type of region?
questions.answer: Administrative region

questions.text: Explain any three causes of regional imbalance within a country.
questions.answer: Causes: (i) Unequal distribution of natural resources such as minerals, fertile soils or water. (ii) Historical factors like colonial policies favouring some ports and regions. (iii) Concentration of industries and infrastructure in few growth centres while other areas remain neglected. (iv) Political decisions, poor governance or lack of investment in backward regions.

questions.text: What is meant by balanced regional development?
questions.answer: Balanced regional development refers to a situation where all regions of a country develop in a reasonably similar way and no region remains permanently backward or highly deprived compared to others.

questions.text: Which of the following is a measure to reduce regional disparities?
options: Concentrating all industries in one metro city
Providing tax incentives to industries in backward areas
questions.answer: Providing tax incentives to industries in backward areas

questions.text: Region A has per capita income of ₹1,20,000 and literacy rate of 85%. Region B has per capita income of ₹60,000 and literacy rate of 65%. Calculate the difference in per capita income and literacy rate between the two regions.
questions.answer: Difference in per capita income = 1,20,000 − 60,000 = ₹60,000. Difference in literacy rate = 85% − 65% = 20 percentage points.

questions.text: Give two examples of natural regions.

questions.text: Define Off-Page SEO and mention any two common Off-Page activities.
questions.answer: Off-Page SEO includes optimisation activities performed outside the website to improve its authority and popularity, such as link building and social bookmarking. Common activities: getting backlinks from other relevant websites, directory submissions, social media sharing.

questions.text: What is a meta description? State the recommended length range for it.
questions.answer: A meta description is a short summary of a web page's content, placed in a <meta name="description"> tag and often shown in search results under the title. It is usually recommended to keep it between about 70 and 160 characters including spaces.

questions.text: Explain how the following elements affect SEO: (i) Title tag, (ii) Heading tags, (iii) Alt attribute of images.
questions.answer: Title tag: Appears as the clickable headline in search results; including main keywords and a clear description helps both ranking and click-through rate. Heading tags (H1–H6): Provide structure to the content; search engines use them to understand page hierarchy and important topics. Alt attribute: Describes images in text form; improves accessibility and helps search engines understand image content, contributing to relevancy for certain keywords.

questions.text: What is keyword stuffing and why should it be avoided?
questions.answer: Keyword stuffing is the practice of excessively repeating keywords in content, meta tags or alt texts only to manipulate search rankings. It should be avoided because it reduces readability, violates search engine guidelines and can lead to penalties or lower ranking.

questions.text: A meta description currently has 210 characters including spaces. If the recommended maximum is 160 characters, by how many characters must it be reduced?

questions.text: List any five good practices to follow while optimising a page structure for SEO.

questions.text: Define a simple statement and a compound statement with one example of each.
questions.answer: Simple statement: cannot be broken into smaller statements, e.g. "5 is odd". Compound statement: formed by combining two or more simple statements using connectives, e.g. "5 is odd and 6 is even".

questions.text: The connective in the compound statement "p or q" is represented symbolically by:

questions.answer:
p q | p ∨ q
T T | T
T F | T
F T | T
F F | F

questions.text: Construct the truth table for (~p ∧ q) → p.
questions.answer:
p q | ~p | ~p ∧ q | (~p ∧ q) → p
T T | F  | F        | T
T F | F  | F        | T
F T | T  | T        | F
F F | T  | F        | T

questions.text: State whether the statement pattern p ∨ ~p is a tautology, contradiction or contingency. Justify briefly.
questions.answer: p ∨ ~p is a tautology because it is true for both possible truth values of p (if p is T, p ∨ ~p is T; if p is F, ~p is T, so disjunction is T).

questions.text: Write the converse and contrapositive of: "If n is even then n² is even".
questions.answer: Converse: If n² is even then n is even. Contrapositive: If n² is not even then n is not even.

questions.text: Write the dual of the statement pattern (p ∧ q) ∨ r.

questions.answer:
Let p: S₁ is ON, q: S₂ is ON. Lamp glows only when both are ON, so expression is p ∧ q.
Switching (truth) table:
p q | p ∧ q
1 1 | 1
1 0 | 0
0 1 | 0
0 0 | 0.

questions.text: Write the negation of the statement: “All integers are rational numbers.”

questions.text: Find the truth value of: p ∨ q, if p is false and q is true.

questions.text: Construct the truth table for p → q.

questions.text: Verify De Morgan’s law: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ (¬p ∨ ¬q).
questions.answer: By constructing truth tables for both sides, the truth values are identical for all combinations of p and q.

questions.text: Check whether the statement p ↔ q is a tautology or not.
questions.answer: By constructing the truth table, p ↔ q is true only when p and q have same truth values; hence it is not a tautology.

questions.answer: A matrix having equal number of rows and columns is called a square matrix.

questions.text: Find the transpose of the matrix A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]].
Show that the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix is neither symmetric nor skew-symmetric in general.
questions.answer: By taking a general symmetric and skew-symmetric matrix and adding them, the resulting matrix does not satisfy either condition.

questions.text: If A is a square matrix, show that (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A.
questions.answer: Transpose of transpose of a matrix gives the original matrix.

questions.text: Find matrix X if A + X = B, where A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]].
Prove that the product of two symmetric matrices need not be symmetric.
questions.answer: By taking suitable symmetric matrices A and B, AB ≠ (AB)ᵀ in general.

chapters.title: Trigonometric Functions
chapters.description: Trigonometric equations and their solutions, principle and general solutions, solution of triangles using sine, cosine and projection rules, area of triangle, and basic properties of inverse trigonometric functions.
topics: Solution of triangle using sine rule
Area of triangle by trigonometric formulae
Inverse trigonometric functions and their ranges
learningObjectives: Solve standard trigonometric equations for principal and general solutions.
Apply sine, cosine and projection rules to solve a triangle.
Use trigonometric formulae for the area of a triangle.
Understand basic definitions and ranges of inverse trigonometric functions.

questions.text: Solve the equation sin x = 1/2 for 0° ≤ x < 360°.
Find the general solution of cos x = 0.
For a triangle ABC, the sine rule is:
options: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
cos A + cos B + cos C = 0
sin(A + B) = sin A + sin B
questions.answer: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C

questions.text: In ΔABC, a = 7 cm, b = 8 cm and angle C = 120°. Find side c using cosine rule.
The sides of a triangle are 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. Find its area using the formula ½ab sin C.
questions.answer: Take sides a=5, b=6, c=7. First find angle C opposite c using cosine rule: cos C = (a² + b² − c²)/(2ab) = (25+36−49)/(60)=12/60=1/5 ⇒ sin C = √(1−1/25)=√(24/25)=2√6/5. Area = ½ab sin C = ½·5·6·(2√6/5)=3·2√6=6√6 cm².

questions.text: State the projection rule relating side a and angles B and C of a triangle ABC.
questions.answer: Projection rule: a = b cos C + c cos B.

questions.text: The principal value of sin⁻¹(√3/2) is:
Write the range of the principal value branch of tan⁻¹x.
questions.answer: Range of tan⁻¹x is (−π/2, π/2).

questions.text: If ΔABC has sides a = 10 cm, b = 12 cm and included angle C = 45°, find the area of the triangle.
Solve the equation 2sin²x − 3sin x + 1 = 0 for 0° ≤ x < 360°.
questions.answer:
Let sin x = t.
2t² − 3t + 1 = 0 ⇒ (2t − 1)(t − 1) = 0 so t = 1/2 or t = 1.
For sin x = 1/2 ⇒ x = 30°, 150°.
For sin x = 1 ⇒ x = 90°.
Solutions: x = 30°, 90°, 150°.

questions.text: The principal value of sin⁻¹(1/2) is:
The domain of y = sin⁻¹x is:
State the principal value range of cos⁻¹x.
questions.answer: The principal value range of cos⁻¹x is [0, π].

questions.text: Find sin(sin⁻¹x).
questions.answer: x, for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1.

questions.text: Evaluate: tan⁻¹(1) + sin⁻¹(1/2).
Show that sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2.
questions.answer: Using principal value ranges, the identity holds for −1 ≤ x ≤ 1.

questions.text: Find the value of tan⁻¹(√3) − sin⁻¹(1/2).
questions.answer: tan⁻¹(√3)=π/3, sin⁻¹(1/2)=π/6, difference=π/6.

questions.text: Find the principal value of cos⁻¹(−√3/2).
Prove that tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹(1/x) = π/2, for x > 0.
questions.answer: Using tangent addition formula and principal value ranges, the identity is proved.

questions.text: Solve: sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹(2x) = π/2.
questions.answer: Using identity sin⁻¹x = π/2 − cos⁻¹x, solution is x = 1/2.

chapters.title: Pair of Straight Lines
chapters.description: Combined equation of two lines, pair of lines passing through origin, angle between lines, condition for parallel and perpendicular lines, and general second degree equation representing pair of lines.
topics: Pair of lines through origin: ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0
Condition for lines to be perpendicular or coincident
General second degree equation and its homogeneous part
Point of intersection of two lines
learningObjectives: Write combined equation of a pair of straight lines in a plane.
Determine angle between lines and conditions for parallelism and perpendicularity.
Find point of intersection of two lines.
Identify when a second degree equation represents a pair of lines.

questions.text: The pair of lines represented by ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 are perpendicular if:
questions.answer: a + b = 0

questions.text: Find the combined equation of the pair of lines passing through origin and making angles 30° and 120° with positive x-axis.
questions.answer:
Lines: y = (tan30°)x = (1/√3)x and y = (tan120°)x = (−√3)x.
Equation: (y − x/√3)(y + √3x) = 0 ⇒ y² + (−√3 + 1/√3)xy − x² = 0 ⇒ y² − (2/√3)xy − x² = 0 (scalar multiple also acceptable).

questions.text: Find the point of intersection of lines 2x + 3y − 5 = 0 and x − y + 1 = 0.
questions.answer: Solve: From second, x = y − 1. Substitute in first: 2(y − 1) + 3y − 5 = 0 ⇒ 5y − 7 = 0 ⇒ y = 7/5, x = 2/5. Intersection: (2/5, 7/5).

questions.text: Find the angle between lines represented by 3x² − 10xy + 3y² = 0.
The general second degree equation ax² + 2hxy + by² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 represents a pair of straight lines if:
options: the homogeneous part factors into two distinct linear factors
questions.answer: the homogeneous part factors into two distinct linear factors

questions.text: Write the condition for ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 to represent a pair of real and distinct lines.
questions.answer: The condition is h² > ab.

questions.text: Resolve 6x² − xy − y² = 0 into two linear factors.
questions.answer:
Compare with ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0. Here a=6, 2h=−1 ⇒ h=−1/2, b=−1. Solve for slopes m from 6 + 2hm + bm² = 0 ⇒ 6 + (−1)m + (−1)m² = 0 ⇒ −m² − m + 6 = 0 ⇒ m² + m − 6 = 0 ⇒ (m+3)(m−2)=0 ⇒ m = −3 or 2.
Lines: y = −3x and y = 2x. So equation: (y + 3x)(y − 2x) = 0.

questions.text: Find the combined equation of lines x + y − 2 = 0 and 2x − 3y + 5 = 0.
questions.answer: Product: (x + y − 2)(2x − 3y + 5) = 0 (expanded form also acceptable).

questions.text: If two non-vertical lines have slopes m₁ and m₂, they are perpendicular when:
questions.answer: m₁m₂ = −1

questions.text: Show that the lines represented by x² − 4xy − 5y² = 0 are perpendicular.
questions.answer:
Here a = 1, 2h = −4 ⇒ h = −2, b = −5. For pair ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0, lines are perpendicular if a + b = 0. Here a + b = 1 − 5 = −4 ≠ 0 so not perpendicular by that check; instead compute slopes:
Equation factors: 1 + 2hm + bm² = 0 ⇒ 1 + 2(−2)m + (−5)m²=0 ⇒ −5m² −4m +1=0 ⇒ 5m² +4m −1=0 ⇒ m = [−4 ± √(16+20)]/(10) = [−4 ± √36]/10 = (−4 ± 6)/10 ⇒ m₁ = 1/5, m₂ = −1.
Product m₁m₂ = (1/5)(−1) = −1/5, so lines are NOT perpendicular. (Note: this shows they are not perpendicular; the condition a + b = 0 must hold for perpendicularity.)

questions.text: The general equation of a pair of straight lines passing through the origin is:
questions.answer: ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0

questions.text: If the pair of lines represented by ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 are perpendicular, then:
questions.answer: a + b = 0

questions.text: What condition represents coincident lines?
questions.answer: For coincident lines, h² = ab.

questions.text: State the condition for the equation to represent real and distinct lines.
questions.answer: The condition is h² > ab.

questions.text: Find the angle between the pair of lines represented by x² − y² = 0.
questions.answer: The given equation represents lines y = x and y = −x, which are perpendicular; angle = 90°.

questions.text: Show that the equation x² + 4xy + y² = 0 represents a pair of coincident lines.
questions.answer: Here a = 1, h = 2, b = 1, so h² = ab, hence the lines are coincident.

questions.text: Find the slopes of the pair of straight lines given by 3x² − 10xy + 3y² = 0.
questions.answer: Comparing with ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 and solving, slopes are m = 3 and m = 1/3.

questions.text: Determine whether the pair of lines represented by 2x² + 5xy + 3y² = 0 are perpendicular.
questions.answer: Since a + b ≠ 0, the lines are not perpendicular.

questions.text: Find the equation of pair of straight lines represented by 6x² − xy − y² = 0 and find the angle between them.
questions.answer: Using tanθ = 2√(h² − ab)/(a + b), the angle is obtained after substitution.

questions.text: Prove that the equation ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 represents two straight lines through the origin.
questions.answer: By factoring into (y − m₁x)(y − m₂x) = 0, the equation represents two straight lines through origin.

chapters.title: Vectors
chapters.description: Scalars and vectors, representation of vectors in 2D and 3D, addition and scalar multiplication, position vectors, dot product, cross product, scalar triple product, and applications to geometry.
topics: Dot product and angle between vectors
Projection of one vector on another
Cross product and area of parallelogram/triangle
Scalar triple product and volume of parallelepiped
learningObjectives: Represent vectors algebraically and geometrically.
Perform basic operations with vectors in component form.
Compute dot product, cross product and scalar triple product.
Use vectors to find lengths, areas, volumes and angles in geometry.

questions.text: Define scalar and vector with one example of each.
questions.answer: Scalar has magnitude only, e.g. mass 5 kg. Vector has both magnitude and direction, e.g. force 10 N acting east.

questions.text: If a⃗ = 3î − 4ĵ, find |a⃗|.
If a⃗ = 2î + 3ĵ − k̂ and b⃗ = î − 2ĵ + 4k̂, find a⃗ + b⃗.
Find the dot product of a⃗ = 2î − 3ĵ + k̂ and b⃗ = î + 4ĵ − 2k̂ and hence the angle between them.
If a⃗ = î + 2ĵ and b⃗ = 3î − 4ĵ, find |a⃗ × b⃗| and interpret it geometrically.
questions.answer:
a⃗ × b⃗ = k̂(det|1 2; 3 −4|) = k̂(1·(−4) − 2·3) = −10k̂.
|a⃗ × b⃗| = 10, which equals the area of the parallelogram formed by a⃗ and b⃗.

questions.text: Find the area of the triangle whose vertices have position vectors a⃗, b⃗, c⃗.
Evaluate the scalar triple product [a⃗ b⃗ c⃗] for a⃗ = î, b⃗ = 2ĵ, c⃗ = 3k̂ and interpret it.
questions.answer:
[a⃗ b⃗ c⃗] = det|1 0 0; 0 2 0; 0 0 3| = 1·2·3 = 6.
This equals the volume of the parallelepiped formed by a⃗, b⃗, c⃗, so volume = 6 units³.

questions.text: State the condition for vectors a⃗ and b⃗ to be perpendicular in terms of dot product.
questions.answer: They are perpendicular if a⃗ · b⃗ = 0.

questions.text: Find the position vector of the point dividing the line segment joining A(1, 2, 3) and B(5, 4, −1) internally in the ratio 1:3.
If a⃗ and b⃗ are parallel non-zero vectors, then a⃗ × b⃗ equals:
questions.answer: zero vector

questions.text: Which of the following quantities is a vector?
questions.answer: Velocity

questions.text: The magnitude of vector 3i − 4j is:
Define a unit vector.
questions.answer: A vector having magnitude equal to one is called a unit vector.

questions.text: Write the position vector of a point (2, −3, 4).
Find the magnitude of vector a = i + 2j + 2k.
Find the unit vector in the direction of vector 4i − 3j.
questions.answer: Unit vector = (4i − 3j)/5

questions.text: Find the angle between vectors a = i + j and b = i − j.
questions.answer: Using dot product, angle = 90°.

questions.text: Find the projection of vector a = 2i + 3j on b = i − j.
questions.answer: Projection = (a·b)/|b|

questions.text: Find the equation of a line passing through point (1, 2, 3) and parallel to vector 2i − j + k.
Show that vectors a + b and a − b are perpendicular if |a| = |b|.
questions.answer: Using dot product (a+b)·(a−b)=|a|²−|b|²=0, hence perpendicular.

chapters.title: Line and Plane
chapters.description: Vector and Cartesian equations of a line in 3D, direction ratios and cosines, angles between lines and planes, various forms of plane equations, conditions for parallelism and perpendicularity, and distance of a point from a plane.
topics: Vector and parametric equations of a line
Cartesian equation of a line in 3D
Equation of a plane in normal form
General form of plane and passing through a point
Distance from a point to a plane
learningObjectives: Write equations of lines and planes in vector and Cartesian forms.
Find angles between lines and between planes.
Determine condition for lines and planes to be parallel or perpendicular.
Compute distance of a point from a plane.

questions.text: Define direction ratios of a line in 3D with an example.
questions.answer: Direction ratios are any three numbers proportional to the components of a direction vector of the line. For line parallel to vector 2î − 3ĵ + k̂, (2, −3, 1) are DRs.

questions.text: Find the vector equation of the line passing through point A(1, 2, −1) and parallel to vector 3î − 4ĵ + k̂.
questions.answer:
Position vector of A is a⃗ = î + 2ĵ − k̂. Direction vector b⃗ = 3î − 4ĵ + k̂.
Line: r⃗ = a⃗ + λb⃗ = (î + 2ĵ − k̂) + λ(3î − 4ĵ + k̂), λ ∈ ℝ.

questions.text: Find the angle between lines whose direction ratios are (1, −2, 2) and (2, 1, −1).
Write the normal form of the equation of a plane at distance p from the origin and having unit normal vector n̂ = (l, m, n).
questions.answer: Plane equation: lx + my + nz = p.

questions.text: Find the equation of a plane passing through point (1, −2, 3) and having normal vector 2î − 3ĵ + 4k̂.
Write the condition for two planes ax + by + cz + d = 0 and a'x + b'y + c'z + d' = 0 to be perpendicular.
questions.answer: Their normal vectors are perpendicular, so aa' + bb' + cc' = 0.

questions.text: Find the angle between planes 2x − y + 2z = 5 and x + 2y − 2z = 3.
Calculate the distance of the point P(2, −1, 3) from the plane x − 2y + 2z − 5 = 0.
A line is parallel to a plane if:
options: its direction vector is perpendicular to the plane’s normal
its direction vector is parallel to the plane’s normal
the line lies entirely in the plane
questions.answer: its direction vector is perpendicular to the plane’s normal

questions.text: Find the angle between the line r⃗ = (î + 2ĵ + 3k̂) + λ(2î − 2ĵ + k̂) and the plane x + y + z = 6.
questions.answer:
Normal to plane: n⃗ = î + ĵ + k̂. Direction vector of line: b⃗ = (2, −2, 1).
Angle between line and plane α satisfies sinα = |b⃗·n⃗|/(|b⃗||n⃗|).
Compute b⃗·n⃗ = 2·1 + (−2)·1 + 1·1 = 1.
|b⃗| = √(4+4+1)=3, |n⃗|=√3.
So sinα = 1/(3√3). α = sin⁻¹(1/(3√3)).

questions.text: The general equation of a plane is:
questions.answer: ax + by + cz + d = 0

questions.text: A line is perpendicular to a plane if its direction ratios are proportional to:
questions.answer: Normal vector of the plane

questions.text: Define direction cosines of a line.
questions.answer: Direction cosines are cosines of angles made by the line with the coordinate axes.

questions.text: What is a normal vector of a plane?
questions.answer: A vector perpendicular to the plane is called its normal vector.

questions.text: Find the direction ratios of the line joining points (1, 2, 3) and (3, 6, 7).
questions.answer: Direction ratios are (2, 4, 4) or simplified (1, 2, 2).

questions.text: Find the equation of the plane passing through the origin and perpendicular to vector i + 2j + 3k.
Find the angle between the planes 2x + y + z = 5 and x − y + 2z = 4.
questions.answer: Angle is found using normals n₁ = (2,1,1) and n₂ = (1,−1,2).

questions.text: Find the equation of the line passing through (1, −1, 2) and parallel to 2i + j − k.
questions.answer: r = (i − j + 2k) + λ(2i + j − k)

questions.text: Find the equation of the plane passing through three points (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1).
questions.answer: The equation is x + y + z = 1.

questions.text: Prove that the angle between a line and a plane is complementary to the angle between the line and the normal to the plane.
questions.answer: Using geometric relations of direction ratios and normal vector, the complementary relation is proved.

chapters.title: Linear Programming
chapters.description: Formulation of linear programming problems in two variables, graphical solution of system of linear inequalities, feasible region, objective function and optimum solution by corner point method.
topics: Graph of linear inequality and half-planes
Feasible region, feasible and basic feasible solutions
Types of solutions: unique, multiple, unbounded, infeasible
learningObjectives: Plot and interpret linear inequalities in two variables.
Formulate real-life optimisation problems as LPPs.
Find feasible region and corner points from the graph.
Use corner point method to obtain optimum solution of an LPP.

questions.text: What is a linear programming problem (LPP)?
questions.answer: An LPP is an optimisation problem in which a linear objective function is maximised or minimised subject to a set of linear inequality constraints.

questions.text: Explain the term feasible region in the context of an LPP.
questions.answer: Feasible region is the common region in the plane that satisfies all the given constraints of the LPP simultaneously.

questions.text: In a two-variable LPP, the optimum value of the objective function (if it exists) occurs at:
options: an interior point of feasible region only
a corner point (vertex) of feasible region
questions.answer: a corner point (vertex) of feasible region

questions.text: Graph the inequality x + 2y ≥ 4 and indicate the feasible half-plane.
questions.answer: Draw line x + 2y = 4 (intercepts: (4,0) and (0,2)). Take test point (0,0): 0 ≥ 4 is false, so the half-plane not containing origin (above/right of the line) is the feasible region.

questions.text: A company produces two products A and B. Profit on A is ₹3 and on B is ₹5 per unit. Each unit of A requires 1 hour of machine time and 2 kg of raw material, while each unit of B requires 2 hours and 1 kg of raw material. The company has at most 8 machine hours and 6 kg raw material per day. Formulate the LPP to maximise profit.
questions.answer:
Let x = units of A, y = units of B.
Objective function to maximise: Z = 3x + 5y.
Constraints from machine time: 1x + 2y ≤ 8.
From raw material: 2x + 1y ≤ 6.
Also x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

questions.text: Solve the LPP: Maximise Z = 5x + 4y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 using graphical method.
questions.answer:
Feasible region is triangle with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (0,4).
Evaluate Z: at (0,0): 0; at (4,0): Z=20; at (0,4): Z=16.
Maximum Z = 20 at (x, y) = (4, 0).

questions.text: Minimise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + 2y ≥ 6, 3x + y ≥ 9, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (graphical). State only the coordinates of corner points and the minimum value.
questions.answer:
Intersect x + 2y = 6 and 3x + y = 9: solving gives x=3, y=1.5.
Other corner points in feasible region (first quadrant, above both lines): (0,6/2=3) on first line, (3,0) on second line.
Z at (0,3): 3·0+2·3=6; at (3,0):9; at (3,1.5):3·3+2·1.5=9+3=12.
Minimum Z = 6 at (0,3).

questions.text: When do we say that an LPP has an unbounded solution?
questions.answer: When the feasible region is open in the direction of optimisation and the value of the objective function can be increased (or decreased) indefinitely without violating any constraint.

questions.text: Explain how you decide the feasible half-plane while graphing a linear inequality ax + by ≥ c.
questions.answer: First draw the line ax + by = c. Then take a convenient test point (usually origin if not on the line). If it satisfies the inequality, the half-plane containing that point is feasible; otherwise, the opposite half-plane is feasible.

questions.text: If the feasible region of an LPP is empty (no common points satisfying all constraints), then:
options: there is a unique optimum solution
the objective function must be constant
questions.answer: the LPP is infeasible

questions.text: A linear programming problem involves:
options: Linear objective function and linear constraints
questions.answer: Linear objective function and linear constraints

questions.text: The feasible region of an LPP is:
questions.answer: The intersection of all constraints

questions.text: Define objective function.
questions.answer: The function which is to be maximized or minimized is called the objective function.

questions.text: What are constraints in LPP?
questions.answer: The conditions expressed as linear inequalities or equations are called constraints.

questions.text: Write the standard form of a linear programming problem.
questions.answer: Maximize or minimize Z = ax + by subject to linear constraints and non-negativity conditions.

questions.text: What is a bounded feasible region?
questions.answer: A feasible region enclosed within finite boundaries is called bounded feasible region.

questions.text: Why does optimal solution occur at a corner point?
questions.answer: Because the objective function achieves maximum or minimum value at one of the vertices of feasible region.

questions.text: Solve the LPP graphically: Maximize Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
questions.answer: Optimal solution occurs at (4,0) giving Z = 12.

questions.text: Solve an LPP by graphical method and find maximum value of objective function.
questions.answer: By plotting constraints, identifying feasible region and evaluating objective function at corner points.

questions.text: Explain unbounded feasible region with an example.
questions.answer: If feasible region extends infinitely and objective function has no maximum or minimum, it is unbounded.

chapters.title: Differentiation
chapters.description: Review of basic derivative rules, derivatives of composite, inverse, implicit, logarithmic and parametric functions, higher order derivatives and geometrical meaning of derivative.
topics: Derivative as limit of increment ratio
Geometrical meaning of derivative (slope of tangent)
Chain rule and derivatives of composite functions
Higher order derivatives of standard functions
learningObjectives: Interpret derivative as instantaneous rate of change and slope of tangent.
Differentiate composite, inverse, implicit and logarithmic functions using chain rule.
Differentiate parametric curves with respect to the parameter.
Compute second and higher order derivatives for standard functions.
Apply derivative rules accurately in algebraic and trigonometric contexts.

questions.text: The derivative of e^{3x} with respect to x is:
Find dy/dx if y = ln(5x + 1).
questions.answer: dy/dx = (5) / (5x + 1) by using derivative of ln u as (1/u)·du/dx.

questions.text: Differentiate y = (x^2 + 1)^5 with respect to x.
questions.answer: dy/dx = 5(x^2 + 1)^4 · 2x = 10x (x^2 + 1)^4 by chain rule.

questions.text: If y = x^x for x > 0, find dy/dx using logarithmic differentiation.
questions.answer: Take ln on both sides: ln y = x ln x. Differentiate: (1/y) dy/dx = ln x + 1. Hence dy/dx = y(ln x + 1) = x^x(ln x + 1).

questions.text: If y = sin(3x^2), find dy/dx and d^2y/dx^2.
questions.answer: dy/dx = cos(3x^2)·6x = 6x cos(3x^2). Then d^2y/dx^2 = derivative of 6x cos(3x^2): 6 cos(3x^2) + 6x[−sin(3x^2)·6x] = 6 cos(3x^2) − 36x^2 sin(3x^2).

questions.text: If y = tan^{-1}(x), show that dy/dx = 1/(1 + x^2).
questions.answer: Let y = tan^{-1}x so x = tan y. Differentiate: dx/dy = sec^2 y = 1 + tan^2 y = 1 + x^2. Hence dy/dx = 1/(dx/dy) = 1/(1 + x^2).

questions.text: Differentiate implicitly: x^2 + y^2 = 25.
questions.answer: Differentiate: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 ⇒ dy/dx = −x/y.

questions.text: If x = a cos t, y = a sin t, find dy/dx in terms of t.
questions.answer: dx/dt = −a sin t, dy/dt = a cos t, so dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = (a cos t)/(−a sin t) = −cot t.

questions.text: For y = (x^2 + 1)/(x − 1), find dy/dx using quotient rule.
Show that the derivative of f(x) = sin^{-1}x + cos^{-1}x is a constant and hence find f(x).
questions.answer: f'(x) = d/dx[sin^{-1}x] + d/dx[cos^{-1}x] = 1/√(1 − x^2) − 1/√(1 − x^2) = 0, so f(x) is constant. Put x = 0: f(0) = sin^{-1}0 + cos^{-1}0 = 0 + π/2 = π/2. Thus f(x) = π/2 for all x in [−1,1].

questions.text: The derivative of sin x with respect to x is:
questions.answer: cos x

questions.text: If y = e^x, then dy/dx equals:
questions.answer: e^x

questions.text: Define derivative of a function.
questions.answer: The derivative of a function represents the rate of change of the function with respect to the variable.

questions.text: Find d/dx (x²).
questions.answer: 2x

questions.text: Differentiate y = ln x.
questions.answer: dy/dx = 1/x

questions.text: Find the derivative of y = sin x + cos x.
questions.answer: dy/dx = cos x − sin x

questions.text: Find dy/dx if y = (x² + 1)/(x).
questions.answer: dy/dx = (x² − 1)/x²

questions.text: Differentiate y = x³ sin x.
questions.answer: dy/dx = 3x² sin x + x³ cos x

questions.text: Find dy/dx if y = ln(sin x).
questions.answer: dy/dx = cot x

questions.text: Differentiate y = (sin x)^x with respect to x.
questions.answer: Using logarithmic differentiation, dy/dx = (sin x)^x [ln(sin x) + x cot x].

chapters.title: Applications of Derivatives
chapters.description: Applications of derivatives to tangents and normals, monotonicity, maxima and minima, approximations and verification of mean value theorems.
topics: Equation of tangent and normal to a curve
Local maxima and minima, critical points
Rolle’s theorem and Lagrange’s mean value theorem (MVT)
learningObjectives: Find equations of tangent and normal to curves at given points.
Determine intervals on which a function is increasing or decreasing.
Identify and classify local maxima and minima using derivatives.
Use linear approximation for small changes.
Verify Rolle’s theorem and Mean Value Theorem for simple functions.
Solve elementary optimization problems from geometry and economics.

questions.text: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve y = x^2 − 4x + 1 at x = 2.
questions.answer: dy/dx = 2x − 4. At x = 2, slope = 2·2 − 4 = 0.

questions.text: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve y = x^3 at the point (1, 1).
questions.answer: dy/dx = 3x^2. At x = 1, slope m = 3. Using point-slope form: y − 1 = 3(x − 1) ⇒ y = 3x − 2.

questions.text: For the same curve y = x^3, find the equation of the normal at (1, 1).
questions.answer: Slope of tangent at (1,1) is 3, so slope of normal = −1/3. Equation: y − 1 = −(1/3)(x − 1) ⇒ 3y − 3 = −x + 1 ⇒ x + 3y − 4 = 0.

questions.text: Define an increasing function on an interval using derivatives.
questions.answer: A function f(x) is increasing on an interval if f'(x) ≥ 0 for every x in that interval and f'(x) > 0 at least at one point.

questions.text: Find the intervals of increase and decrease of f(x) = x^3 − 3x.
questions.answer: f'(x) = 3x^2 − 3 = 3(x^2 − 1) = 3(x − 1)(x + 1). Critical points: x = −1, 1. Test intervals: for x < −1, f'(x) > 0 (increasing); between −1 and 1, f'(x) < 0 (decreasing); for x > 1, f'(x) > 0 (increasing).

questions.text: Find the local maxima and minima of f(x) = x^3 − 6x^2 + 9x and classify them using second derivative test.
State Rolle’s Theorem.
questions.answer: If f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b) and f(a) = f(b), then there exists at least one c in (a, b) such that f'(c) = 0.

questions.text: Verify Rolle’s Theorem for f(x) = x^2 − 4x + 3 on [1, 3].
questions.answer: f is polynomial ⇒ continuous and differentiable. f(1) = 1 − 4 + 3 = 0, f(3) = 9 − 12 + 3 = 0 ⇒ f(1) = f(3). f'(x) = 2x − 4. Set 2x − 4 = 0 ⇒ x = 2 in (1,3). Thus Rolle’s Theorem is verified.

questions.text: Use differential approximation to estimate (4.02)^2.
A rectangle has perimeter 40 m. Find the dimensions of the rectangle of maximum area.
questions.answer: Let sides be x and y with 2(x + y) = 40 ⇒ y = 20 − x. Area A = xy = x(20 − x) = 20x − x^2. Then A'(x) = 20 − 2x. For extrema, 20 − 2x = 0 ⇒ x = 10. A''(x) = −2 < 0 so maximum. Then y = 20 − 10 = 10. Thus the rectangle of maximum area is a square of side 10 m.

questions.text: If f′(x) > 0 for all x in an interval, then the function f(x) is:
questions.answer: Increasing

questions.text: A point where f′(x) = 0 is called:
questions.answer: Critical point

questions.text: Define local maximum.
questions.answer: A function has a local maximum at a point if its value there is greater than values at nearby points.

questions.text: What is a point of inflection?
questions.answer: A point where the concavity of the curve changes is called a point of inflection.

questions.text: Find intervals of increase for f(x) = x³.
questions.answer: f′(x) = 3x² ≥ 0 for all x, so function increases everywhere.

questions.text: Find the critical points of f(x) = x² − 4x.
State the second derivative test.
questions.answer: If f′(a)=0 and f″(a)<0 then local maximum; if f″(a)>0 then local minimum.

questions.text: Find the maxima or minima of f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 4.
questions.answer: Critical points x = 0, 2. f″(0)<0 → maxima, f″(2)>0 → minima.

questions.text: Find the maximum value of f(x) = x(10 − x).
questions.answer: f′(x)=10−2x=0 ⇒ x=5, maximum value = 25.

questions.text: A rectangle is formed by using 20 m of fencing. Find maximum area.
questions.answer: Maximum area occurs for a square of side 5 m, area = 25 m².

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ (3x^2 − 4) dx.
questions.answer: ∫ 3x^2 dx = x^3, ∫ (−4) dx = −4x. So integral = x^3 − 4x + C.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ cos x dx.
questions.answer: ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ (2x)/(x^2 + 1) dx.
questions.answer: Let u = x^2 + 1 ⇒ du = 2x dx. Then integral = ∫ du/u = ln|u| + C = ln(x^2 + 1) + C.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ e^{2x} dx.
questions.answer: Let u = 2x ⇒ du = 2 dx ⇒ dx = du/2. Then ∫ e^{2x} dx = (1/2)∫ e^u du = (1/2) e^{2x} + C.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ x e^x dx using integration by parts.
questions.answer: Take u = x, dv = e^x dx. Then du = dx, v = e^x. So ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + C = e^x(x − 1) + C.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ (x^2)/(x^3 + 1) dx.
Resolve 3x + 5 over x^2 − 4 as partial fractions and hence integrate ∫ (3x + 5)/(x^2 − 4) dx.
Evaluate ∫ sec^2 x dx and ∫ cosec^2 x dx.
questions.answer: ∫ sec^2 x dx = tan x + C;  ∫ cosec^2 x dx = −cot x + C.

questions.text: What is meant by a family of curves represented by an indefinite integral?
questions.answer: The indefinite integral ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C represents a family of curves obtained by varying the constant C; all these curves are parallel vertical shifts of the graph of F(x).

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ x ln x dx using integration by parts.
questions.answer: Let u = ln x, dv = x dx. Then du = (1/x) dx, v = x^2/2. So ∫ x ln x dx = (x^2/2) ln x − ∫ (x^2/2)·(1/x) dx = (x^2/2) ln x − (1/2)∫ x dx = (x^2/2) ln x − (1/2)(x^2/2) + C = (x^2/2) ln x − x^2/4 + C.

questions.text: ∫ dx is equal to:
questions.answer: x + C

questions.text: ∫ e^x dx equals:
questions.answer: e^x + C

questions.text: What is the constant of integration?
questions.answer: An arbitrary constant added to an integral is called the constant of integration.

questions.text: Find ∫ cos x dx.
questions.answer: sin x + C

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ x dx.
questions.answer: x²/2 + C

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ sin x cos x dx.
questions.answer: Using substitution, integral equals (sin²x)/2 + C.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ 1/(1 + x²) dx.
questions.answer: tan⁻¹x + C

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ (2x)/(x² + 1) dx.
questions.answer: ln(x² + 1) + C

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ x e^x dx.
questions.answer: Using integration by parts, integral equals x e^x − e^x + C.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫ ln x dx.
questions.answer: Using integration by parts, ∫ ln x dx = x ln x − x + C.

chapters.title: Definite Integration
chapters.description: Definite integral as limit of sum, evaluation using antiderivatives, properties of definite integrals and fundamental theorem of calculus.
topics: Definite integral as limit of Riemann sums
Notation and interpretation of ∫_a^b f(x) dx
learningObjectives: Interpret definite integral as limit of sum and as area under curve.

Handle integrals with variable upper or lower limits.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫_0^1 x dx.
Evaluate ∫_0^{π} sin x dx.
questions.answer: Integral of sin x is −cos x. So value = [−cos x]_0^{π} = (−cos π) − (−cos 0) = (1) − (−1) = 2.

questions.text: State the fundamental theorem of calculus for definite integrals.
questions.answer: If F is an antiderivative of continuous function f on [a, b], then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a).

questions.text: Evaluate ∫_1^3 (2x + 1) dx.
Evaluate ∫_0^{π/2} cos^2 x dx using identity.
Using property, evaluate ∫_{-2}^2 x^3 dx.
questions.answer: x^3 is an odd function and limits are symmetric about 0, so ∫_{-2}^2 x^3 dx = 0.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫_0^1 (3x^2 + 2x) dx using fundamental theorem of calculus.
Evaluate ∫_0^{π/2} e^{sin x} ⋅ cos x dx using substitution.
questions.answer: Let u = sin x ⇒ du = cos x dx. Limits: when x = 0, u = 0; when x = π/2, u = 1. Thus integral = ∫_0^1 e^u du = [e^u]_0^1 = e − 1.

questions.text: Show that ∫_a^b f(x) dx = −∫_b^a f(x) dx.
questions.answer: By definition of definite integral with reversed limits, ∫_b^a f(x) dx = −∫_a^b f(x) dx, hence the result.

questions.text: If F(x) = ∫_0^x (t^2 + 1) dt, find dF/dx and F(2).
questions.answer: By fundamental theorem, dF/dx = x^2 + 1. Also F(2) = ∫_0^2 (t^2 + 1) dt = [t^3/3 + t]_0^2 = (8/3 + 2) − 0 = 14/3.

questions.text: If ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = k, then ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx is:
questions.answer: k

questions.text: The value of ∫₀ᵃ [f(x) + f(a − x)] dx is:
questions.answer: 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx

questions.text: State the property: ∫₋ᵃᵃ f(x) dx = 0.
questions.answer: If f(x) is an odd function, then ∫₋ᵃᵃ f(x) dx = 0.

questions.text: What is the value of ∫₋ᵃᵃ f(x) dx if f(x) is even?
questions.answer: 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx

questions.text: Evaluate ∫₀^π sin x dx.
questions.answer: ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2

questions.text: Evaluate ∫₀^π cos x dx.
questions.answer: ∫₀^π cos x dx = 0

questions.text: Using properties, evaluate ∫₀ᵃ x f(x) dx if f(x) is even.
questions.answer: Since x f(x) is odd, the integral equals 0.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫₀^π x sin x dx.
questions.answer: Using integration by parts, ∫₀^π x sin x dx = π.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫₀^π/2 sin²x dx.
questions.answer: Using identity, value = π/4.

questions.text: Evaluate ∫₀ᵃ (x² + 2x + 1) dx.
questions.answer: Value = [x³/3 + x² + x]₀ᵃ = a³/3 + a² + a.

chapters.title: Application of Definite Integration
chapters.description: Application of definite integrals to find area under a curve and area between curves in simple cases.
topics: Area under a curve y = f(x) above x-axis
Area between a curve and a line
Geometric interpretation of sign of integral
learningObjectives: Interpret area under a curve as a definite integral.
Set up and evaluate definite integrals to find region areas.
Find area between curves by taking appropriate difference.
Use symmetry to simplify area calculations.
Understand when area is taken as absolute value of integral.

questions.text: Write the formula for the area under the curve y = f(x) between x = a and x = b (f(x) ≥ 0).
questions.answer: Area A = ∫_a^b f(x) dx, provided f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b].

questions.text: Find the area under the curve y = x between x = 0 and x = 2.
questions.answer: Area = ∫_0^2 x dx = [x^2/2]_0^2 = (4/2) − 0 = 2 square units.

questions.text: Find the area bounded by the curve y = x^2 and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 3.
Find the area enclosed between the lines y = 0, x = 1, x = 3 and the curve y = 2x.
questions.answer: Area = ∫_1^3 2x dx = [x^2]_1^3 = 9 − 1 = 8 square units.

questions.text: Find the area between the curves y = x and y = x^2 from x = 0 to x = 1.
Find the area bounded by the parabola y = x^2 and the line y = 4.
questions.answer: Intersection points from x^2 = 4 ⇒ x = −2, 2. Area between line (upper) and curve (lower) = ∫_{−2}^2 (4 − x^2) dx. Compute: ∫_{−2}^2 4 dx = 4·(4) = 16, ∫_{−2}^2 x^2 dx = [x^3/3]_{−2}^2 = (8/3 − (−8/3)) = 16/3. So area = 16 − 16/3 = (48 − 16)/3 = 32/3 square units.

questions.text: Find the area bounded by y = sin x and x-axis between x = 0 and x = π.
questions.answer: Area = ∫_0^π sin x dx = [−cos x]_0^π = (−cos π) − (−cos 0) = 1 − (−1) = 2 square units.

questions.text: Why do we sometimes take absolute value of a definite integral when computing area?
questions.answer: Because area is always non-negative, but the definite integral can be negative when the curve lies below the x-axis; we take the absolute value to represent actual area.

questions.text: Find the area enclosed between the curves y = |x| and y = 2 − |x|.
questions.answer: Intersection from |x| = 2 − |x| ⇒ 2|x| = 2 ⇒ |x| = 1. So region symmetric, integrate from 0 to 1 and double. For 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, |x| = x, 2 − |x| = 2 − x. Area = 2∫_0^1 [(2 − x) − x] dx = 2∫_0^1 (2 − 2x) dx = 2[2x − x^2]_0^1 = 2[(2 − 1) − 0] = 2 square units.

questions.text: Show that the area enclosed between the parabola y^2 = 4ax and the line x = a is 8a^2 square units.
questions.answer: For parabola y^2 = 4ax ⇒ x = y^2/(4a). The line x = a intersects when a = y^2/(4a) ⇒ y^2 = 4a^2 ⇒ y = ±2a. Area between x = a (right) and parabola (left) from y = −2a to 2a is ∫_{−2a}^{2a} [a − y^2/(4a)] dy. Compute: ∫ a dy = a·(4a) = 4a^2; ∫ y^2 dy from −2a to 2a = [y^3/3]_{−2a}^{2a} = (8a^3/3 − (−8a^3/3)) = 16a^3/3. So area = 4a^2 − (1/(4a))·(16a^3/3) = 4a^2 − (16a^2/12) = 4a^2 − (4a^2/3) = (12a^2 − 4a^2)/3 = 8a^2/3 *? Wait*, check: (1/(4a))*16a^3/3 = 4a^2/3; thus 4a^2 − 4a^2/3 = (12a^2 − 4a^2)/3 = 8a^2/3. However the standard result is 8a^2/3; so the enclosed area equals 8a^2/3 square units.

questions.text: Area bounded by a curve and x-axis is given by:
questions.answer: ∫ y dx

questions.text: Area between the curve y = f(x) and x-axis from x=a to x=b is:
questions.answer: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

questions.text: Define area under a curve.
questions.answer: The area enclosed between a curve, x-axis, and ordinates is called area under the curve.

questions.text: Which method is used to find area between two curves?
questions.answer: Definite integration method.

questions.text: Find the area under the curve y = x from x = 0 to x = 2.
questions.answer: Area = ∫₀² x dx = 2.

questions.text: Find the area bounded by y = x², x-axis and x = 1.
questions.answer: Area = ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3.

questions.text: State the formula for area between two curves y=f(x) and y=g(x).
questions.answer: Area = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x) − g(x)] dx, where f(x) ≥ g(x).

questions.text: Find the area between curves y = x² and y = x from x = 0 to x = 1.
questions.answer: Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/6.

questions.text: Find the area bounded by y = sin x, x-axis and x = 0 to π.
questions.answer: Area = ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2.

questions.text: Find the area enclosed between y = x² and y = 4.
questions.answer: Intersection at x = ±2; Area = ∫₋₂² (4 − x²) dx = 32/3.

chapters.title: Differential Equations
chapters.description: Definition, order and degree of differential equation, formation of differential equations and solutions of first order first degree differential equations using various methods.

Linear differential equation of type dy/dx + Py = Q
Applications to growth and decay, simple modelling

questions.text: Define the order of a differential equation.
questions.answer: Order of a differential equation is the highest order of derivative of the dependent variable occurring in the equation.

questions.text: Find the order and degree of the differential equation d^2y/dx^2 + (dy/dx)^3 = 0.
questions.answer: Highest derivative is d^2y/dx^2 ⇒ order 2. Powers of derivatives are integers and equation is polynomial in derivatives; highest power of highest derivative is 1 ⇒ degree 1.

questions.text: Form the differential equation of the family y = C e^{2x}.
questions.answer: Differentiate: dy/dx = 2C e^{2x} = 2y. Eliminate C to get dy/dx − 2y = 0.

questions.text: Solve dy/dx = 3x^2.
questions.answer: Integrate: dy = 3x^2 dx ⇒ y = x^3 + C.

questions.text: Solve the differential equation dy/dx = (x + 1)/(y + 1).
questions.answer: Separate variables: (y + 1) dy = (x + 1) dx. Integrate: ∫(y + 1) dy = ∫(x + 1) dx ⇒ (y^2/2 + y) = (x^2/2 + x) + C. Multiply by 2: y^2 + 2y = x^2 + 2x + C'.

questions.text: Solve the linear differential equation dy/dx + y = e^x.
questions.answer: Here P = 1, Q = e^x. Integrating factor IF = e^{∫P dx} = e^x. Then solution: y·e^x = ∫ e^x·e^x dx + C = ∫ e^{2x} dx + C = (1/2) e^{2x} + C. So y = (1/2)e^{x} + C e^{-x}.

questions.text: Solve dy/dx − 2y = 0 given that y(0) = 3.
questions.answer: Linear with P = −2, Q = 0. IF = e^{∫−2 dx} = e^{−2x}. Then y·e^{−2x} = ∫0 dx + C = C. So y = C e^{2x}. Use y(0) = 3 ⇒ C = 3. Thus y = 3e^{2x}.

questions.text: What is a general solution and a particular solution of a differential equation?
questions.answer: General solution contains arbitrary constant(s), representing a family of solutions. Particular solution is obtained from general solution by assigning specific values to constants using given conditions.

questions.text: Solve the homogeneous differential equation dy/dx = (x + y)/(x − y).
questions.answer: Homogeneous; put y = vx ⇒ dy/dx = v + x dv/dx. Then v + x dv/dx = (x + vx)/(x − vx) = (1 + v)/(1 − v). So x dv/dx = (1 + v)/(1 − v) − v = [(1 + v) − v(1 − v)]/(1 − v) = [1 + v − v + v^2]/(1 − v) = (1 + v^2)/(1 − v). Thus (1 − v)/(1 + v^2) dv = dx/x. Integrate: ∫(1 − v)/(1 + v^2) dv = ∫ dx/x. Split: ∫ 1/(1 + v^2) dv − ∫ v/(1 + v^2) dv = tan^{-1}v − (1/2)·ln(1 + v^2) = ln|x| + C. Substitute v = y/x.

questions.text: In a certain chemical reaction, the rate of decay of a substance is proportional to the amount present at time t. If initially the amount is A_0, set up the differential equation and write its solution.
questions.answer: Let A(t) be amount at time t. Statement gives dA/dt ∝ −A ⇒ dA/dt = −kA, k > 0. This is linear: dA/dt + kA = 0. Solution: A = C e^{−kt}. Using A(0) = A_0 gives C = A_0. So A(t) = A_0 e^{−kt}.

questions.text: The order of the differential equation (d²y/dx²) + dy/dx = 0 is:
The general solution of a differential equation contains:
options: As many constants as the order
questions.answer: As many constants as the order

questions.text: Define order of a differential equation.
questions.answer: The highest order of derivative present in the differential equation is called its order.

questions.text: What is a particular solution?
questions.answer: A solution obtained by assigning specific values to the constants in the general solution is called a particular solution.

questions.text: Find the degree of the differential equation (d²y/dx²)² + dy/dx = 0.
questions.answer: Degree is 2.

questions.text: Solve: dy/dx = x.
questions.answer: Integrating, y = x²/2 + C.

questions.text: Form the differential equation of the family y = Cx².
questions.answer: Differentiating gives dy/dx = 2Cx = 2y/x.

questions.text: Solve the differential equation: dy/dx = y.
questions.answer: Separating variables, ln y = x + C or y = Ce^x.

questions.text: Solve: dy/dx + y = e^x.
questions.answer: Using integrating factor, solution is y = (x + C)e^x.

questions.text: Solve the differential equation: (1 + y²) dx + x dy = 0.
questions.answer: Rewriting and integrating gives x² + ln(1 + y²) = C.

questions.text: Define a random variable.
questions.answer: A random variable is a real-valued function that assigns to each outcome of a random experiment a real number.

questions.text: Which of the following is a discrete random variable?
options: Time taken to complete an exam
Height of students in a class
Number of heads in 3 coin tosses
Amount of rainfall in a day
questions.answer: Number of heads in 3 coin tosses

questions.text: A discrete random variable X takes values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities P(X=0)=0.2, P(X=1)=0.5 and P(X=2)=0.3. Find E(X).
For the random variable in Q3, find Var(X).
A fair die is rolled once. Let X be the score. Write the probability distribution of X.
questions.answer: X takes values 1,2,3,4,5,6 each with probability 1/6. So P(X = k) = 1/6 for k = 1,2,3,4,5,6.

questions.text: A discrete random variable X has the following probability distribution: X: 1, 2, 3, 4 with P(X=1)=k, P(X=2)=2k, P(X=3)=3k, P(X=4)=4k. Find k and E(X).
How is variance of a discrete random variable defined in terms of its distribution?
questions.answer: Variance Var(X) is defined as Var(X) = Σ (x − μ)^2 P(X = x), where μ = E(X). Equivalently Var(X) = E(X^2) − [E(X)]^2.

questions.text: Let a continuous random variable X have probability density function f(x) = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2 and 0 otherwise. Find P(0.5 ≤ X ≤ 1.5).
What is the relation between probability density function (PDF) and distribution function (CDF) of a continuous random variable?
questions.answer: For a continuous random variable X with PDF f(x), the CDF F(x) is given by F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = ∫_{−∞}^x f(t) dt. Conversely, f(x) is the derivative of F(x) wherever derivative exists.

questions.text: A continuous random variable X has PDF f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2 and 0 otherwise. Find k, the distribution function F(x) and E(X).
The sum of probabilities of all possible values of a random variable is:
If X is a random variable, then P(X = x) is called:
questions.answer: Probability distribution

questions.text: Define a random variable.
questions.answer: A random variable is a function that assigns a real number to each outcome of a random experiment.

questions.text: What is a discrete random variable?
questions.answer: A random variable that takes countable values is called a discrete random variable.

questions.text: Define probability distribution of a random variable.
questions.answer: It is a table or function that gives probability for each possible value of the random variable.

questions.text: Find the mean of a discrete random variable X with distribution: X: 0,1,2; P(X): 1/6, 1/2, 1/3.
Write the formula for variance of a discrete random variable.
questions.answer: Var(X) = Σx²P(x) − [ΣxP(x)]².

questions.text: Find the variance of X if X takes values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3.
questions.answer: Mean = 2.1, Variance = 0.49.

questions.text: Find the mean and variance of a probability distribution given in tabular form.
questions.answer: Mean and variance are calculated using standard formulas ΣxP(x) and Σx²P(x) − μ².

questions.text: Show that the variance of a random variable is always non-negative.
questions.answer: Since variance is the expected value of squared deviation, it is always ≥ 0.
