questions.text: State the conditions under which a binomial distribution is applicable.
questions.answer: Conditions: (i) Fixed number n of trials, (ii) Each trial has two possible outcomes (success or failure), (iii) Probability of success p is constant for every trial, (iv) Trials are independent.

questions.text: Write the probability mass function of a binomial distribution with parameters n and p.
A coin is tossed 4 times. Assuming a fair coin, find the probability of getting exactly 2 heads.
Find the mean and variance of a binomial distribution with parameters n and p.
questions.answer: Mean = E(X) = np, variance = Var(X) = np(1 − p).

questions.text: In a binomial distribution B(10, 0.3), find P(X = 0) and P(X = 10).
A die is thrown 5 times. What is the probability of getting exactly three times a '4'?
A manufacturer of bulbs finds that 5% of the bulbs are defective. If he packs 20 bulbs in a box, what is the expected number of defective bulbs per box?
questions.answer: Here n = 20, p = 0.05. Expected number of defective bulbs = np = 20·0.05 = 1.

questions.text: If X ~ B(n, p), express the standard deviation of X in terms of n and p.
questions.answer: Standard deviation σ = √[Var(X)] = √[np(1 − p)].

questions.text: For a binomial distribution, n = 8 and p = 0.4. Find P(X ≥ 6).
questions.answer:
P(X ≥ 6) = P(X = 6) + P(X = 7) + P(X = 8).
P(X = 6) = C(8,6)0.4^6·0.6^2 = 28·0.4^6·0.6^2.
P(X = 7) = C(8,7)0.4^7·0.6 = 8·0.4^7·0.6.
P(X = 8) = C(8,8)0.4^8 = 0.4^8.
Students may compute the numerical value using calculator if allowed.

questions.text: In a binomial distribution B(n, p), it is known that mean is 4 and variance is 3. Find n and p.
questions.answer: Mean np = 4, variance np(1 − p) = 3. From np = 4 ⇒ p = 4/n. Substitute: np(1 − p) = 4(1 − 4/n) = 3 ⇒ 4 − 16/n = 3 ⇒ 4 − 3 = 16/n ⇒ 1 = 16/n ⇒ n = 16. Then p = 4/16 = 1/4.

questions.text: In a binomial distribution, the number of trials is:
questions.answer: Fixed

questions.text: If p is the probability of success, then q equals:
State the probability mass function of binomial distribution.
questions.answer: P(X = x) = ⁿCₓ pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ, where x = 0,1,2,…,n.

questions.text: What is the mean of a binomial distribution?
questions.answer: Mean = np.

questions.text: Write the variance of a binomial distribution.
questions.answer: Variance = npq.

questions.text: Find the mean of a binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.4.
Find the variance if n = 8 and p = 0.5.
questions.answer: Variance = npq = 8 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 2.

questions.text: Find P(X = 3) for a binomial distribution with n = 5 and p = 0.4.
Find the mean and variance of a binomial distribution with n = 6 and p = 1/3.
questions.answer: Mean = np = 2, Variance = npq = 4/3.

questions.text: A coin is tossed 4 times. Find the probability of getting exactly two heads.
questions.answer: Using binomial distribution, P(X=2)=⁴C₂(1/2)⁴ = 3/8.

chapters.title: Rotational Dynamics
chapters.description: Uniform and non-uniform circular motion, centripetal and centrifugal forces, banking of roads, conical pendulum, vertical circular motion, moment of inertia, radius of gyration and basic theorems for moment of inertia.
topics: Vehicle on level and banked roads
Moment of inertia and radius of gyration
Theorems of parallel and perpendicular axes
learningObjectives: Describe kinematics of circular motion using angular variables.
Explain centripetal and centrifugal forces with real-life examples.
Apply concepts of banking and friction to calculate safe speeds on curves.
Analyse conical and vertical pendulum motion using energy and force diagrams.
Define and calculate moment of inertia for simple rigid bodies.
Use theorems of parallel and perpendicular axes to find moment of inertia.

questions.text: The force responsible for circular motion of a stone tied to a string and whirled in a horizontal circle is:
options: Normal reaction of air on the stone
questions.answer: Tension providing centripetal force

questions.text: Define centripetal acceleration and write its expression for a body in uniform circular motion.
questions.answer: Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration directed towards the centre of the circular path which changes only the direction of velocity. Its magnitude is aᵣ = v²/r = ω²r.

questions.text: A car of mass 1000 kg takes a turn on a level road of radius 50 m at a speed of 10 m/s. Find the minimum coefficient of static friction required between tyres and road so that the car does not skid.
questions.answer:
Centripetal force = mv²/r = 1000×10²/50 = 2000 N.
Maximum friction = μₛN = μₛmg = μₛ×1000×9.8.
Equate: μₛ×1000×9.8 = 2000 ⇒ μₛ = 2000/9800 ≈ 0.204.

questions.text: A vehicle moves on a smooth banked road of radius 100 m and banking angle 30°. Find the speed at which no friction is required for safe turning (g = 9.8 m/s²).
questions.answer:
For no friction: v = √(rg tanθ) = √(100 × 9.8 × tan30°)
= √(980 × 1/√3) ≈ √(566) ≈ 23.8 m/s (approximately).

questions.text: What is a conical pendulum? Write the expression for its time period.
questions.answer: A conical pendulum is a pendulum in which the bob describes a horizontal circle while the string traces the surface of a cone. For string length L and semi-vertical angle θ, period T = 2π√(L cosθ / g).

questions.text: A small mass is whirled in a vertical circle of radius 1 m using a light string. Find the minimum speed at the highest point so that the string just remains taut (g = 9.8 m/s²).
questions.answer: At top: T_min = 0, so mg = mv²/r ⇒ v² = gr ⇒ v = √(9.8×1) ≈ 3.13 m/s.

questions.text: Define moment of inertia and write its expression for a system of discrete particles.
questions.answer: Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass; it measures opposition to change in rotational motion about an axis. For discrete particles: I = Σ mᵢ rᵢ².

questions.text: Moment of inertia of a thin ring of mass M and radius R about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is:
questions.answer: MR²

questions.text: State the theorem of parallel axes for moment of inertia.
questions.answer: The moment of inertia I about any axis parallel to an axis through the centre of mass is I = I_cm + Md², where I_cm is moment of inertia about the parallel axis through centre of mass and d is the perpendicular distance between the axes.

questions.text: A uniform disc of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m rotates about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane with angular speed 10 rad/s. Calculate its moment of inertia and rotational kinetic energy.
The moment of inertia of a disc of radius R and mass M about its central axis is:
questions.answer: MR²/2

questions.text: A body performing uniform circular motion has constant:
questions.answer: kinetic energy

questions.text: Define centripetal force.
questions.answer: The force acting towards the centre of a circular path that keeps a body in circular motion is called centripetal force.

questions.text: Define moment of inertia of a rotating rigid body. State its SI unit.
questions.answer: Moment of inertia is the rotational inertia of a body about an axis. Its SI unit is kg m².

questions.text: State and prove the principle of conservation of angular momentum.
questions.answer: If no external torque acts on a system, its angular momentum remains constant.

questions.text: An electron revolves in a circular orbit of radius 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m with speed 3 × 10⁶ m/s. Find its angular momentum.
questions.answer: Angular momentum = mvr = 9.1×10⁻³¹ × 3×10⁶ × 5.3×10⁻¹¹ = 1.45×10⁻³⁴ kg m²/s

questions.text: A torque of 400 Nm acting on a body of mass 40 kg produces angular acceleration of 20 rad/s². Find the moment of inertia.
questions.answer: Moment of inertia I = τ/α = 400/20 = 20 kg m²

questions.text: Derive an expression for the kinetic energy of a body rotating with uniform angular velocity.
questions.answer: K.E. = ½ Iω², derived by summing kinetic energies of particles forming the rigid body.

questions.text: Derive expressions for linear velocity at lowest, mid and top positions of a particle in vertical circular motion.
questions.answer: Using energy conservation, minimum velocity at top is √(gr), expressions follow accordingly.

chapters.title: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
chapters.description: Pressure in fluids, Pascal’s law, hydraulic devices, atmospheric pressure and barometer, surface tension, capillarity, contact angle, viscosity, streamline and turbulent flow, Bernoulli’s theorem and applications.
topics: Streamline vs turbulent flow, Reynolds number
learningObjectives: Explain how pressure varies with depth in a fluid and use Pascal’s law in devices.
Discuss atmospheric pressure measurement using a barometer.
Define surface tension and explain related phenomena like capillary rise.
Describe viscosity and distinguish streamline and turbulent flow.
Apply Bernoulli’s theorem to simple fluid flow situations.

questions.text: State Pascal’s law for fluids.
questions.answer: Pascal’s law: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every portion of the fluid and to the walls of the containing vessel.

questions.text: A liquid of density 800 kg/m³ is filled in a tank. Find the pressure at a depth of 2 m below the free surface (g = 9.8 m/s²).
The rise of liquid in a capillary tube is due to:
questions.answer: Surface tension and adhesion

questions.text: Define surface tension. State its SI unit.
questions.answer: Surface tension is the force per unit length acting along the surface of a liquid at right angles to a line drawn in the surface. SI unit: N/m.

questions.text: Calculate the excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius 2 mm. Surface tension of soap solution is 0.03 N/m.
Differentiate between streamline flow and turbulent flow.
questions.answer: In streamline flow, each fluid particle follows a smooth, well-defined path and paths do not cross; velocity at a point is steady. In turbulent flow, motion is irregular with eddies; velocity and direction change randomly with time.

questions.text: Water flows steadily through a pipe of cross-sectional area 4×10⁻⁴ m² with speed 2 m/s. The pipe narrows to an area of 1×10⁻⁴ m². Find the speed in the narrow portion.
questions.answer: By continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ ⇒ v₂ = A₁v₁/A₂ = (4×10⁻⁴×2)/(1×10⁻⁴) = 8 m/s.

questions.text: Using Bernoulli’s theorem, explain why the roof of a house may be blown off during a storm when wind speed above the roof is very high.
questions.answer: High wind speed above roof ⇒ high v ⇒ lower pressure above according to Bernoulli (P + ½ρv² = constant). Pressure inside room remains nearly atmospheric. So greater pressure inside pushes roof upward; if force exceeds weight and fixtures, roof may be lifted.

questions.text: The SI unit of coefficient of viscosity is:
questions.answer: Pa·s

questions.text: Define Reynolds number. What does a low value of Reynolds number signify about the flow?
questions.answer: Reynolds number Re = ρvd/η, where v is characteristic speed, d is diameter, ρ is density and η is viscosity. Low Re (typically < 1000) indicates predominantly streamline (laminar) flow.

questions.text: The SI unit of coefficient of viscosity is:
questions.answer: Pa s

questions.text: Viscosity of liquids generally ______ with increase in temperature.
questions.answer: decreases

questions.text: Define viscosity.
questions.answer: Viscosity is the property of a fluid by virtue of which it resists relative motion between its layers.

questions.text: State Pascal’s law.
questions.answer: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions.

questions.text: Explain surface tension.
questions.answer: Surface tension is the force per unit length acting tangentially on the surface of a liquid.

questions.text: Why do liquids rise in a capillary tube?
questions.answer: Due to surface tension and adhesive forces between liquid and tube walls.

questions.text: Calculate excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius 2 mm if surface tension is 0.03 N/m.
questions.answer: Excess pressure = 4T/r = 4×0.03 / 2×10⁻³ = 60 N/m²

questions.text: Find the terminal velocity of a sphere of radius 1 mm falling through a liquid of viscosity η.
questions.answer: Using Stokes’ law: v = 2r²(ρ−σ)g / 9η

questions.text: Derive an expression for terminal velocity of a sphere moving through a viscous fluid.
questions.answer: At terminal velocity, gravitational force equals viscous force; using Stokes’ law leads to v = 2r²(ρ−σ)g / 9η.

questions.text: Explain Bernoulli’s theorem and state its applications.
questions.answer: Bernoulli’s theorem states that total energy of a fluid remains constant along a streamline. Applications include lift on airplane wings and venturimeter.

chapters.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
chapters.description: Ideal gas equation, assumptions of kinetic theory, pressure of an ideal gas, mean free path, degrees of freedom, equipartition theorem, specific heats, real gases and van der Waals equation, thermal radiation, black body, Stefan–Boltzmann law and Wien’s law.
topics: Ideal gas and kinetic theory assumptions
Pressure and temperature in kinetic theory
Mean free path and collision frequency
Degrees of freedom and equipartition of energy
Specific heats of monoatomic and diatomic gases
Real gases and van der Waals equation
Black body radiation and Stefan–Boltzmann law
learningObjectives: State the assumptions of kinetic theory and derive expression for pressure of an ideal gas.
Explain mean free path and factors affecting it.
Use equipartition theorem to calculate internal energy and specific heats.
Distinguish between ideal and real gases and write van der Waals equation.
Describe characteristics of black body radiation and apply Stefan–Boltzmann law.

questions.text: Write the ideal gas equation and define each symbol used.
questions.answer: Ideal gas equation: PV = nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is number of moles, R is universal gas constant and T is absolute temperature.

questions.text: State any two assumptions of kinetic theory of gases.
questions.answer: Examples: (1) Gas consists of a large number of identical molecules moving in random directions. (2) Volume of molecules is negligible compared to container volume. (3) Intermolecular forces are negligible except during collisions. (Any two.)

questions.text: Show that average translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas is (3/2)kT.
questions.answer:
From kinetic theory, PV = (1/3)Nm⟨c²⟩ and also PV = NkT.
Equate: (1/3)Nm⟨c²⟩ = NkT ⇒ (1/2)m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT, so average KE = (3/2)kT.

questions.text: What is mean free path? On which factors does it depend?
questions.answer: Mean free path is the average distance traveled by a molecule between successive collisions. It depends on number density of molecules, size (diameter) of molecules and temperature/pressure of gas.

questions.text: Using law of equipartition, find molar specific heat at constant volume Cᵥ for a monoatomic ideal gas.
questions.answer:
Monoatomic gas has 3 translational degrees of freedom ⇒ average energy per mole = (f/2)RT = (3/2)RT.
By definition U = nCᵥT for 1 mol ⇒ Cᵥ = (1/U)(dU/dT) = (3/2)R.

questions.text: For a diatomic ideal gas at room temperature, the approximate ratio Cₚ/Cᵥ is:
Write van der Waals equation for n moles of a real gas and explain the significance of constants a and b.
questions.answer:
Equation: (P + a(n/V)²)(V − nb) = nRT.
Here a accounts for intermolecular attractions (corrects pressure) and b represents excluded volume due to finite size of molecules.

questions.text: State Stefan–Boltzmann law of radiation.
questions.answer: Total radiant energy emitted per unit area per unit time by a black body is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature: E = σT⁴.

questions.text: According to Wien’s displacement law, λₘT = constant, where λₘ is:
questions.answer: Maximum wavelength emitted (peak)

questions.text: The maximum intensity of radiation from a black body occurs at 580 nm. Estimate its surface temperature using Wien’s law (b = 2.9×10⁻³ m·K).
The root mean square speed of gas molecules is proportional to:
questions.answer: √T

questions.text: Which of the following laws relates pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature?
questions.answer: Boyle’s law

questions.text: Define absolute zero temperature.
questions.answer: Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature at which molecular motion ceases, equal to 0 K.

questions.text: State Avogadro’s law.
questions.answer: Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules.

questions.text: Explain mean free path of gas molecules.
questions.answer: Mean free path is the average distance travelled by a molecule between two successive collisions.

questions.text: Why real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure?
questions.answer: Because intermolecular forces and finite size of molecules become significant at high pressure.

questions.text: Calculate the rms speed of oxygen molecules at 300 K. (Molecular mass = 32 g/mol)
questions.answer: v_rms = √(3RT/M) ≈ 484 m/s

questions.text: Find the pressure exerted by an ideal gas if number density and mean square speed are given.
questions.answer: Using P = (1/3)ρ⟨c²⟩

questions.text: Derive the expression for pressure of an ideal gas using kinetic theory.
questions.answer: By considering molecular collisions with container walls, pressure P = (1/3)ρ⟨c²⟩ is obtained.

questions.text: Explain black body radiation and Wien’s displacement law.
questions.answer: A black body absorbs all radiation. Wien’s law states λ_max T = constant.

chapters.title: Thermodynamics
chapters.description: Thermodynamic system, variables, processes, first law of thermodynamics, work and heat, specific heats, second law, reversible and irreversible processes, heat engines, Carnot cycle, refrigerator and efficiency.
topics: Thermodynamic system, state variables and equation of state
Isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isochoric processes
Heat engine, efficiency and Carnot cycle
learningObjectives: Define thermodynamic system and distinguish various thermodynamic processes.
Apply first law to calculate heat, work and internal energy changes.
Use PV diagrams to represent processes and cycles.
Describe second law and limitations on conversion of heat into work.
Explain working of heat engines, Carnot cycle and refrigerator.

questions.text: State the first law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: First law: The heat supplied to a system is used to change its internal energy and to do work on the surroundings: ΔQ = ΔU + W.

questions.text: In an isothermal process for an ideal gas:
questions.answer: Temperature remains constant

questions.text: Distinguish between isochoric and isobaric processes.
questions.answer: Isochoric: volume constant, so no work is done; pressure and temperature may change. Isobaric: pressure constant, so system expands or contracts; both volume and temperature change.

questions.text: An ideal gas is taken through a process in which 500 J of heat is supplied and 200 J of work is done by the system. Find the change in internal energy.
State Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: It is impossible to construct a device operating in a cycle that converts all the heat absorbed from a single reservoir completely into work without any other effect.

questions.text: A heat engine absorbs 1000 J of heat from a source and rejects 600 J to the sink in one cycle. Calculate the efficiency of the engine.
questions.answer: Work done W = Q₁ − Q₂ = 1000 − 600 = 400 J. Efficiency η = W/Q₁ = 400/1000 = 0.4 = 40%.

questions.text: A Carnot engine operates between 600 K and 300 K. Calculate its efficiency. If it absorbs 900 J of heat from the source, how much work does it perform?
Define coefficient of performance (COP) of a refrigerator.
questions.answer: COP of a refrigerator is the ratio of heat removed from the cold reservoir per cycle to the work done on the system per cycle: COP = Q₂/W.

questions.text: In an adiabatic process for an ideal gas:
options: No heat is exchanged with surroundings
questions.answer: No heat is exchanged with surroundings

questions.text: Explain with a labelled PV diagram the working of a Carnot engine and derive the expression for its efficiency in terms of source and sink temperatures.
questions.answer: Answer should include: description of four reversible steps (isothermal expansion at T₁, adiabatic expansion T₁→T₂, isothermal compression at T₂, adiabatic compression T₂→T₁); PV diagram showing cycle; use of first law for isothermals giving Q₁ and Q₂; derivation η = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ = 1 − T₂/T₁ for ideal gas.

questions.text: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of conservation of:
questions.answer: energy

questions.text: In an isothermal process, the temperature of the system:
questions.answer: remains constant

questions.text: Define thermodynamic system.
questions.answer: A thermodynamic system is a specified quantity of matter or a region in space chosen for thermodynamic study.

questions.text: State the first law of thermodynamics.
questions.answer: Heat supplied to a system equals the increase in internal energy plus work done by the system.

questions.text: What is an adiabatic process?
questions.answer: An adiabatic process is one in which no heat is exchanged between the system and surroundings.

questions.text: Why is the efficiency of a heat engine always less than 100%?
questions.answer: Because some heat is always rejected to the sink as required by the second law of thermodynamics.

questions.text: An ideal gas absorbs 300 J of heat and does 100 J of work. Find the change in internal energy.
Calculate the efficiency of a Carnot engine working between 400 K and 300 K.
Derive an expression for work done during an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas.
questions.answer: Work done W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁) derived using Boyle’s law and integration.

questions.text: Explain the second law of thermodynamics and its significance.
questions.answer: The second law states that heat flows naturally from hot to cold bodies and introduces the concept of entropy and irreversibility.

chapters.title: Oscillations
chapters.description: Simple harmonic motion (SHM), differential equation of SHM, energy in SHM, damped and forced oscillations, resonance, simple pendulum and related concepts.
topics: Simple harmonic motion and restoring force
learningObjectives: Identify SHM and write its displacement equation.
Use differential equation approach to describe SHM.
Calculate velocity, acceleration and energy of a SHM at different positions.
Describe damped and forced oscillations and the phenomenon of resonance.
Derive expression for time period of a simple pendulum.

questions.text: Define simple harmonic motion and give one example.
questions.answer: SHM is oscillatory motion in which the restoring force is directly proportional to displacement and always directed towards mean position. Example: small oscillations of a simple pendulum.

questions.text: In SHM, acceleration is:
options: Directly proportional to displacement and opposite in direction
questions.answer: Directly proportional to displacement and opposite in direction

questions.text: A particle performing SHM has amplitude 0.05 m and time period 2 s. Write its displacement equation if at t = 0, it is at mean position and moving in positive direction.
questions.answer:
Angular frequency ω = 2π/T = π rad/s.
Since x(0) = 0 and motion towards +ve, x = A sin(ωt) ⇒ x = 0.05 sin(πt) m.

questions.text: For a SHM, maximum speed is 0.4 m/s and amplitude is 0.08 m. Find its angular frequency and time period.
Write the expressions for potential and kinetic energy of a particle executing SHM.
questions.answer: For mass m, angular frequency ω and displacement x: potential energy U = (1/2)kx = (1/2)mω²x²; kinetic energy K = (1/2)m(v²) = (1/2)mω²(A² − x²).

questions.text: What is damping? Give one example of damped oscillations.
questions.answer: Damping is reduction in amplitude of oscillations with time due to resistive forces. Example: oscillations of a pendulum in air, vibrating tuning fork in air, etc.

questions.text: Define resonance. State one useful and one harmful effect of resonance.
questions.answer: Resonance is the phenomenon in which a system oscillates with large amplitude when driven by a periodic force of frequency close to its natural frequency. Useful: tuning in radio, resonance in musical instruments. Harmful: collapse of structures like bridges when forced near natural frequency.

questions.text: Derive the expression for time period of a simple pendulum executing small oscillations.
questions.answer: For small angle θ, restoring torque ≈ −mglθ, and angular acceleration θ¨ = −(g/l)θ ⇒ SHM with ω = √(g/l). Therefore T = 2π√(l/g). (Steps showing small angle approximation and SHM form should be included.)

questions.text: A simple pendulum of length 1 m has time period 2.0 s. Find its acceleration due to gravity from this data.
questions.answer: T = 2π√(l/g) ⇒ g = 4π²l/T² = 4π²×1 / 4 = π² ≈ 9.87 m/s².

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT change when damping is introduced in a weakly damped oscillator?
questions.answer: Frequency (approximately)

questions.text: The SI unit of angular frequency is:
questions.answer: rad s⁻¹

questions.text: The time period of a simple pendulum depends on:
questions.answer: length of pendulum

questions.text: Define simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer: Simple harmonic motion is a periodic motion in which the restoring force is directly proportional to displacement and acts towards the mean position.

questions.text: Write the expression for time period of a simple pendulum.
questions.answer: T = 2π√(l/g)

questions.text: What is angular frequency? Give its relation with time period.
questions.answer: Angular frequency ω = 2π/T

questions.text: Why is the motion of a simple pendulum approximately SHM for small oscillations?
questions.answer: For small angles, sinθ ≈ θ, making restoring force proportional to displacement.

questions.text: Find the time period of a simple pendulum of length 1 m. (g = 9.8 m/s²)
A particle executes SHM with frequency 2 Hz. Find its angular frequency.
questions.answer: ω = 2πf = 4π rad/s

questions.text: Derive the expression for time period of a simple pendulum.
questions.answer: Using torque and small-angle approximation, T = 2π√(l/g) is derived.

questions.text: Obtain expressions for velocity and acceleration of a particle in SHM.
questions.answer: v = ω√(A² − x²) and a = −ω²x

chapters.title: Superposition of Waves
chapters.description: Progressive waves, principle of superposition, interference of waves, formation of stationary waves in strings and pipes, beats and their applications.
topics: Stationary waves in strings and air columns
learningObjectives: Describe progressive waves and their basic properties.
Apply the principle of superposition for wave pulses and continuous waves.
Distinguish between constructive and destructive interference and calculate resultant amplitude.
Explain formation of stationary waves in strings and air columns.
Define beats and determine beat frequency in simple situations.

questions.text: In a progressive mechanical wave, which of the following is transferred?
questions.answer: Only energy and momentum

questions.text: State the principle of superposition of waves.
questions.answer: When two or more waves overlap in space, the resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of displacements due to each wave acting independently.

questions.text: Two waves of amplitudes 3 cm and 4 cm superpose in phase. Find the resultant amplitude and resultant intensity (in terms of I₀, the intensity due to 1 cm amplitude).
questions.answer: Resultant amplitude A = 3 + 4 = 7 cm. Intensity ∝ A², so I = 7² I₀ = 49 I₀.

questions.text: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. What is the beat frequency? How much time is required between successive maxima of sound intensity?
questions.answer: Beat frequency = |260 − 256| = 4 Hz. Time between successive maxima = 1/4 s = 0.25 s.

questions.text: What are stationary waves? State one condition for their formation on a stretched string.
questions.answer: Stationary waves are waves in which certain points (nodes) have zero displacement and others (antinodes) have maximum displacement, with no net energy transfer along the medium. They form when two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose, usually due to reflection at fixed ends.

questions.text: A string of length 1.2 m is fixed at both ends and vibrates in its fundamental mode with a wave speed of 60 m/s. Find its fundamental frequency.
questions.answer: For fundamental, λ = 2L = 2 × 1.2 = 2.4 m. f = v/λ = 60 / 2.4 = 25 Hz.

questions.text: Two waves y₁ = A sin(ωt) and y₂ = A sin(ωt + π) superpose. Find the expression for the resultant displacement and its amplitude.
questions.answer: Resultant y = y₁ + y₂ = A[sin(ωt) + sin(ωt + π)] = A[sin(ωt) − sin(ωt)] = 0. Resultant amplitude is zero (complete destructive interference).

questions.text: List any two properties of a progressive wave travelling in an elastic medium.
questions.answer: Any two: (i) Each particle performs SHM about its mean position. (ii) All particles have same amplitude and frequency. (iii) There is a phase difference between neighbouring particles. (iv) Energy is transported along the direction of propagation.

questions.text: The amplitude of each of two interfering waves is A. Show that the ratio of maximum intensity to minimum intensity in the interference pattern is (I_max / I_min) = ∞ when the amplitudes are equal and nonzero.
questions.answer: Resultant amplitude A_R = 2A for constructive interference and 0 for destructive interference. Intensities: I_max ∝ (2A)² = 4A², I_min ∝ 0² = 0, so I_max / I_min = 4A² / 0 → ∞.

questions.text: Explain the formation of stationary waves on a string fixed at both ends. Derive the condition for the frequencies of the harmonics in terms of string length and wave speed.
questions.answer: A wave travelling along the string reflects from the fixed ends and superposes with the incoming wave. For certain frequencies, nodes form at both fixed ends and standing patterns appear. The distance between adjacent nodes is λ/2. For a string of length L fixed at both ends, allowed wavelengths are λ_n = 2L/n (n = 1,2,3,...). Since v = f_n λ_n, we get f_n = n(v/2L). These are the harmonic frequencies of the string.

questions.text: The phenomenon of interference is due to:
questions.answer: Superposition of waves

questions.text: In Young’s double slit experiment, bright fringes are formed due to:
questions.answer: Constructive interference

questions.text: State the principle of superposition of waves.
questions.answer: When two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of individual displacements.

questions.text: What is interference of waves?
questions.answer: Interference is the phenomenon of redistribution of energy due to superposition of two coherent waves.

questions.text: Define coherent sources.
questions.answer: Coherent sources emit waves of same frequency having constant phase difference.

questions.text: Why do interference fringes disappear when one slit is closed?
questions.answer: Because interference requires superposition of waves from two coherent sources.

questions.text: Calculate fringe width if wavelength = 600 nm, distance between slits = 0.5 mm and screen distance = 1 m.
Find the position of the first dark fringe in YDSE.
questions.answer: First dark fringe occurs at path difference λ/2 from central maximum.

questions.text: Explain Young’s double slit experiment with necessary theory.
questions.answer: YDSE demonstrates wave nature of light by forming alternate bright and dark fringes due to interference.

questions.text: Derive expression for fringe width in Young’s double slit experiment.
questions.answer: Fringe width β = λD/d derived using path difference and constructive interference condition.

learningObjectives: Explain the need for wave theory of light and state Huygens’ principle.
Describe coherent sources and conditions for sustained interference.

Explain diffraction patterns and factors affecting fringe width and intensity.
Describe plane polarization and applications of polarizing devices.

questions.text: In Young’s double-slit experiment, fringe width is directly proportional to:
questions.answer: Wavelength and distance to screen

questions.text: What is meant by coherent sources of light?
questions.answer: Coherent sources are two or more sources that emit light waves of the same frequency and a constant phase difference between them.

questions.text: In a double-slit experiment, the slit separation is 0.5 mm and the screen is 2 m away. If the fringe width is 2.4 mm, calculate the wavelength of light used.
State Malus’ law for polarization of light.
questions.answer: When completely plane-polarized light is incident on an analyser, the transmitted intensity I is given by I = I₀ cos²θ, where θ is the angle between the transmission directions of the polarizer and analyser.

questions.text: Light of intensity I₀ is incident on two ideal polarizers. The angle between their transmission axes is 60°. Find the transmitted intensity.
questions.answer: After first polarizer intensity is I₀/2. After second, I = (I₀/2) cos²60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = I₀/8.

questions.text: Differentiate between interference and diffraction of light (any two points).
questions.answer: Interference: due to superposition of waves from two or more coherent sources; fringe width is uniform; occurs over entire screen. Diffraction: due to bending of light around edges/apertures; fringes are generally not equally spaced; usually produced by a single aperture or obstacle.

questions.text: In a single-slit diffraction experiment, the first minimum is observed at an angle of 30′ (30 minutes) when light of wavelength 500 nm is used. Estimate the slit width.
What is meant by resolving power of a telescope?
questions.answer: Resolving power is the ability of a telescope to distinguish two closely spaced point objects as separate. Quantitatively it is the reciprocal of the angular separation of the just-resolved images.

questions.text: Explain how Young’s double-slit experiment supports the wave nature of light.
questions.answer: In YDSE, light from a single source is split into two coherent waves, which superpose on the screen to produce alternating bright and dark fringes. Bright fringes correspond to constructive interference and dark fringes to destructive interference. Such a stable interference pattern can arise only when light behaves as a wave capable of superposition; corpuscular theory cannot explain the regular pattern of maxima and minima in intensity.

questions.text: State Huygens’ principle. Using it, briefly explain the laws of reflection of light.
questions.answer: Huygens’ principle: Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets that spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave; the new wavefront at a later time is the common tangent (envelope) to these secondary wavelets. For reflection from a plane mirror, incident and reflected wavefronts make equal angles with the reflecting surface, and the construction using secondary wavelets shows that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection and that the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.

questions.text: The phenomenon of bending of light around obstacles is called:
questions.answer: Diffraction

questions.text: Which of the following waves can be polarised?
questions.answer: Light waves

questions.text: Define diffraction of light.
questions.answer: Diffraction is the bending of light waves around obstacles and apertures comparable to their wavelength.

questions.text: What is polarisation of light?
questions.answer: Polarisation is the phenomenon of restricting the vibrations of light waves to a particular plane.

questions.text: State Brewster’s law.
questions.answer: Brewster’s law states that tanθB = μ, where θB is Brewster angle and μ is refractive index of the medium.

questions.text: Why is sky light partially polarised?
questions.answer: Because of scattering of sunlight by air molecules in the atmosphere.

questions.text: Find Brewster angle for glass of refractive index 1.5.
Calculate angular width of central maximum in single slit diffraction.
questions.answer: Angular width = 2λ/a

questions.text: Explain diffraction of light due to a single slit.
questions.answer: Single slit diffraction produces a central bright maximum with alternating dark and weaker bright fringes.

questions.text: Explain polarisation of light and its applications.
questions.answer: Polarisation confirms transverse nature of light and is used in sunglasses, photography and glare reduction.

questions.text: Electric flux through a surface depends on:
options: Charge enclosed and permittivity of medium
Distance of charge from surface only
questions.answer: Area vector and electric field

questions.text: State Gauss’s law in electrostatics.
questions.answer: The net electric flux through any closed surface is equal to 1/ε₀ times the total charge enclosed by the surface: ∬E·dA = Q_enclosed / ε₀.

questions.text: A point charge of 2×10⁻⁸ C is placed at the centre of a spherical Gaussian surface of radius 0.2 m in air. Find the electric flux through the sphere.
Define electric potential at a point. How is it related to the electric field?
questions.answer: Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity to that point, against the electric field. The electric field is the negative gradient of potential: **E = −dV/dr** (in one dimension).

questions.text: The potential difference between two points is 50 V. How much work is done in moving a charge of 2 μC from lower to higher potential?
A parallel-plate capacitor has plate area 0.02 m² and plate separation 1 mm in air. Find its capacitance (ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m).
What is an electric dipole? Define its dipole moment.
questions.answer: An electric dipole consists of two equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance. Dipole moment **p** is defined as the product of magnitude of one charge and the separation vector from negative to positive charge: **p = q·2a** (in magnitude).

questions.text: Three capacitors 2 μF, 3 μF and 6 μF are connected in series across a 12 V battery. Find the equivalent capacitance and the charge on each capacitor.
questions.answer: 1/C_eq = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = (3+2+1)/6 = 1 ⇒ C_eq = 1 μF. Charge Q = C_eq V = 1 μF × 12 V = 12 μC. In series, charge is same on each capacitor: 12 μC on each.

questions.text: How does the introduction of a dielectric slab between the plates of an isolated, charged capacitor affect (i) its capacitance, (ii) its potential difference, and (iii) its stored energy?
questions.answer: (i) Capacitance increases by factor k (dielectric constant). (ii) As charge remains constant, V decreases by factor k. (iii) Energy U = Q²/(2C) decreases by factor k.

questions.text: Using Gauss’s law, derive an expression for electric field intensity due to an infinitely long, uniformly charged straight wire.
questions.answer: Consider a long wire of linear charge density λ. Choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L coaxial with the wire. By symmetry, electric field E is radial and same at all points on curved surface; flux through end caps is zero. Total flux = E(2πrL). Charge enclosed = λL. By Gauss’s law, E(2πrL) = λL/ε₀ ⇒ E = λ/(2π ε₀ r), radially outward.

questions.text: The SI unit of electric charge is:
questions.answer: Coulomb

questions.text: The force between two point charges varies inversely as:
questions.answer: square of distance

questions.text: Define electric field intensity.
questions.answer: Electric field intensity is the force experienced per unit positive charge placed at a point.

questions.text: State Coulomb’s law.
questions.answer: The electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to square of distance between them.

questions.text: Define electric potential.
questions.answer: Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to that point.

questions.text: Why electric field inside a conductor is zero?
questions.answer: Because charges rearrange themselves on the surface so that the net field inside becomes zero.

questions.text: Calculate force between two charges of 5 μC each placed 10 cm apart in air.
Find electric potential at a point due to a charge of 2 μC placed 1 m away.
Derive an expression for electric field intensity due to a point charge.
questions.answer: Using Coulomb’s law, E = kq/r² directed radially outward or inward.

questions.text: Explain electric potential energy of a system of charges.
questions.answer: Electric potential energy is the work done in assembling charges from infinity to their respective positions.

questions.text: Kirchhoff’s current law is based on the principle of:
questions.answer: Conservation of charge

questions.text: State Ohm’s law. Under what conditions is it valid?
questions.answer: At constant physical conditions (temperature, pressure, etc.), the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it (V ∝ I or V = IR). It holds for ohmic conductors within a certain range of temperature and field.

questions.text: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. Find their equivalent resistance.
The potential difference across a 4 Ω resistor is 12 V. Calculate the current through it and the power dissipated.
State Kirchhoff’s voltage law (KVL).
questions.answer: The algebraic sum of all potential differences around any closed loop in an electrical circuit is zero, i.e., ΣΔV = 0.

questions.text: In a meter bridge, the balancing length is 40 cm when the known resistance is 5 Ω. Find the value of the unknown resistance.
questions.answer: Let R be unknown. For balance, R / 5 = 40 / 60 ⇒ R = 5 × (40/60) = 5 × 2/3 = 10/3 ≈ 3.33 Ω.

questions.text: Explain how a potentiometer can be used to compare the emfs of two cells.
questions.answer: Connect the potentiometer wire in series with a driving cell and a rheostat. Connect cell E₁ using a galvanometer and jockey, obtain balancing length l₁ where galvanometer shows zero current. Replace E₁ with E₂ and get balancing length l₂. Since no current flows through the cell at balance, E ∝ balancing length, so E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂.

questions.text: Define resistivity of a material. How is it related to conductivity?
questions.answer: Resistivity ρ of a material is the resistance of a conductor of that material having unit length and unit cross-sectional area. Conductivity σ is the reciprocal of resistivity: σ = 1/ρ.

questions.text: A copper wire 2 m long and of cross-sectional area 1×10⁻⁶ m² has a resistance of 0.034 Ω. Find the resistivity of copper.
Derive the relation between drift velocity of electrons and current in a conductor. Hence obtain the expression for electrical conductivity.
questions.answer: Consider a conductor of length L, area A, containing n free electrons per unit volume, each of charge e and drift velocity v_d. Charge passing per second through area A is q = (number of electrons crossing per second) × e = (nAv_d) e. Thus current I = nAe v_d. Comparing with J = I/A gives J = ne v_d. Using Ohm’s microscopic form J = σE, we get σ = ne²τ/m (using v_d = eEτ/m).

questions.text: The SI unit of electric current is:
questions.answer: Ampere

questions.text: Ohm’s law relates:
questions.answer: Voltage and current

questions.text: Define electric current.
questions.answer: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor.

questions.text: State Ohm’s law.
questions.answer: At constant temperature, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.

questions.text: Define resistance and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of current. Its SI unit is ohm.

questions.text: Why are alloys used for making standard resistances?
questions.answer: Because alloys have high resistivity and low temperature coefficient of resistance.

questions.text: Find the current flowing through a conductor of resistance 10 Ω when potential difference applied is 20 V.
Calculate equivalent resistance of two resistances 4 Ω and 6 Ω connected in series.

questions.answer: Using Ohm’s law and current distribution, 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...

questions.text: The magnetic force on a moving charge is maximum when the angle between velocity and magnetic field is:
State the expression for force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a uniform magnetic field.
questions.answer: For a straight conductor of length **L** carrying current I in a magnetic field **B**, the force is **F = I (L × B)**. Magnitude F = I L B sinθ, where θ is the angle between L and B.

questions.text: An electron moves with a speed of 2×10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.01 T. Find the radius of the circular path. (e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg)
State Biot–Savart law for the magnetic field due to a current element.
questions.answer: It states that the magnetic field d**B** at a point due to a current element I d**l** is directly proportional to current I, length element dl, sine of angle between dl and line joining element to point, and inversely proportional to square of distance r: dB = (μ₀/4π)(I dl sinθ / r²).

questions.text: Find the magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of radius 0.1 m having 50 turns and carrying a current of 2 A.
What is a cyclotron? Name the basic fields used in it.
questions.answer: Cyclotron is a device used to accelerate charged particles to high energies using a combination of a uniform perpendicular magnetic field and a rapidly alternating electric field.

questions.text: Using Ampere’s law, show that the magnetic field inside a very long solenoid is B = μ₀ n I, where n is the number of turns per unit length.
questions.answer: Consider a rectangular Amperian loop partly inside the solenoid. Outside field ≈ 0. Line integral ∮B·dl = B·L (inside segment) + 0 (others) = μ₀ I_enc. Current enclosed I_enc = nL I. Thus B L = μ₀ n L I ⇒ B = μ₀ n I.

questions.text: Why is a radial magnetic field used in a moving-coil galvanometer?
questions.answer: A radial magnetic field keeps the plane of the coil always parallel to the field lines so that torque τ = NIAB sinθ is maximum and independent of θ, making deflection proportional to current.

questions.text: A moving-coil galvanometer has a resistance of 50 Ω and gives full-scale deflection for 2 mA. How can it be converted into a 10 V voltmeter?
questions.answer: For full-scale, current I_g = 2 mA. Required series resistance R_s satisfies V = I_g (R_s + 50). So 10 = 2×10⁻³ (R_s + 50) ⇒ R_s + 50 = 5000 ⇒ R_s = 4950 Ω.

questions.text: Derive an expression for the torque acting on a rectangular current-carrying coil placed in a uniform magnetic field. Define magnetic dipole moment of the coil.
questions.answer: Consider a coil of N turns, area A, carrying current I in a uniform field B. Only the two opposite sides experience equal and opposite forces producing torque. For each side, F = I l B sinθ; torque of pair τ = F·b = I l B sinθ·b = IAB sinθ. For N turns, τ = N I A B sinθ. Magnetic dipole moment is defined as **m = N I A n̂**, so torque is **τ = m × B**.

questions.text: The SI unit of magnetic field is:
questions.answer: Tesla

questions.text: The magnetic field around a current carrying straight conductor is:
questions.answer: Circular

questions.text: State Fleming’s right hand rule.
questions.answer: If the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the right hand are mutually perpendicular, then the forefinger indicates magnetic field, thumb indicates motion of conductor and middle finger indicates induced current.

questions.text: State Biot–Savart law.
questions.answer: The magnetic field due to a small current element is directly proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the square of distance from it.

questions.text: Define magnetic permeability.
questions.answer: Magnetic permeability is the measure of ability of a material to support the formation of magnetic field within it.

questions.text: Why are magnetic field lines continuous closed curves?
questions.answer: Because magnetic monopoles do not exist; field lines neither start nor end but form closed loops.

questions.text: Calculate magnetic field at a distance of 2 cm from a long straight conductor carrying 10 A current.
questions.answer: B = μ₀I / 2πr = 1×10⁻⁴ T

questions.answer: Using Biot–Savart law, B = μ₀I / 2r is obtained at the centre of the coil.

questions.answer: It works on the principle that a current carrying coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a torque.

questions.text: Define magnetization of a material.
questions.answer: Magnetization M is the magnetic moment per unit volume of a material: M = μ_total / V.

questions.text: Which of the following is ferromagnetic at room temperature?
questions.answer: Iron

questions.text: What is magnetic susceptibility? How is it related to relative permeability?
questions.answer: Magnetic susceptibility χ is the ratio of magnetization M to magnetic intensity H: χ = M/H. Relative permeability μ_r is related as μ_r = 1 + χ.

questions.text: Give any two properties of diamagnetic materials.
questions.answer: Any two: (i) Weakly repelled by magnetic fields. (ii) χ is small and negative. (iii) μ_r is slightly less than 1. (iv) Independent of temperature.

questions.text: Why does a ferromagnetic material lose its ferromagnetic property above Curie temperature?
questions.answer: Above Curie temperature, thermal agitation becomes strong enough to randomize the orientation of magnetic domains, destroying spontaneous magnetization; the material behaves as paramagnetic.

questions.text: Distinguish between soft and hard magnetic materials based on their hysteresis loops and typical uses.
questions.answer: Soft materials: narrow hysteresis loop, small coercivity and remanence, low energy loss per cycle; used in transformer and electromagnet cores. Hard materials: wide hysteresis loop, large coercivity and remanence, high energy loss but retain magnetization; used for permanent magnets, recording media.

questions.text: A paramagnetic material has susceptibility 2×10⁻³. Find its relative permeability.
Explain the origin of permanent magnetism in ferromagnetic materials in terms of domains.
questions.answer: Ferromagnetic materials consist of small regions called magnetic domains, in each of which atomic magnetic moments are strongly aligned due to exchange interaction. In an unmagnetized specimen, domains are randomly oriented, resulting in zero net magnetization. When an external field is applied, domains aligned with the field grow at the expense of others, giving large net magnetization that can persist even after the field is removed.

questions.text: Why are transformer cores laminated?
questions.answer: They are laminated to reduce eddy currents and thereby decrease energy loss and heating in the core.

questions.text: Draw a typical hysteresis loop for a ferromagnetic material and explain the terms retentivity and coercivity.
questions.answer: On a B–H graph, the loop shows how B changes as H is cycled. Retentivity (remanence) is the value of B remaining when H is reduced to zero after saturation. Coercivity is the value of reverse H required to bring B to zero from its remanent value. Larger retentivity means a stronger permanent magnet; larger coercivity indicates greater resistance to demagnetization.

learningObjectives: Describe Faraday–Henry experiments and infer the conditions for induction.

questions.text: State Faraday’s first law of electromagnetic induction.
questions.answer: Whenever there is a change of magnetic flux linked with a closed circuit, an emf is induced in the circuit; if the circuit is closed, an induced current flows.

questions.text: State Lenz’s law. How does it express conservation of energy?
questions.answer: Lenz’s law: The direction of induced current is such that the magnetic field produced by it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced the current. This ensures that the induced current opposes the cause, so extra mechanical work is required, conserving energy.

questions.text: The magnetic flux through a coil of 100 turns changes from 0.02 Wb to 0 in 0.1 s. Find the magnitude of induced emf.
A straight conductor of length 0.5 m moves in a uniform magnetic field of 0.8 T with a speed of 3 m/s, such that it cuts the field lines normally. Calculate the induced emf between its ends.
Define self inductance of a coil.
questions.answer: Self inductance L is the property of a coil by virtue of which it opposes any change in current through it by inducing an emf proportional to the rate of change of current: e = −L di/dt.

questions.text: A coil has self inductance 0.5 H. What emf is induced in it when the current changes from 2 A to 5 A in 0.1 s?
What is meant by eddy currents? Give one useful application.
questions.answer: Eddy currents are loops of induced current produced in bulk conductors exposed to changing magnetic flux. They are used in electromagnetic braking, induction furnaces, and damping of moving-coil instruments.

questions.text: An ideal transformer has 1000 turns in the primary and 100 turns in the secondary. The primary is connected to 220 V AC. Calculate (i) the secondary voltage, (ii) the primary current when secondary current is 2 A.
questions.answer: (i) e_s/e_p = N_s/N_p ⇒ e_s = e_p (N_s/N_p) = 220 × 100/1000 = 22 V (step-down). (ii) For ideal transformer, power in = power out ⇒ e_p i_p = e_s i_s ⇒ 220 i_p = 22 × 2 = 44 ⇒ i_p = 0.2 A.

questions.text: Why are the cores of transformers laminated?
questions.answer: To reduce eddy currents induced in the core by the alternating flux. Laminations increase resistance to circulating currents and hence reduce energy loss and heating.

questions.text: Explain the Faraday disc dynamo and obtain the expression for the induced emf between the centre and the rim of a rotating conducting disc in a perpendicular magnetic field.
questions.answer: A conducting disc of radius R rotates with angular speed ω in a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to its plane. A radial element at distance r from centre has linear speed v = ωr, so induced emf across small element dr is dε = B v dr = B ω r dr. Integrating from 0 to R gives ε = ∫₀^R B ω r dr = ½ B ω R². The device demonstrates motional emf where mechanical rotation in a magnetic field produces a steady emf.

questions.text: Electromagnetic induction is the phenomenon of:
options: Production of magnetic field due to current
Production of emf due to change in magnetic flux
Force on a current carrying conductor
questions.answer: Production of emf due to change in magnetic flux

questions.text: The negative sign in Faraday’s law represents:
questions.answer: Lenz’s law

questions.text: Define magnetic flux.
questions.answer: Magnetic flux is the product of magnetic field and area perpendicular to the field.

questions.text: State Faraday’s laws of electromagnetic induction.
questions.answer: Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an emf is induced; its magnitude is proportional to rate of change of flux.

questions.text: State Lenz’s law.
questions.answer: The induced current flows in a direction such that it opposes the cause producing it.

questions.text: Why is eddy current loss undesirable in transformers?
questions.answer: Because it causes energy loss in the form of heat.

questions.text: Calculate induced emf if magnetic flux changes from 5 Wb to 1 Wb in 2 seconds.
questions.answer: emf = ΔΦ/Δt = (5 − 1)/2 = 2 V

questions.text: Find self-inductance if emf of 10 V is induced when current changes at rate 2 A/s.
questions.answer: L = emf / (di/dt) = 10 / 2 = 5 H

questions.text: Derive expression for induced emf using Faraday’s law.
questions.answer: Induced emf e = −dΦ/dt derived from change in magnetic flux linked with circuit.

questions.text: Explain principle, construction and working of a transformer.
questions.answer: Transformer works on mutual induction; alternating current in primary induces emf in secondary coil.

questions.text: For a sinusoidal AC, the relation between RMS value and peak value is:
questions.answer: I_rms = I₀/√2

questions.text: Write expressions for inductive and capacitive reactances.
questions.answer: Inductive reactance: X_L = ωL = 2π f L. Capacitive reactance: X_C = 1/(ωC) = 1/(2π f C).

questions.text: An AC source of emf 220 V, 50 Hz is applied to a pure resistor of 44 Ω. Find the peak current and RMS current through the resistor.
questions.answer: I_rms = V_rms / R = 220 / 44 = 5 A. Peak current I₀ = √2 I_rms ≈ 7.07 A.

questions.text: Find the inductive reactance of a 0.2 H inductor connected to a 50 Hz AC supply.
Define power factor. What is its value for (i) pure resistor and (ii) pure inductor?
questions.answer: Power factor cosφ is the cosine of phase angle between voltage and current. For pure resistor cosφ = 1; for pure inductor cosφ = 0.

questions.text: An LCR series circuit has R = 20 Ω, L = 0.2 H, C = 50 μF. It is connected to a 200 V, 50 Hz AC source. Calculate the impedance and current in the circuit.
What is resonance in an LCR series circuit? Write the condition for resonance.
questions.answer: Resonance is the condition in an LCR series circuit when current amplitude becomes maximum and impedance is minimum. It occurs when X_L = X_C, i.e., ω₀L = 1/(ω₀C) or ω₀ = 1/√(LC).

questions.text: In a series LCR circuit at resonance, R = 50 Ω and applied RMS voltage is 100 V. Find (i) RMS current, (ii) average power absorbed.
questions.answer: (i) At resonance Z = R, so I_rms = V_rms/R = 100/50 = 2 A. (ii) Power P = V_rms I_rms cosφ = 100 × 2 × 1 = 200 W.

questions.text: Why is power factor improvement important in AC power systems? Name one method of improving it.
questions.answer: Low power factor increases current for a given power, causing higher losses and voltage drops. Improving power factor reduces current and losses. It can be improved by connecting shunt capacitors or synchronous condensers to compensate the lagging reactive power.

questions.text: Derive the expression for the average power absorbed in an AC circuit in terms of RMS values and power factor.
questions.answer: For voltage v = V₀ sinωt and current i = I₀ sin(ωt − φ), instantaneous power p = v i = V₀ I₀ sinωt sin(ωt − φ). Using identity, p = (V₀ I₀/2)[cosφ − cos(2ωt − φ)]. Average of cosine term with double frequency over a cycle is zero, leaving P_avg = (V₀ I₀/2) cosφ = V_rms I_rms cosφ.

questions.text: The rms value of alternating current is:
questions.answer: I₀/√2

questions.text: In an AC circuit, impedance plays the role similar to ______ in DC circuits.
questions.answer: Resistance

questions.text: Define inductive reactance.
questions.answer: Inductive reactance is the opposition offered by an inductor to the flow of alternating current.

questions.text: Write expression for capacitive reactance.
questions.answer: Xc = 1 / (2πfC)

questions.text: What is resonance in AC circuits?
questions.answer: Resonance occurs when inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance, resulting in maximum current.

questions.text: Why is power factor important in AC circuits?
questions.answer: It determines the efficiency of power transfer; low power factor leads to energy losses.

questions.text: Calculate inductive reactance of a coil of inductance 0.2 H at frequency 50 Hz.
questions.answer: XL = 2πfL = 62.8 Ω

questions.text: Find capacitive reactance of a capacitor of 10 μF connected to 50 Hz AC supply.
Derive expression for impedance of a series LCR circuit.
questions.answer: Z = √[R² + (XL − XC)²]

questions.text: Explain resonance in series LCR circuit with phasor diagram.
questions.answer: At resonance XL = XC, impedance is minimum and current is maximum; voltage and current are in phase.

chapters.title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
chapters.description: Photoelectric effect and Einstein’s explanation, particle aspects of radiation, de Broglie hypothesis, wave nature of matter and applications like electron microscope. :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}
topics: de Broglie wavelength of matter waves
learningObjectives: Describe key observations of photoelectric effect and their significance.
Use Einstein’s equation to relate stopping potential, frequency and work function.
Explain need for photon concept and dual nature of light.
Calculate de Broglie wavelength for particles and relate to momentum.
Explain qualitatively the working of an electron microscope.

questions.text: In the photoelectric effect, the photocurrent mainly depends on:
questions.answer: Intensity of light only

questions.text: Define work function of a metal.
questions.answer: Work function φ is the minimum energy required to just liberate an electron from the surface of a metal.

questions.text: The threshold frequency for a metal is 6×10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate its work function in eV. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s, 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J)
Write Einstein’s photoelectric equation and explain each term.
questions.answer: hν = φ + ½ m v_max² = φ + eV_s, where hν is photon energy, φ is work function, ½ m v_max² is maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons and V_s is stopping potential.

questions.text: Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal surface with work function 2 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons (in eV).
questions.answer: Photon energy E = hc/λ ≈ (1240 eV·nm)/400 nm = 3.1 eV. So K_max = 3.1 − 2.0 = 1.1 eV.

questions.text: State de Broglie relation for matter waves.
questions.answer: The de Broglie wavelength associated with a particle of momentum p is λ = h/p.

questions.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s, mₑ = 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C)
Why could classical wave theory not explain the existence of a threshold frequency in the photoelectric effect?
questions.answer: Classical theory predicts that energy delivered to electrons depends only on intensity and time, so even low-frequency light should eject electrons if intensity is high or exposure is long. But experimentally no electrons are emitted below a certain frequency regardless of intensity, which contradicts classical predictions.

questions.text: How does Davisson–Germer experiment support the wave nature of electrons?
questions.answer: In the experiment, electrons scattered by a nickel crystal produced intensity maxima at certain angles, similar to X-ray diffraction by crystals. The positions of maxima agreed with Bragg’s law using de Broglie wavelength, confirming that electrons behave as waves.

questions.text: Explain qualitatively how the resolving power of an electron microscope is higher than that of an optical microscope.
questions.answer: Resolving power is inversely proportional to wavelength of radiation used. Optical microscopes use visible light (λ ≈ 400–700 nm). Electrons accelerated to high voltages have de Broglie wavelengths of the order of picometres to Angstroms (10⁻¹²–10⁻¹⁰ m), much smaller than visible wavelengths. Using electromagnetic lenses, electron microscopes form images with much smaller diffraction limits, hence higher resolving power.

questions.text: The phenomenon which supports particle nature of light is:
questions.answer: Photoelectric effect

questions.text: The energy of a photon is given by:
questions.answer: E = hν

questions.text: Define work function.
questions.answer: Work function is the minimum energy required to eject an electron from the surface of a metal.

questions.text: State Einstein’s photoelectric equation.
questions.answer: hν = φ + ½mv²

questions.text: What is threshold frequency?
questions.answer: Threshold frequency is the minimum frequency of incident radiation required to eject electrons from a metal surface.

questions.text: Why does photoelectric current increase with intensity of incident light?
questions.answer: Because higher intensity means more photons striking the surface per second, ejecting more electrons.

questions.text: Calculate energy of a photon of frequency 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz.
Find de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V.
questions.answer: λ = h/√(2meV)

questions.text: Explain the photoelectric effect with necessary graphs.
questions.answer: Photoelectric effect is emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of frequency above threshold is incident.

questions.text: Derive expression for de Broglie wavelength of a particle.
questions.answer: Using momentum p = mv, λ = h/p = h/mv.

chapters.title: Structure of Atoms and Nuclei
chapters.description: Rutherford and Bohr atomic models, energy levels and spectra, nuclear composition and binding energy, radioactivity and nuclear reactions including fission and fusion. :contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}
topics: Energy levels, orbits and spectral lines
Composition of nucleus and nuclear forces
learningObjectives: Compare Rutherford and Bohr atomic models and their limitations.
Use Bohr’s formula to calculate radii and energies of hydrogen-like atoms.
Define mass defect and binding energy and compute BE per nucleon.
Explain radioactive decay law and half-life calculations.
Describe basic principles of nuclear fission, fusion and energy generation.

questions.text: State any two postulates of Bohr’s model of the hydrogen atom.
questions.answer: Any two: (i) Electrons revolve in certain stable orbits without radiating energy. (ii) Angular momentum of electron is quantized: mvr = nħ. (iii) Radiation is emitted or absorbed only when an electron jumps between stationary orbits, with hν = E₂ − E₁.

questions.text: Calculate the radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen. (Take ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m, h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s, mₑ = 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.answer: Using standard result, r₁ = 4π ε₀ ħ² / (mₑ e²) ≈ 0.53 Å = 5.3×10⁻¹¹ m.

questions.text: Define mass defect and binding energy of a nucleus.
questions.answer: Mass defect Δm is the difference between the sum of masses of individual nucleons and the actual mass of the nucleus. Binding energy is the energy required to separate all nucleons of a nucleus completely; BE = Δm c².

questions.text: The mass of ⁴He nucleus is 4.0015 u, while masses of proton and neutron are 1.0073 u and 1.0087 u respectively. Calculate the binding energy per nucleon of ⁴He. (1 u = 931 MeV)
State the radioactive decay law.
questions.answer: The rate of decay of radioactive nuclei at any instant is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present: dN/dt = −λN, leading to N = N₀ e⁻ˡᵃᵐᵇᵈᵃᵗ.

questions.text: A radioactive substance has a half-life of 10 years. What fraction of the original activity will remain after 30 years?
questions.answer: After n half-lives, remaining fraction = (1/2)ⁿ; here n = 30/10 = 3, so fraction = (1/2)³ = 1/8.

questions.text: What is nuclear fission? Name one fissionable isotope commonly used in reactors.
questions.answer: Nuclear fission is the process in which a heavy nucleus splits into two (or more) lighter nuclei with the release of large energy and neutrons. Example of a fissionable isotope: ²³⁵U or ²³⁹Pu.

questions.text: Mention any two differences between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
questions.answer: Fission: heavy nucleus splits; can be controlled in reactors; requires slow neutrons. Fusion: light nuclei combine; occurs at very high temperature and pressure; difficult to control but releases more energy per nucleon.

questions.text: What is meant by chain reaction in a nuclear reactor? How is it controlled?
questions.answer: A chain reaction is a self-sustaining sequence of fission reactions where neutrons from one fission cause further fissions. It is controlled by using control rods (e.g., cadmium, boron) that absorb excess neutrons, keeping the reaction rate steady.

questions.text: Explain Rutherford’s α-scattering experiment and how it led to the nuclear model of the atom.
questions.answer: Rutherford bombarded thin gold foil with α-particles and observed that most passed through undeflected, some were deflected at small angles, and a few at large angles (>90°). This could not be explained by Thomson’s plum-pudding model. Rutherford concluded that most of the atom is empty space, positive charge and most mass are concentrated in a small, dense nucleus, and electrons revolve around it. This led to the planetary (nuclear) model of the atom.

questions.text: The atomic model that explains hydrogen spectrum is:
questions.answer: Bohr model

questions.text: The SI unit of binding energy is:
questions.answer: Both J and eV

questions.text: Define mass defect.
questions.answer: Mass defect is the difference between the sum of masses of constituent nucleons and the actual mass of the nucleus.

questions.text: State Bohr’s postulates.
questions.answer: Electrons revolve in fixed orbits without radiating energy and angular momentum is quantized.

questions.text: Define binding energy of a nucleus.
questions.answer: Binding energy is the energy required to separate a nucleus into its constituent nucleons.

questions.text: Why are heavier nuclei unstable?
questions.answer: Due to large repulsive Coulomb forces between protons overpowering nuclear force.

questions.text: Calculate energy of electron in first orbit of hydrogen atom.
questions.answer: E₁ = −13.6 eV

questions.text: Find binding energy if mass defect of nucleus is 0.02 u.
questions.answer: Binding energy = 0.02 × 931 MeV = 18.62 MeV

questions.text: Derive expression for radius of Bohr orbit.
questions.answer: Using Coulomb force and quantization, rₙ = n²a₀ is obtained.

questions.text: Explain nuclear fission and fusion with energy considerations.
questions.answer: Fission splits heavy nuclei while fusion combines light nuclei, both releasing energy due to mass defect.

learningObjectives: Differentiate between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors.
Explain forward and reverse biasing of a p–n junction and interpret its I–V characteristics.
Describe Zener breakdown and use of Zener diode as voltage regulator.
Explain operation of half-wave and full-wave rectifier circuits and role of filters.
Describe construction and working of LEDs, photodiodes, solar cells and BJTs.

questions.text: In an n-type semiconductor, the majority carriers are:
questions.answer: Electrons

questions.text: What is meant by forward biasing of a p–n junction diode?
questions.answer: When the p-side of the diode is connected to the positive terminal of a battery and the n-side to the negative terminal so that the potential barrier is reduced and current flows easily, the diode is said to be forward biased.

questions.text: Define breakdown voltage of a Zener diode.
questions.answer: Breakdown voltage is the reverse bias voltage at which the Zener diode conducts a large current with only a small further increase in voltage, entering the breakdown region without damage.

questions.text: A half-wave rectifier uses a diode with forward resistance 100 Ω connected to a load of 900 Ω. If the peak secondary voltage is 20 V, find approximate peak load current.
questions.answer: Total forward resistance ≈ 100 + 900 = 1000 Ω. Peak current I₀ ≈ V₀ / R_total = 20 / 1000 = 0.02 A = 20 mA.

questions.text: Mention any two advantages of LEDs over conventional lamps.
questions.answer: Any two: high efficiency and low power consumption; long life; small size and robust; no warm-up time; environmentally friendly (no mercury).

questions.text: Name the three regions of a bipolar junction transistor and state their relative doping levels.
questions.answer: Emitter (heavily doped), base (thin and lightly doped), collector (moderately doped, area larger than emitter).

questions.text: Write the approximate relation between emitter current, base current and collector current in a transistor.
questions.answer: I_E = I_B + I_C and usually I_C ≈ I_E (since I_B is very small).

questions.text: In a common-emitter transistor amplifier, the input current changes from 100 μA to 140 μA and the corresponding output current changes from 5 mA to 7 mA. Find the current gain β.
Explain how a Zener diode can be used as a voltage regulator.
questions.answer: Zener diode is reverse-biased and operated in breakdown region where its voltage remains nearly constant over a wide range of current. By connecting it in parallel with the load and using a series resistor to limit current, the output voltage across the Zener (and load) is held approximately constant despite variations in input voltage or load current.

questions.text: Describe the working of a full-wave bridge rectifier. Draw the circuit diagram and explain the conduction during both half-cycles of AC.
questions.answer: Bridge rectifier uses four diodes in a bridge. During positive half-cycle of AC, two opposite diodes conduct, say D₁ and D₃, connecting the load in one direction; during negative half-cycle, the other pair D₂ and D₄ conducts, again making current through load flow in the same direction. Thus both halves of the AC input are used, giving pulsating DC at the output with frequency twice the input frequency.

questions.text: Which of the following is a semiconductor?
questions.answer: Germanium

questions.text: In an n-type semiconductor, the majority charge carriers are:
questions.answer: Electrons

questions.text: Define intrinsic semiconductor.
questions.answer: An intrinsic semiconductor is a pure semiconductor with equal number of electrons and holes.

questions.text: What is a p–n junction diode?
questions.answer: A p–n junction diode is a semiconductor device formed by joining p-type and n-type semiconductors.

questions.text: Explain forward biasing of a p–n junction diode.
questions.answer: In forward biasing, p-side is connected to positive terminal and n-side to negative terminal, reducing barrier potential.

questions.text: Why is a semiconductor diode used as a rectifier?
questions.answer: Because it allows current to flow in one direction and blocks it in the opposite direction.

questions.text: Find the barrier potential of a silicon diode.
questions.answer: Barrier potential of silicon diode is approximately 0.7 V.

questions.text: Calculate output voltage of a half-wave rectifier for given input.
questions.answer: Output voltage depends on peak input voltage and diode drop; Vout ≈ Vmax − 0.7 V.

questions.text: Explain the construction and working of a p–n junction diode with neat diagram.
questions.answer: A p–n junction diode is formed by joining p-type and n-type semiconductors; it conducts in forward bias and blocks in reverse bias.

questions.text: Explain working of a transistor as an amplifier.
questions.answer: In amplifier mode, a small input signal at base produces large output at collector due to current gain of transistor.
